vocabulary.definition: The quality of evoking a strong emotional response or connection. It often relates to how well an idea or message aligns with the audience's values or experiences.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and branding, resonance is crucial for creating campaigns that effectively connect with target audiences, enhancing brand loyalty and engagement.

insight.nuance: Resonance implies a deeper connection than mere agreement; it suggests that the message strikes a chord with the audience's beliefs or feelings.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: You want to diagnose with data and treat with design. So data is not a tool that's going to tell you what you should build. I don't actually think a lot of the fast growing companies are using data well at this point.
keySentence: Diagnose with data and treat with design; instincts won't sustain growth.
text_ko: 데이터(data)로 진단하고 디자인(design)으로 해결하세요. 그러니까 데이터는 뭘 만들어야 할지 알려주는 도구는 아니에요. 솔직히 지금 많은 빠르게 성장하는 회사들이 데이터를 제대로 활용하고 있다고 보진 않아요.
text_zh: 要用数据(data)来诊断问题，再用设计(design)来解决。不要把数据(data)当成会直接告诉你该做什么的工具。说实话，我觉得现在很多快速成长的公司，其实还没把数据(data)用好。
text_es: La idea es diagnosticar con datos (data) y tratar con diseño (design). Pero los datos no son una herramienta que te diga qué deberías construir. De hecho, no creo que muchas de las empresas de rápido crecimiento estén usando bien los datos a estas alturas.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie about her transition from being head of design at Facebook to now running a data analytics startup. Julie explains her philosophy on the relationship between data and design, arguing that many fast-growing AI companies today haven't had time to build proper data infrastructure because they've scaled so quickly. She believes data should inform what problems to solve, but design creativity is still needed to determine the solutions.

vocabulary.definition: To identify the nature or cause of a problem or condition through analysis.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, diagnosing often refers to analyzing data or performance metrics to understand underlying issues affecting a product or service.

insight.nuance: While commonly used in medical contexts, in business it implies a systematic approach to problem-solving rather than a casual observation.

vocabulary.definition: To take action to improve or resolve a problem or condition.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, treating a problem might involve implementing solutions or strategies based on the diagnosis to enhance performance or user experience.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a proactive approach to problem-solving, often implying a level of care or consideration in the actions taken.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by rapid expansion or increase in size, revenue, or market share over a short period.
vocabulary.businessContext: Fast-growing companies are often startups that quickly scale their operations and customer base, typically attracting significant investment and attention in the market.

insight.nuance: While it conveys positive momentum, it can also imply challenges related to sustainability and management of growth.

vocabulary.definition: The effective and strategic application of data to inform decision-making and drive business outcomes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, using data well means leveraging analytics to gain insights that guide product development, marketing strategies, and operational improvements.

insight.nuance: This phrase emphasizes not just the collection of data, but its thoughtful analysis and application, distinguishing between mere data usage and data-driven decision-making.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: I really believe that it's never a bad thing, it's always a better thing to have more feedback.
keySentence: it's always a better thing to have more feedback.
text_ko: 피드백은 많을수록 나쁜 건 전혀 없고, 항상 더 나아진다고 정말 믿어요.
text_zh: 我真心觉得，多点反馈永远没坏处，反而更有用。
text_es: De verdad creo que la retroalimentación (feedback) nunca está de más; cuanta más haya, mejor.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie about how companies should structure product review meetings and design critiques. Julie explains her philosophy on gathering feedback during product development. She emphasizes that feedback collection should be an ongoing process rather than a single decisive meeting, and that getting diverse perspectives from different groups (designers, team members, external users, target customers) will all provide valuable but potentially contradictory insights.

vocabulary.definition: Feedback refers to information or criticism about a person's performance or a product's effectiveness, intended to guide future improvements.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, feedback is crucial for refining products, enhancing customer satisfaction, and driving employee performance.

insight.nuance: While feedback is generally positive and constructive, it can sometimes be perceived as negative if not delivered thoughtfully.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: Management is still really critical. You have a north star, you have a vision, and you're just trying to figure out how to use the resources that you have to get that thing done.
keySentence: Management is still really critical.
text_ko: 그래도 매니지먼트(management)는 여전히 정말 중요해요. 북극성(north star) 같은 방향과 비전(vision)이 있고, 그걸 해내기 위해 가진 자원(resources)을 어떻게 써야 할지 알아가는 과정이에요.
text_zh: 管理还是很关键。你得有个北极星（north star）、有个愿景（vision），然后琢磨着怎么用手头的资源把它落地。
text_es: La gestión sigue siendo clave. Tienes una estrella polar (north star), una visión, y estás intentando averiguar cómo aprovechar los recursos que tienes para sacarlo adelante.
fullContext: Lenny mentions how organizations are flattening and many middle managers are being let go, questioning whether we still need managers. Julie explains that while the nature of management is changing with AI, the core principles remain the same - having a vision and coordinating resources to achieve it. The key difference is that instead of managing only people, managers now need to orchestrate both people and AI models with different capabilities.

vocabulary.definition: Essential or of great importance; crucial for success or failure.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, being critical often refers to the need for decisive management and strategic decision-making that can significantly impact a company's trajectory.

insight.nuance: While 'critical' can imply urgency, it can also suggest a level of scrutiny that may not always be constructive.

vocabulary.definition: A guiding principle or goal that provides direction and focus for an organization or project.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, a 'north star' often refers to a long-term vision or objective that aligns team efforts and strategies towards achieving a common aim.

insight.nuance: The term conveys a sense of unwavering guidance, suggesting that while tactics may change, the overarching goal remains constant.

vocabulary.definition: Assets or materials that can be utilized to achieve objectives, including financial, human, and technological assets.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and businesses, managing resources effectively is crucial for maximizing productivity and ensuring sustainable growth.

insight.nuance: The term can imply both tangible and intangible assets, and it is often used in discussions about optimization and allocation.

vocabulary.definition: A clear and compelling long-term goal or aspiration that an organization aims to achieve.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a strong vision is essential for inspiring teams, guiding strategic planning, and communicating purpose to stakeholders.

insight.nuance: While 'vision' suggests a positive and forward-thinking outlook, it can also imply a level of idealism that may not always align with practical realities.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: The number one advice that I always have for people when talking about product sensor or product thinking is it's just really about observation and it's about curiosity and can start by first observing yourself.
keySentence: it's just really about observation and it's about curiosity
text_ko: 프로덕트 센서(product sensor)나 프로덕트 씽킹(product thinking)에 대해 얘기할 때 제가 항상 하는 가장 중요한 조언은 결국 관찰하고 호기심을 갖는 거예요. 그리고 그 시작은 자기 자신을 먼저 관찰하는 것에서부터 할 수 있어요.
text_zh: 每次跟别人聊产品嗅觉(product sensor)或产品思维(product thinking)时，我最常给的首要建议就是：多观察、多保持好奇，先从观察自己开始。
text_es: Mi consejo número uno cuando hablo de sentido de producto (product sensor) o mentalidad de producto (product thinking) es que, en realidad, todo se reduce a observar y a tener curiosidad; puedes empezar simplemente observándote a ti mismo.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie for advice on how people can develop better product sense and product thinking skills. Julie explains that developing product intuition starts with careful self-observation - paying attention to your own user experience when trying new products or services. This involves reflecting on emotions, assumptions, and behaviors at each step of the user journey, from what motivated you to try something to where you got confused or excited during the experience.

vocabulary.definition: The act of carefully watching or monitoring something to gain information or insights.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, observation is crucial for understanding user behavior, market trends, and product performance, enabling data-driven decision-making.

insight.nuance: While observation implies a passive act of watching, it can also suggest an active engagement in analyzing the observed phenomena.

vocabulary.definition: A strong desire to learn or know more about something, often leading to exploration and inquiry.
vocabulary.businessContext: Curiosity drives innovation and problem-solving in startups, as it encourages teams to ask questions and seek new solutions to challenges.

insight.nuance: Curiosity can have a positive connotation of openness and eagerness to learn, but it may also imply a lack of focus if not directed appropriately.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: It's always been manager's job to manage change. I just think the rate of change is accelerating. Today management is really about this idea of be sturdy while being flexible. So I think about this metaphor a lot of the willow tree.
keySentence: Management is about being sturdy while being flexible amid the accelerating rate of change.
text_ko: 예전부터 관리자(manager)의 역할은 변화를 관리하는 것이었어요. 다만 변화의 속도(rate of change)가 점점 빨라지고 있다고 생각해요. 요즘의 매니지먼트(management)는 단단하면서도 유연함을 유지하는 게 핵심이라고 봐요. 그래서 저는 버드나무(willow tree)라는 비유를 자주 떠올려요.
text_zh: 做管理的，一直就是要应对变化。我只是觉得变化的速度在加快。现在的管理，关键是既要稳健又要灵活。我经常用柳树这个比喻——要像柳树一样顶得住风，又能随风摆动。
text_es: Siempre ha sido trabajo de los gerentes gestionar el cambio. Creo que el ritmo de los cambios se está acelerando. Hoy la gestión consiste en mantenerse firme sin perder flexibilidad. Por eso recurro mucho a la metáfora del sauce.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie what she feels is the biggest change in the role and daily work of managers with the rise of AI. Julie explains that while managing change has always been part of a manager's job, the pace of change is now much faster, creating more uncertainty and fear among employees. She uses the metaphor of a willow tree to describe the balance managers need - being strong enough to weather storms while remaining flexible enough to adapt.

vocabulary.definition: To oversee and facilitate the process of transformation within an organization, ensuring that adjustments are implemented effectively and efficiently.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, managing change is crucial during periods of organizational restructuring, technological upgrades, or shifts in market strategy, requiring leaders to guide employees through transitions.

insight.nuance: This phrase implies a proactive approach to change, emphasizing the importance of leadership and communication in navigating challenges.

vocabulary.definition: Increasing in speed or rate; happening more quickly than before.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business, accelerating often refers to the rapid pace of market changes, technological advancements, or the growth of startups that require swift adaptation and response.

insight.nuance: While it generally has a positive connotation of progress, it can also imply pressure and urgency, which may lead to stress if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: Capable of bending easily without breaking; adaptable to new conditions or changes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, flexibility refers to an organization's ability to adjust its strategies, operations, or workforce in response to changing market demands or internal challenges.

insight.nuance: Flexibility is often viewed positively, as it suggests resilience and adaptability, but excessive flexibility can lead to a lack of direction or consistency.

vocabulary.definition: A figure of speech that implies a comparison between two unrelated things, suggesting that one thing embodies the qualities of another.
vocabulary.businessContext: Metaphors are frequently used in business communication to illustrate complex ideas, inspire teams, or convey messages in a relatable manner, enhancing understanding and engagement.

insight.nuance: While metaphors can enrich communication, they should be used judiciously to avoid confusion or misinterpretation, especially in formal contexts.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: Being in an uncomfortable situation, being in a position where you feel like, Hey, do I really know how to do this? I've not prepared for it is kind of coin sides with the fastest and most intense periods of growth in one's career.
keySentence: Uncomfortable situations coin sides with intense growth periods.
text_ko: 불편한 상황에 놓여 있거나 ‘정말 이걸 잘할 수 있을까? 준비가 안 됐는데…’라고 느낄 때가 경력에서 가장 빠르고 강하게 성장하는 시기와 맞닿아 있어요.
text_zh: 处在让人不舒服、怀疑自己能不能胜任、感觉没准备好的时候，往往恰恰就是职业生涯里成长最快、最剧烈的阶段。
text_es: Estar en una situación incómoda, en la que te preguntas «¿de verdad sé hacerlo? ¿No estoy preparado?», suele ir de la mano con los periodos de crecimiento profesional más rápidos e intensos.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie about her rapid career progression from designer to VP of Design at Facebook, and how others can achieve similar success. Julie explains that she experienced imposter syndrome for 7-8 years, constantly feeling unprepared for her roles. However, she came to realize that feeling uncomfortable and unprepared is actually the flip side of experiencing rapid professional growth - when you're constantly challenged by new situations, you're forced to learn and develop quickly.

vocabulary.definition: A scenario that causes feelings of unease or anxiety, often due to unfamiliarity or high stakes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an uncomfortable situation may arise during high-pressure meetings, negotiations, or when facing unexpected challenges that test one's skills and adaptability.

insight.nuance: This phrase often implies a need for personal growth or resilience, and is typically used in contexts where overcoming discomfort leads to positive outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: Times characterized by heightened activity, pressure, or focus, often leading to significant outcomes or changes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate world, intense periods can occur during product launches, fiscal year-end closing, or when meeting critical deadlines, requiring teams to work at a heightened pace.

insight.nuance: This term suggests a temporary state that can lead to both stress and substantial growth, and is often used to describe phases of rapid development or transformation.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: We need to dissolve the boundaries of these traditional roles and call ourselves builders. I'd love for us to get to the world where that's the title.
keySentence: Dissolve the boundaries of traditional roles; we are all builders now.
text_ko: 우리는 전통적인 역할의 경계를 허물고 스스로를 '빌더(builder)'라고 불러야 해요. 그런 호칭이 당연한 세상이 오면 좋겠어요.
text_zh: 我们要打破这些传统角色的界限，直接把自己称作建设者(builders)。我很希望有一天这能成为我们的正式头衔。
text_es: Tenemos que romper las barreras entre estos roles tradicionales y llamarnos constructores (builders). Me encantaría que llegáramos a un punto en el que ese fuera nuestro título.
fullContext: Lenny discusses the trend of organizational flattening where everyone is becoming an individual contributor again. Julie argues that AI is empowering individuals to take on multiple roles that previously required different specialists. Instead of having traditional job titles like engineer, designer, or product manager, she believes we should all consider ourselves 'builders' who can use AI tools to perform various functions previously requiring separate team members.

vocabulary.definition: To formally end or eliminate something, often a structure or organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'dissolve' can refer to the process of disbanding a team, project, or even a company to allow for new structures or approaches.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a connotation of transformation or change rather than mere termination.

vocabulary.definition: Limits or borders that define the scope of authority, responsibility, or interaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate environment, boundaries can refer to the delineation of roles, departments, or even inter-company collaborations that define how teams interact.

insight.nuance: While boundaries can provide clarity, they may also imply rigidity, which can hinder collaboration and innovation.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: The most important feedback I would say is focus on identifying the problem and making it really clear for the other person, the person you're giving feedback to, what is the problem. There's a lot of assumptions that are already in place.
keySentence: Focus on identifying the problem and making it clear.
text_ko: 제가 보기엔 가장 중요한 피드백(feedback)은 문제를 정확히 파악하고, 피드백을 받는 사람에게 그 문제가 무엇인지 아주 분명하게 전달하는 데 집중하는 거예요. 이미 많은 가정이 깔려 있는 경우가 많거든요.
text_zh: 我觉得最重要的是，在给反馈(feedback)时先把问题弄清楚，然后把问题讲得很明白，让对方（也就是接受反馈的人）知道到底出在哪儿。很多时候大家带着太多默认的假设。
text_es: Lo más importante, diría, es que te centres en identificar el problema y dejarle muy claro a la persona que recibe la retroalimentación (feedback) en qué consiste. Hay demasiadas suposiciones que se dan por hechas.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie for advice on how colleagues (PMs, engineers, data scientists) should give feedback to designers during critiques. Julie emphasizes that people should focus on clearly articulating the underlying problem rather than jumping straight to solutions. She explains that when people say things like 'make the logo purple' or 'add this feature,' they're making assumptions about solutions without first establishing what specific problem needs to be solved.

vocabulary.definition: Beliefs or statements taken for granted without proof or evidence.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, assumptions can influence decision-making and strategy development, often requiring validation to ensure they are accurate and relevant.

insight.nuance: Assumptions can carry a negative connotation when they lead to misjudgments or oversights, so it's important to challenge them regularly.

vocabulary.definition: Information or criticism about a person's performance or a product's effectiveness, intended to guide improvement.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, feedback is essential for personal development and organizational growth, enabling teams to refine processes and enhance productivity.

insight.nuance: Feedback can be constructive or negative, and the manner in which it is delivered can significantly impact its reception and effectiveness.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: If you ask a company to do this, we'll know that this is challenging for humans.
keySentence: this is challenging for humans.
text_ko: 회사에 이걸 해 달라고 부탁하면 사람들이 하기엔 쉽지 않다는 걸 알게 돼요.
text_zh: 要是你让公司去做这件事，我们就会知道这对人来说挺有挑战性的。
text_es: Si le pides a una empresa que haga esto, nos daremos cuenta de que supone un reto para las personas.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie about which management skills are most valuable when working with AI agents and tools. Julie explains that defining clear goals and success criteria is crucial - the same skill needed for managing people. She points out that even in human organizations, alignment is difficult because people often have different interpretations of what success means, making this skill even more critical when working with AI systems that need precise instructions.

vocabulary.definition: Difficult in a way that tests one's abilities or resources; demanding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business environment, 'challenging' is frequently used to describe tasks, projects, or market conditions that require significant effort and innovation to overcome.

insight.nuance: The term carries a connotation of potential growth and opportunity, making it suitable for motivating teams, but should be used carefully to avoid discouragement.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: you have a lot of really great ideas...but whenever there's a large room...you're just sort of quiet and you're not really telling your perspective.
keySentence: You're not telling your perspective in larger forums.
text_ko: 정말 좋은 아이디어가 많은데, 사람 많은 자리나 큰 회의에서는 좀 조용해져서 본인의 관점을 잘 말하지 않아요.
text_zh: 你有很多很棒的想法，但每次一到人多的会议里你就比较沉默，不怎么把自己的观点说出来。
text_es: Tienes muchas ideas muy buenas, pero en reuniones grandes te quedas callado y no compartes tu punto de vista.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie about what got her started with writing and what impact it has had on her career. Julie explains that her writing journey began as a response to performance feedback about her reluctance to speak up in large meetings. Her manager pointed out that while she was engaged in small group discussions, she became quiet in larger forums with 7-15 people, and suggested she work on contributing her perspective in those settings.

vocabulary.definition: A particular attitude or way of considering something; a viewpoint. It often reflects an individual's unique experiences and beliefs.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, sharing one's perspective can lead to innovative solutions and collaborative decision-making, especially in team settings.

insight.nuance: While 'perspective' is generally positive, it can imply subjectivity, so it is important to support one's viewpoint with data or rationale.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: I think the real promise and magic of AI that we're seeing in the workplace is that it leads us to each individual is far more empowered.
keySentence: The real promise and magic of AI empowers individuals to perform multiple jobs.
text_ko: 제가 보기엔, 직장에서 인공지능(AI)이 보여주는 진짜 약속과 마법은 결국 각 개인이 훨씬 더 권한을 갖고 역량을 발휘할 수 있게 된다는 점인 것 같아요.
text_zh: 我觉得人工智能（AI）在职场上的真正价值和魔力，就是让每个人都更有能力、更有影响力。
text_es: Creo que la verdadera promesa y la magia de la IA (AI) en el entorno laboral es que empodera mucho más a cada persona.
fullContext: Lenny asks about the trend of organizational flattening and whether we even need managers in the future. Julie explains that AI is fundamentally changing how work gets done by empowering individuals to perform tasks that previously required specialists. While someone might not reach the top 1% skill level in every area, AI can help them achieve competency levels that were previously impossible, reducing the need for large specialized teams.

vocabulary.definition: Having the authority or power to make decisions and take action independently.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being empowered often refers to employees who are given the autonomy to innovate and contribute to decision-making processes, enhancing productivity and job satisfaction.

insight.nuance: While 'empowered' conveys a sense of strength and capability, it is important to ensure that empowerment is accompanied by adequate support and resources.

vocabulary.definition: A declaration or assurance that something will happen or be done; potential for future success or benefits.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'promise' often refers to the anticipated benefits or capabilities of a product, service, or innovation, particularly in terms of its impact on efficiency and productivity.

insight.nuance: While 'promise' conveys optimism and potential, it should be used cautiously to avoid overhyping capabilities that may not yet be realized.

speaker: Julie Zhuo
text: Write because you're trying to work on a particular key skill... make it a goal, but make it an action goal.
keySentence: make it a goal, but make it an action goal.
text_ko: 특정 핵심 역량(key skill)을 키우려고 글을 쓰세요. 그것을 목표로 삼되, 단순한 목표가 아니라 실제로 실행할 수 있는 행동 목표(action goal)로 만드세요.
text_zh: 写的时候要有针对性——为练某项关键技能而写。把它当成一个目标，但要设成具体可执行的行动目标 (action goal)。
text_es: Escribe porque quieres mejorar una habilidad clave en concreto; ponte una meta, pero que implique acciones concretas.
fullContext: Lenny asks Julie if she would recommend writing as a tool for others who want to work on specific skills like clarity of communication. Julie responds with advice for people who want to start writing but find it difficult. She emphasizes that writing should be driven by personal development goals rather than external validation like likes or views, since you can't control audience response but you can control your own actions and skill development.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to a specific item or detail rather than a general one.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, 'particular' is often used to highlight specific requirements, features, or aspects of a project or product that need attention.

insight.nuance: While 'particular' emphasizes specificity, it can sometimes imply a level of exclusivity or importance that may not be present in broader discussions.

vocabulary.definition: A desired result or outcome that a person or organization aims to achieve within a specified timeframe.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, setting goals is crucial for strategic planning, performance measurement, and motivating teams to achieve desired outcomes.

insight.nuance: The term 'goal' often carries a sense of ambition and purpose, and is typically associated with measurable objectives, unlike more vague aspirations.

vocabulary.definition: A specific type of goal that emphasizes the steps or actions required to achieve a desired outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, action goals are often used in project management to ensure that team members focus on concrete tasks that lead to achieving broader objectives.

insight.nuance: Action goals are typically more dynamic and process-oriented than traditional goals, highlighting the importance of taking measurable steps rather than just envisioning an end result.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: Model training is more an art than a science. And in a lot of ways we, as model trainers, think a lot about data quality.
keySentence: Model training is more an art than a science, focusing on data quality.
text_ko: 모델 학습(model training)은 과학이라기보다 예술에 더 가깝다고 생각해요. 그리고 여러 면에서 저희 모델 트레이너(model trainers)들은 데이터 품질(data quality)을 많이 신경 써요.
text_zh: 模型训练 (model training) 更像是一门艺术，而不是一门科学。作为模型训练者 (model trainers)，我们很多时候都把注意力放在数据质量上。
text_es: El entrenamiento de modelos (model training) es más un arte que una ciencia. Y, en muchos sentidos, nosotros, como entrenadores de modelos (model trainers), prestamos mucha atención a la calidad de los datos.
fullContext: Lenny asks Karina what people most misunderstand about how AI models are created. Karina explains that model training involves a careful balance of teaching models contradictory information - like telling them they don't have physical bodies while also teaching them to perform functions like setting alarms. She emphasizes that the process requires constant debugging and balancing between making models helpful versus preventing harmful behavior.

vocabulary.definition: Data quality refers to the accuracy, completeness, reliability, and relevance of data used in analysis and decision-making processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, high data quality is essential for effective analytics, ensuring that insights derived from data are valid and actionable.

insight.nuance: While 'data quality' often implies a focus on technical aspects, it also encompasses the importance of context and usability in decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: Model training is the process of teaching a machine learning model to make predictions or decisions based on input data by adjusting its parameters through algorithms.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech startups and businesses, model training is crucial for developing predictive analytics tools, enhancing customer experiences, and automating decision-making processes.

insight.nuance: The term 'model training' suggests a blend of technical skill and creative intuition, highlighting that success often relies on both data and the trainer's expertise.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: When you taught the model, some of the self-knowledge of you actually don't have a physical body to operate in the physical world, the model would get extremely confused.
keySentence: The model would get extremely confused without self-knowledge of a physical body.
text_ko: 모델(model)을 가르칠 때, '나는 실제로 물리적 세계에서 활동할 물리적 몸이 없다'는 식의 자기 인식(self-knowledge)을 포함하면 그 모델이 엄청 혼란스러워해요.
text_zh: 在你训练模型(model)的时候，如果把你那部分“没有实体、无法在现实世界行动”的自我认知(self-knowledge)也教给它，它就会非常困惑。
text_es: Cuando entrenabas al modelo, algunas nociones de su autoconocimiento (self-knowledge) —como la de no tener un cuerpo físico para operar en el mundo real— lo confundían muchísimo.
fullContext: Lenny asks what people misunderstand about model creation. Karina shares a specific example from training Claude 3 where they discovered conflicts in the training data. The model was taught it has no physical body, but also learned function calls for tasks like setting alarms, creating confusion about what it could actually do. This illustrates the complex debugging process required in model training.

vocabulary.definition: Self-knowledge refers to an individual's awareness and understanding of their own character, feelings, motives, and desires.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, self-knowledge is crucial for leaders and employees to understand their strengths and weaknesses, which can enhance decision-making and team dynamics.

insight.nuance: While self-knowledge is often seen as a positive trait, excessive self-awareness can lead to overthinking or self-doubt in professional settings.

vocabulary.definition: Confused describes a state of being unable to think clearly or understand something due to a lack of clarity or information.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, confusion can arise during complex project discussions or when instructions are not communicated effectively, potentially leading to errors or inefficiencies.

insight.nuance: While confusion can indicate a lack of understanding, it can also signal the need for further clarification or training in a professional environment.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: I think there are two questions here. We can unpack one at a time. But people say we are hitting the data wall.
keySentence: We can unpack one at a time; people say we are hitting the data wall.
text_ko: 여기서 질문이 두 개 있는 것 같아요. 하나씩 차근차근 풀어볼게요. 그런데 사람들은 우리가 데이터 장벽(data wall)에 부딪히고 있다고 말해요.
text_zh: 我觉得这儿有两个问题，我们可以一个个拆开来说。不过大家都说我们正碰到数据瓶颈（data wall）。
text_es: Creo que aquí hay dos preguntas. Podemos ir abordándolas una por una. Pero la gente dice que nos estamos topando con el muro de datos (data wall).
fullContext: Lenny asks about the concern that AI models will stop getting smarter because they're running out of training data. Karina addresses the misconception about the 'data wall' - the idea that models can't improve further because they've already been trained on all available internet data. She argues this view is too narrow and focuses only on pre-training phases.

vocabulary.definition: To analyze or break down a complex idea or issue into its constituent parts for better understanding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'unpacking' is often used to clarify multifaceted problems or strategies, allowing teams to address each component systematically.

insight.nuance: While 'unpack' can imply a thorough examination, it is often used informally; in more formal contexts, alternatives like 'analyze' may be preferred.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: But I think what's happening right now with new paradigm of o1 series is that the scaling in post-training itself is not hitting the wall.
keySentence: The new paradigm shows scaling in post-training is not hitting the wall.
text_ko: 제 생각엔 지금 o1 시리즈(o1 series)의 새로운 패러다임에서 벌어지고 있는 건, 사후 학습(post-training)에서의 스케일링(scaling) 자체가 아직 한계에 부딪히지 않았다는 점이에요.
text_zh: 我觉得就o1系列（o1 series）的新模式来说，后训练（post-training）本身的扩展还没碰到瓶颈。
text_es: Pero creo que ahora mismo, con el nuevo paradigma de la serie o1, el escalado (scaling) en el post-entrenamiento (post-training) no está tocando techo.
fullContext: Lenny asks about synthetic data and whether models will continue getting smarter despite data limitations. Karina explains why she believes the 'data wall' concern is misguided. The o1 series represents a new paradigm where models can be taught infinite tasks during post-training through reinforcement learning, rather than being limited by finite internet data during pre-training.

vocabulary.definition: A paradigm is a typical example or pattern of something; a model that represents a framework for understanding a particular concept or phenomenon.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, a paradigm shift refers to a fundamental change in approach or underlying assumptions, often leading to new methods or innovations.

insight.nuance: While 'paradigm' often implies a significant change, it can also refer to established norms that may not be questioned.

vocabulary.definition: Scaling refers to the process of increasing the capacity or size of a business, system, or technology to accommodate growth or demand.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, scaling is crucial as it involves expanding operations, increasing production, or enhancing service delivery to meet market needs without compromising quality.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a positive connotation of growth and success, but it can also imply challenges related to resource management and operational efficiency.

vocabulary.definition: Hitting the wall is an idiomatic expression that describes reaching a point of exhaustion or a barrier that prevents further progress.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, it can refer to a situation where a project or initiative encounters significant obstacles that hinder advancement or success.

insight.nuance: This phrase often conveys a sense of frustration and urgency, typically used in discussions about challenges faced during rapid growth or intense competition.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: Creative thinking and you kind of want to generate a bunch of ideas and filter through them and not just build the best product experience.
keySentence: Creative thinking involves generating a bunch of ideas and filtering through them.
text_ko: 창의적으로 생각할 때는 여러 아이디어를 많이 내서 하나하나 걸러 보는 게 좋아요. 그냥 최고의 제품 경험(product experience)만 만드는 데 그치면 안 돼요.
text_zh: 做创意思考的时候，你会想先把一堆点子抛出来、筛一筛，而不是只想着把产品体验(product experience)做得最好。
text_es: Con pensamiento creativo, lo que quieres es generar un montón de ideas, filtrarlas y no quedarte solo en construir la mejor experiencia de producto (product experience).
fullContext: Lenny asks what skills will be most valuable for product teams as AI advances. Karina emphasizes that creative thinking will become increasingly important - the ability to generate many ideas and filter through them effectively. She explains that current AI models struggle with aesthetic judgment, high-quality visual design, and truly creative writing, making these human skills more valuable.

vocabulary.definition: To produce or create something, often through a systematic process or method.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, generating ideas or solutions is crucial for innovation and problem-solving, particularly during brainstorming sessions or product development phases.

insight.nuance: While 'generate' implies a proactive approach to creation, it may not always convey the quality or feasibility of the output.

vocabulary.definition: To remove unwanted elements from a set of data or ideas, allowing only the most relevant or useful components to remain.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, filtering is often applied during decision-making processes to narrow down options and focus on the most viable strategies or products.

insight.nuance: The term 'filter' suggests a careful selection process, but it can also imply that some potentially valuable ideas may be overlooked.

vocabulary.definition: The overall interaction and satisfaction a user has with a product, encompassing usability, functionality, and emotional response.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech companies, enhancing the product experience is vital for customer retention and brand loyalty, influencing design and development strategies.

insight.nuance: The phrase carries a holistic connotation, suggesting that every aspect of a product's use contributes to the user's perception and satisfaction.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to generate innovative ideas and solutions by thinking outside conventional frameworks and exploring new possibilities.
vocabulary.businessContext: Creative thinking is essential in business environments for fostering innovation, developing unique products, and solving complex problems effectively.

insight.nuance: While often associated with artistic endeavors, creative thinking is equally valuable in analytical and strategic contexts, emphasizing flexibility and open-mindedness.

speaker: Karina Nguyen
text: For Canvas, for example, it came down to three main behaviors. It was how do you trigger Canvas for prompts like, 'Write me a long essay,' when the user intention is mostly iterating over long documents?
keySentence: Canvas behaviors came down to user intention and iterating over long documents.
text_ko: 예를 들어 Canvas의 경우는 결국 세 가지 주요 행동으로 정리됐어요. 사용자의 의도가 주로 긴 문서를 반복해서 다루는 것일 때, '긴 에세이를 써줘' 같은 프롬프트(prompt)로 Canvas를 어떻게 활성화(activate)하느냐가 관건이었어요.
text_zh: 拿 Canvas 举例，我们把它归结为三种主要行为。问题是，当用户的目的主要是反复修改长文档时，像“给我写一篇长文”这样的提示（prompts）应该怎么触发 Canvas？
text_es: En Canvas, por ejemplo, todo se redujo a tres comportamientos clave. La pregunta era: ¿cómo activas Canvas para peticiones (prompts) como "Escríbeme un ensayo largo" (Write me a long essay) cuando la intención del usuario es más bien iterar sobre documentos largos?
fullContext: Lenny asks how Canvas was created using synthetic data training. Canvas is OpenAI's collaborative document editing interface that changes from a chat to a visual editor. Karina explains they identified three core behaviors to teach the model: when to trigger the Canvas interface, how to edit documents, and how to make comments. The first behavior involved teaching the model to distinguish between requests that need document iteration versus simple Q&A.

vocabulary.definition: To initiate or activate a process or action in response to a specific event or condition.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'trigger' often refers to actions that start automated processes, such as alerts or workflows in software applications.

insight.nuance: While 'trigger' can imply a sudden action, it is often used in a technical context to describe deliberate initiation rather than random occurrences.

vocabulary.definition: The underlying goal or purpose that a user aims to achieve when interacting with a product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding user intention is crucial for product development and marketing, as it helps businesses tailor their offerings to meet customer needs effectively.

insight.nuance: The phrase 'user intention' emphasizes the importance of empathy in design, highlighting that products should align with users' goals rather than just their actions.

vocabulary.definition: The process of making repeated adjustments or refinements to a product or idea based on feedback or testing.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech development, iterating is a fundamental practice in agile methodologies, allowing teams to quickly adapt and improve their products in response to user feedback.

insight.nuance: While 'iterating' suggests a cycle of improvement, it can imply a continuous process rather than a one-time adjustment, which is essential in fast-paced environments.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: My belief is that, like any domain or industry, the more it matters, the more the design matters.
keySentence: The more it matters, the more design matters; the bar is so high.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 다른 어떤 분야나 산업과 마찬가지로, 중요할수록 디자인이 더 큰 차이를 만들어요.
text_zh: 我觉得，和任何行业一样，越重要的事，设计就越关键。
text_es: Creo que, como en cualquier sector, cuanto más importante es algo, más crítico resulta el diseño.
fullContext: Lenny asks Karri about when design can be enough of a differentiator against incumbents and whether founders should invest heavily in design versus other areas like distribution or technology. Karri explains his theory about how design becomes increasingly important as markets mature and become more crowded. He argues that in new paradigms like mobile or web, early products don't need great design since they're first to market, but as competition increases, the design bar rises significantly.

vocabulary.definition: Design refers to the process of creating a plan or convention for the construction of an object or system, encompassing aesthetics, functionality, and user experience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, design is crucial for product development, branding, and user interface, as it directly impacts customer satisfaction and market success.

insight.nuance: While design often emphasizes visual aspects, it also encompasses strategic thinking about usability and user engagement, making it a multifaceted concept.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: I think today it's almost a very basic thing now. Pretty much from the very beginning, you need pretty high level design for people to even pay attention or consider you seriously.
keySentence: High level design is necessary to pay attention and consider you seriously.
text_ko: 요즘엔 이게 거의 기본이에요. 처음부터 사람들의 관심을 끌고 진지하게 고려되려면 꽤 높은 수준의 디자인(high-level design)이 필요해요.
text_zh: 我觉得现在这几乎成了基本门槛。一开始就得有相当高水准的设计(design)，别人才能注意你、把你当回事。
text_es: Hoy en día eso ya es casi algo básico: prácticamente desde el principio necesitas un diseño de alto nivel (high-level design) para que la gente siquiera te preste atención o te tome en serio.
fullContext: Karri continues explaining why design has become crucial for modern startups. He points out that unlike older companies like Google or YouTube that launched with very basic websites, today's startups need high-quality design from day one just to get noticed. He acknowledges this creates an unfair barrier where good products might be dismissed simply due to poor visual design, even when the underlying functionality is solid.

vocabulary.definition: To think carefully about something, typically before making a decision.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business environment, 'consider' is often used when evaluating options, strategies, or proposals before taking action.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a thoughtful and deliberate process, often implying that multiple factors are being weighed.

vocabulary.definition: An abstract representation of a system or product that outlines its architecture and components without delving into detailed implementation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup settings, 'high level design' is crucial for communicating the overall vision and structure of a project to stakeholders and team members.

insight.nuance: This term emphasizes the strategic overview rather than technical specifics, making it suitable for discussions with non-technical stakeholders.

vocabulary.definition: To focus one's mind on something; to give careful consideration or notice to a particular matter.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'pay attention' often refers to the need for stakeholders, employees, or customers to be aware of important information or changes that could impact their decisions.

insight.nuance: This phrase can imply a call to action, suggesting that the subject matter is significant enough to warrant focused observation.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: So I think similarly, with startups or SaaS, it's like your landing page or some of the other things.
keySentence: it's like your landing page or some of the other things.
text_ko: 저도 비슷하게 생각해요. 스타트업(startups)이나 SaaS(SaaS) 쪽에서는 랜딩 페이지(landing page)나 그런 다른 요소들이 중요한 편이에요.
text_zh: 我觉得对初创公司(startups)或软件即服务(SaaS)来说也是这样，像你的落地页(landing page)或其他一些环节就很关键。
text_es: Creo que con las startups o con el software como servicio (SaaS) pasa algo parecido: tu página de aterrizaje (landing page) y otras cosas.
fullContext: Karri draws an analogy between product packaging (like Apple's attention to unboxing experiences) and startup design elements like landing pages. He explains that design serves as the first impression that sets user expectations before they even try the product. This is particularly valuable for unknown startups that need to establish credibility and quality perception from the first interaction, making design a powerful form of leverage in the early stages.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: So for every project there's a project lead. That lead can be engineer or designer. It's not a formal role or it's not based on your whatever level or it's just like you need to be certain title that you can be that.
keySentence: That lead can be engineer or designer.
text_ko: 프로젝트마다 프로젝트 리드(project lead)가 있어요. 그 리드는 엔지니어(engineer)일 수도 있고 디자이너(designer)일 수도 있어요. 정식 직책이나 경력 레벨에 따라 정해지는 건 아니고, 특정 타이틀이 있어야만 맡을 수 있는 역할도 아니에요.
text_zh: 每个项目都会有个项目负责人(project lead)，可以是工程师也可以是设计师。这不是一个正式的职位，也不是按你的级别或头衔来定的，没必要非得有某个特定头衔才能担任。
text_es: Así que para cada proyecto hay un responsable del proyecto (project lead). Ese responsable puede ser un ingeniero o un diseñador. No es un rol formal ni depende de tu nivel ni de tener un título concreto para poder serlo.
fullContext: Lenny asks how Linear functions with only one product manager across the entire company. Karri explains their project-based leadership model where engineers and designers take turns being project leads. This isn't a formal hierarchy based on seniority or titles, but rather a rotating assignment system where someone takes responsibility for driving a specific project forward, coordinating with the team, and managing communications about progress.

vocabulary.definition: A project lead is an individual responsible for overseeing and guiding a specific project from inception to completion, ensuring that objectives are met and resources are utilized effectively.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, the project lead coordinates team efforts, manages timelines, and communicates with stakeholders to ensure project success.

insight.nuance: While the title of project lead may not always be formalized, it implies a level of authority and accountability that is crucial for project execution.

vocabulary.definition: A formal role refers to an officially recognized position within an organization, typically defined by specific responsibilities and authority.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate structures, formal roles delineate job functions, helping to establish clear lines of responsibility and accountability among employees.

insight.nuance: The term 'formal role' suggests a level of hierarchy and structure, which may not always apply in more fluid or collaborative work environments.

vocabulary.definition: An engineer or designer refers to professionals who apply technical and creative skills to develop products, systems, or solutions, often collaborating closely in project settings.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology and design firms, engineers and designers play critical roles in the development process, contributing their expertise to ensure that projects are both functional and aesthetically pleasing.

insight.nuance: The phrase suggests a collaborative relationship between technical and creative disciplines, highlighting the importance of both perspectives in successful project outcomes.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: I think sometimes people use data a lot or too much because they're worrying or they're afraid that, will I make the wrong choice? And I'm using data to make the choice for me.
keySentence: people use data a lot or too much because they're worrying or they're afraid that, will I make the wrong choice?
text_ko: 사람들이 가끔 데이터를(data)를 많이, 심지어 과하게 쓰는 건 '내가 잘못된 선택을 할까?' 하는 불안이나 두려움 때문이라고 생각해요. 그래서 스스로 선택하기보다 데이터를 통해 선택을 대신하게끔 하는 거예요.
text_zh: 我觉得有时候人们会把数据用得很多、甚至过头了，因为害怕会做错决定，就让数据替自己做主。
text_es: Creo que a veces la gente se apoya demasiado en los datos (data) porque tiene miedo de equivocarse: se preguntan "¿voy a tomar la decisión equivocada?" y acaban dejando que los datos decidan por ellos.
fullContext: Lenny asks about Linear's approach of not using metrics-based goals or A/B testing, which differs from many other companies. Karri explains his philosophy that over-reliance on data often stems from fear of making wrong decisions. He argues that leaders should make decisions based on customer understanding and intuition rather than letting data make choices for them, emphasizing the importance of taking ownership of decisions rather than hiding behind metrics.

vocabulary.definition: To select an option or course of action that leads to an undesirable or negative outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, making the wrong choice can have significant repercussions, affecting everything from project success to financial stability.

insight.nuance: This phrase emphasizes the potential for error in decision-making, often highlighting the fear or anxiety associated with uncertainty.

speaker: Karri Saarinen
text: I think there's always things that you're supposed to do or it sounds like a good idea to do. And it could be like, yeah, come to this podcast. And I actually think before it wasn't like...
keySentence: You're supposed to do things that sound like a good idea, but timing matters.
text_ko: 늘 해야 할 것 같거나, 하면 좋을 것 같은 일들이 있는 것 같아요. 예를 들어 '이 팟캐스트에 나와보세요' 같은 제안일 수 있죠. 근데 사실 전에는 꼭 그렇게 생각하지 않았어요.
text_zh: 我觉得总有些事别人觉得你应该做，或者听起来是个好主意。比如有人会说，“来上这个播客 (podcast) 吧”。但我其实觉得以前并不是那样……
text_es: Creo que siempre hay cosas que se supone que tienes que hacer o que parecen buena idea. Puede ser algo como: “sí, ven a este pódcast (podcast)”. Y, la verdad, creo que antes no era así...
fullContext: Lenny asks Karri about his exceptional focus and ability to avoid distractions, noting how difficult it was to get him on the podcast initially. Karri shares his decision-making framework for maintaining focus, explaining that he constantly evaluates whether activities are important to do now versus later. He uses the podcast example to illustrate how he delayed this interview until Linear reached a stage where the conversation would be more valuable and interesting.

vocabulary.definition: A suggestion or proposal that is considered beneficial or advantageous in a particular context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, identifying a 'good idea' can lead to innovative solutions, improved processes, or new product developments.

insight.nuance: While 'good idea' is a positive endorsement, it can be subjective and may require further validation or analysis before implementation.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: And so I came in swinging ready to go, and then about a month into my time there, I got a meeting on my calendar.
keySentence: I came in swinging ready to go
text_ko: 그래서 저는 시작부터 의욕적으로 뛰어들었어요. 그런데 그곳에서 일한 지 한 달쯤 됐을 때 제 캘린더에 회의가 잡혔어요.
text_zh: 所以我一进公司就干劲十足准备大干一场，结果干了差不多一个月，我收到了一个会议邀请。
text_es: Y entonces llegué con todas las ganas, listo para arrancar, y como al mes de estar ahí, me aparece una reunión en el calendario.
fullContext: Lenny asks Katie about a significant failure in her leadership career. Katie describes her first month as head of design at Airbnb, where she tried to make rapid changes to improve the team's low engagement scores and collaboration issues. However, five team members scheduled a formal meeting with HR to read from papers listing everything they thought she was doing wrong as a leader.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: The use of the word beauty in books that have been digitized by Google has decreased, like pretty dramatically. And it's aligned with this idea of, "Well, functionality is king.
keySentence: functionality is king.
text_ko: 구글이 디지털화한 책들에서 '아름다움'이라는 단어가 눈에 띄게 줄었어요. 그리고 그건 '기능이 최고다'라는 생각과 맞물려 있어요.
text_zh: 被谷歌数字化（digitized by Google）的书里，“美”这个词用得明显少了，下降幅度挺大的。这和“功能为王（functionality is king）”这种说法是一致的。
text_es: El uso de la palabra "belleza" en los libros que Google ha digitalizado ha bajado muchísimo. Y eso va de la mano con la idea de que, bueno, la funcionalidad manda.
fullContext: Lenny asks Katie about the importance of beauty in product design and whether it's just subjective opinion or has objective value. Katie references research from Stefan Sagmeister and Jessica Walsh's book that shows the word "beauty" has declined in usage over the past 200 years as people have come to see functionality and beauty as opposing forces. Katie argues that this is a false dichotomy - functionality and beauty actually work together to create better user experiences.

vocabulary.definition: In agreement or cooperation with a particular goal or standard.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, 'aligned' often refers to ensuring that team objectives, strategies, or values are in harmony with the overall mission of the organization.

insight.nuance: While 'aligned' suggests a positive coordination, it can imply a lack of independent thought or creativity if overused.

vocabulary.definition: The range of operations that can be performed by a system or product; its practical utility.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, 'functionality' is crucial as it determines how effectively a product meets user needs and drives customer satisfaction.

insight.nuance: While 'functionality' emphasizes practical use, it can sometimes overshadow aesthetic or emotional aspects of a product.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: And regardless of each individual thing, what was very clear was that the missing piece, the theme that was across all of that is that I hadn't earned their trust.
keySentence: the missing piece, the theme that was across all of that is that I hadn't earned their trust.
text_ko: 각각의 사안을 떠나서, 분명한 건 모든 경우에 공통된 한 가지는 제가 그들의 신뢰를 얻지 못했다는 점이었어요.
text_zh: 不管具体是哪件事，有一点很明确，就是所有这些问题的根源都指向一个问题——我还没有赢得他们的信任。
text_es: Y más allá de cada cosa en particular, lo que quedó clarísimo es que lo que faltaba, el hilo conductor de todo eso, era que no me había ganado su confianza.
fullContext: Katie explains her realization after receiving harsh feedback from her design team at Airbnb. The team had formally complained about her leadership approach through HR after just one month. Katie reflects on what she learned from this difficult experience about the importance of building trust as a foundation for effective leadership.

vocabulary.definition: An essential element or factor that is absent and necessary for achieving a complete understanding or successful outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: Identifying the missing piece in a project or strategy can lead to breakthroughs in problem-solving and innovation within a business context.

insight.nuance: This phrase often conveys a sense of incompleteness or urgency, implying that addressing the missing piece is critical for success.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: And the other piece of it that is not talked about in business as often is just the importance of how people feel. Things that are more beautiful, increase trust.
keySentence: the importance of how people feel.
text_ko: 그리고 비즈니스에서 잘 얘기되지 않는 또 하나는 사람들이 어떻게 느끼는지가 얼마나 중요한가예요. 더 보기 좋고 아름다운 것들은 신뢰를 더 쌓아줘요.
text_zh: 还有一点在商界很少说的，就是人们的感受很重要。更有美感的东西会更容易建立信任。
text_es: Otra cosa que no se suele hablar tanto en el mundo de los negocios es la importancia de cómo se sienten las personas: las cosas más bonitas inspiran más confianza.
fullContext: Katie continues explaining why beauty matters in business products, particularly in B2B contexts. She argues that beautiful design signals quality and trustworthiness to users. When customers see that a company has invested painstaking effort in the visible details of their product, it creates confidence that the same level of care has been applied to the technical details they cannot see.

vocabulary.definition: The state or fact of being of great significance or value.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding the importance of various factors, such as employee satisfaction or customer feedback, can drive strategic decisions and enhance overall performance.

insight.nuance: While 'importance' conveys a general sense of value, it can imply varying degrees of urgency or priority depending on the context.

vocabulary.definition: A firm belief in the reliability, truth, or ability of someone or something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, trust is essential for building strong relationships with clients, partners, and employees, often influencing brand loyalty and collaboration.

insight.nuance: Trust can be fragile and is built over time; it is crucial to maintain transparency and consistency to foster it effectively.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: I had some version of a panic attack, walked off stage, I was still mic'd up, cursed. I was laughing. I was like, 'Geez, are they laughing at me.
keySentence: I was like, 'Geez, are they laughing at me.
text_ko: 어떤 식으론 공황발작 비슷한 게 왔어요. 무대에서 내려왔는데도 마이크가 아직 붙어 있어서 욕이 나왔어요. 웃음도 나왔고, '아이구, 사람들이 나 보고 웃는 걸까?'라고 생각했어요.
text_zh: 我当时差点panic attack，直接走下台了，麦克风还开着呢，嘴里骂骂咧咧的。我还在那儿笑，心想"天哪，他们是在笑我吗？"
text_es: Tuve algo así como un ataque de pánico, me bajé del escenario, todavía tenía el micrófono puesto, dije groserías. Me estaba riendo. Y pensé, 'Dios mío, ¿se están burlando de mí?'
fullContext: Lenny asks Paul about a memorable failure that scarred him for life. Paul describes freezing during a keynote speech at the world's biggest advertising festival in Cannes, representing Facebook. He had to walk off stage in front of thousands of people, and because his microphone was still on, the audience heard him curse. Despite this nightmare scenario, he managed to return and successfully complete his presentation.

vocabulary.definition: A sudden episode of intense fear or anxiety that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger or apparent cause.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, a panic attack may occur during high-pressure situations such as public speaking or critical meetings, impacting an individual's performance and decision-making.

insight.nuance: While often associated with mental health issues, the term can also imply a loss of control in stressful situations, making it important to use with sensitivity.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: The gravitational pull is to mediocrity. It is very easy to fall into a path of a baseline, where what is required to go to that next level where something feels truly great is certainly a lot of effort, and it's a concerted effort.
keySentence: The gravitational pull leads to mediocrity; concerted effort is needed.
text_ko: 사람들은 평범함으로 끌리는 중력 같은 게 있어요. 기준선(baseline)에 머무는 길로 빠지는 건 정말 쉽고, 다음 단계로 올라가서 진짜 훌륭하다고 느껴질 수준에 닿으려면 확실히 많은 노력, 특히 의도적이고 집중적인 노력이 필요해요.
text_zh: 人都容易向平庸靠拢，这就像地心引力一样。很容易就走上了一条得过且过的路，但要想上一个台阶，做出真正出色的东西，那就需要付出很大的努力，而且必须是持续的、有目标的努力。
text_es: La tendencia natural es hacia la mediocridad. Es muy fácil caer en una zona de confort donde haces lo mínimo, y para llegar a ese siguiente nivel donde realmente sientes que algo está increíble, pues requiere mucho esfuerzo, y tiene que ser un esfuerzo constante y enfocado.
fullContext: Lenny asks Katie about how teams can operationalize quality and maintain high design standards. Katie explains one of the core challenges in maintaining quality - that there's a natural tendency for teams and products to drift toward mediocre, baseline solutions because achieving true greatness requires sustained, coordinated effort from multiple people and teams working together intentionally.

vocabulary.definition: Mediocrity refers to the state of being average or unremarkable, often implying a lack of excellence or quality. It suggests a complacency in performance or achievement.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, mediocrity can hinder innovation and growth, as organizations may settle for satisfactory results rather than striving for exceptional performance.

insight.nuance: While mediocrity can be seen as a safe or comfortable position, it often carries a negative connotation, suggesting a failure to reach one's full potential.

vocabulary.definition: A baseline is a standard or reference point used for comparison, often established to measure progress or performance over time. It serves as a foundation for evaluating changes or improvements.
vocabulary.businessContext: In project management and performance analysis, establishing a baseline is crucial for tracking outcomes and determining the effectiveness of strategies or interventions.

insight.nuance: While a baseline is essential for measurement, it can also imply a minimum standard that may not inspire ambition or growth if adhered to rigidly.

vocabulary.definition: A concerted effort refers to a coordinated and collaborative approach to achieving a specific goal, involving multiple parties working together towards a common objective. It emphasizes teamwork and shared commitment.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a concerted effort is often necessary for successful project execution, requiring alignment among various departments or stakeholders to drive results effectively.

insight.nuance: The term conveys a sense of urgency and importance, suggesting that individual efforts alone are insufficient to achieve the desired outcome.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: I think a lot of the motivation for those projects came from a place of fear. It didn't come from a place of let's make a great product for people, let's really understand the things people struggle with when communicating with family and friends.
keySentence: a lot of the motivation for those projects came from a place of fear.
text_ko: 제 생각에 그 프로젝트들에 대한 동기 대부분은 두려움에서 나온 것 같아요. 사람들이 진짜로 필요로 하는 좋은 제품을 만들자거나, 가족·친구와 소통할 때 사람들이 어떤 어려움을 겪는지 제대로 이해해 보자는 마음에서 나온 건 아니었어요.
text_zh: 我觉得那些项目很多都是出于恐惧心理在做。不是真的想着怎么给用户做个好产品，怎么真正去了解大家跟家人朋友交流时会遇到什么困难。
text_es: Creo que gran parte de la motivación de esos proyectos venía del miedo. No venía de un lugar de "vamos a crear un producto genial para la gente", de realmente entender con qué luchan las personas cuando se comunican con familia y amigos.
fullContext: Lenny asks Paul about his time working on failed social projects at Google like Google Buzz and Google+. Paul reflects on why these products failed, explaining that the motivation behind building them was fundamentally flawed. Instead of focusing on solving real user problems, the projects were driven by competitive fear of Facebook's success in social networking.

vocabulary.definition: The reason or reasons one has for acting or behaving in a particular way; the driving force behind actions and decisions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, motivation often refers to the underlying factors that inspire teams to pursue projects, innovate, and achieve goals, which can significantly impact productivity and company culture.

insight.nuance: While motivation can stem from positive incentives, it can also arise from fear or pressure, which may lead to short-term results but potentially harm long-term engagement.

vocabulary.definition: To grasp the meaning, significance, or nature of something; to comprehend fully.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, understanding customer needs and market dynamics is crucial for developing effective strategies and products that resonate with target audiences.

insight.nuance: Understanding often implies a deeper level of insight beyond surface knowledge, and it is essential for effective decision-making and relationship-building.

vocabulary.definition: The act of conveying information or expressing thoughts and feelings to others through verbal, non-verbal, or written means.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective communicating is vital in business for collaboration, negotiation, and maintaining relationships with clients, stakeholders, and team members.

insight.nuance: Communicating encompasses not only the transmission of information but also the clarity and effectiveness of the message, which can greatly influence outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: To make strenuous or violent efforts to get free of restraint or resist attack; to experience difficulty or hardship.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business environment, struggle often refers to the challenges faced by individuals or teams in overcoming obstacles, achieving goals, or adapting to change.

insight.nuance: Struggle can imply a sense of conflict or difficulty, and while it may indicate a negative experience, it can also lead to growth and resilience when addressed constructively.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: Performance equals potential minus interference.
keySentence: Performance equals potential minus interference.
text_ko: 성과(performance)는 잠재력(potential)에서 방해 요인(interference)을 뺀 거예요.
text_zh: 表现其实就是你的潜力被各种干扰削弱后的结果。
text_es: El rendimiento es el potencial menos todo lo que lo interfiere.
fullContext: Lenny asks Katie about lessons she's learned from scaling design teams at multiple hypergrowth companies. Katie shares a formula she learned at Airbnb that has guided her leadership approach: Performance = Potential - Interference. She explains that leaders can improve team performance in two ways: increasing potential through hiring great people and developing talent, and decreasing interference by removing obstacles that prevent great people from doing their best work.

vocabulary.definition: The execution of a task or the ability to achieve results effectively and efficiently.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, performance often refers to how well an organization, team, or individual meets established goals and objectives, frequently measured through key performance indicators (KPIs).

insight.nuance: While 'performance' can imply a high level of achievement, it may also suggest a need for improvement when used in contexts of evaluation.

vocabulary.definition: The inherent ability or capacity for growth, development, or future success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, potential often refers to the untapped capabilities of employees, markets, or products that could lead to significant advancements or profits if properly harnessed.

insight.nuance: The term 'potential' carries a positive connotation, suggesting optimism about future possibilities, but can also imply that current performance is lacking.

vocabulary.definition: The act of hindering or obstructing progress or development.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business realm, interference can refer to factors that disrupt workflow, such as bureaucratic processes, external market conditions, or internal conflicts that impede productivity.

insight.nuance: Interference often has a negative connotation, suggesting unwanted or unnecessary obstacles that detract from efficiency and effectiveness.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: The critique that is often leveled at Pets.com or at least at the time, was like, this is just a stupid business. They're shipping dog food around. You could never make that work, and that's just wrong. You absolutely can make it work.
keySentence: The critique that is often leveled at Pets.com was that it was a stupid business.
text_ko: 당시 Pets.com에 대해 자주 나오던 비판은 “그건 그냥 말도 안 되는 사업이야. 개 사료를 배송한다고? 절대 성공할 수 없어”라는 식이었어요. 그런데 그건 틀렸어요. 충분히 성공시킬 수 있어요.
text_zh: 当时大家对Pets.com最大的质疑就是，这生意太蠢了，就是把狗粮快递来快递去的，这怎么可能赚钱嘛，但这种想法是错的。这个模式绝对是能跑通的。
text_es: La crítica que siempre le hacían a Pets.com, o al menos en ese momento, era algo como "este negocio no tiene sentido, están mandando comida para perros por todo el país, eso jamás va a funcionar", y eso está completamente equivocado. Claro que se puede hacer funcionar.
fullContext: Lenny discusses how Tom took Pets.com from nothing to a public company to completely out of business in 19 months. Tom defends the business model, noting that Chewy later proved online pet retail could work with a $9 billion valuation. Tom explains that timing was crucial - Pets.com launched when internet adoption was still very limited, making the logistics and customer acquisition much more challenging than it would be later.

vocabulary.definition: A detailed analysis and assessment of something, typically a literary, artistic, or academic work.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a critique often refers to feedback on a product, service, or strategy, helping organizations identify strengths and weaknesses.

insight.nuance: While critiques can be constructive, they may also carry a negative connotation if perceived as overly harsh or dismissive.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: One of the biggest examples that I've seen of business impact through quality is actually in the checkout experience. We've done research on the checkout experience in some of the top e-commerce sites.
keySentence: One of the biggest examples that I've seen of business impact through quality is actually in the checkout experience.
text_ko: 제가 본 품질로 인한 비즈니스 영향 사례 중 가장 큰 것 중 하나는 사실 결제 경험(checkout experience)에서 나왔어요. 상위 이커머스(e-commerce) 사이트 몇 곳의 결제 경험을 조사해봤어요.
text_zh: 我见过的通过质量带来业务影响最明显的例子之一，其实是在结账体验(checkout experience)上。我们对几家顶级电商网站(e-commerce sites)的结账体验做过研究。
text_es: Uno de los ejemplos más claros que he visto de cómo la calidad impacta en el negocio es la experiencia de pago (checkout experience). Hemos investigado esa experiencia en varios de los principales sitios de comercio electrónico (e-commerce).
fullContext: Lenny asks Katie about making the ROI case for design quality versus just shipping new features quickly. Katie provides a concrete example from Stripe's work on checkout experiences. She explains that Stripe researched major e-commerce sites and discovered that nearly all of them had quality issues in their checkout flows that were actually hurting their business metrics. By fixing these design quality issues, businesses saw measurable improvements in conversion rates.

vocabulary.definition: Business impact refers to the effect that a particular action, decision, or event has on a company's performance and operations. It encompasses both positive and negative outcomes that can influence revenue, reputation, and overall success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, assessing business impact is crucial for decision-making, as it helps organizations prioritize initiatives that drive growth and mitigate risks.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a measurable outcome, making it more suitable in discussions involving data analysis or strategic planning.

vocabulary.definition: Checkout experience refers to the process and user interface that a customer interacts with when finalizing a purchase in an online or physical store. It includes elements such as payment options, ease of navigation, and overall customer satisfaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In e-commerce, optimizing the checkout experience is vital for reducing cart abandonment rates and enhancing customer loyalty, as it directly influences sales conversions.

insight.nuance: This term emphasizes the customer's perspective and is often used in discussions about user experience (UX) design and customer journey mapping.

vocabulary.definition: Research is the systematic investigation into a subject to establish facts, gather information, and develop new insights or solutions. It can be qualitative or quantitative in nature.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, research is essential for market analysis, product development, and strategic planning, as it provides the data needed to make informed decisions.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a connotation of rigor and thoroughness, making it more appropriate in formal contexts or when discussing academic or scientific inquiries.

vocabulary.definition: E-commerce, or electronic commerce, refers to the buying and selling of goods and services over the internet. It encompasses various online transactions, including retail, wholesale, and services.
vocabulary.businessContext: E-commerce has transformed traditional retail by enabling businesses to reach a global audience, streamline operations, and leverage digital marketing strategies for growth.

insight.nuance: While commonly associated with online retail, e-commerce also includes B2B and B2C transactions, making it a broad term that should be specified when discussing particular segments.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: For me, failure is not that you didn't drive revenue, failure is not learning. So it's really important that you learn when you fail.
keySentence: failure is not learning.
text_ko: 제게 있어 실패는 수익(revenue)을 만들지 못한 게 아니라 거기서 배우지 못하는 거예요. 그래서 실패했을 땐 꼭 배우는 게 중요해요.
text_zh: 在我看来，失败不是因为你没有带来收入，真正的失败是没有从中学到东西。所以当你失败的时候，关键是要从中吸取教训。
text_es: Para mí, fracasar no es que no hayas generado ingresos, fracasar es no aprender nada. Por eso es súper importante que cuando las cosas no salen bien, saques algo en limpio.
fullContext: Lenny asks Sri about creating a culture where people aren't afraid to take risks, given that growth experiments typically have only a 30% success rate. Sri explains his philosophy that the real failure isn't when experiments don't drive revenue - it's when teams don't learn from their failed attempts. He emphasizes the importance of designing conclusive tests to avoid repeatedly trying the same ineffective approaches.

vocabulary.definition: Failure is the lack of success in achieving a desired outcome or goal, often resulting in setbacks or losses.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, failure is frequently viewed as a learning opportunity, encouraging teams to analyze mistakes and pivot strategies rather than simply focusing on negative results.

insight.nuance: While 'failure' carries a negative connotation, in entrepreneurial contexts, it can also signify a crucial step towards eventual success and growth.

vocabulary.definition: Learning is the process of acquiring knowledge, skills, or understanding through experience, study, or instruction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business realm, continuous learning is essential for adapting to market changes, improving processes, and fostering innovation within teams.

insight.nuance: The term 'learning' emphasizes the importance of reflection and adaptation, particularly in contexts where mistakes have been made.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: So I started to make pretty fast change and still moving in the direction that was necessary for the org to make the really large impact in how we were operating, but bringing folks along with me.
keySentence: bringing folks along with me.
text_ko: 그래서 저는 꽤 빠르게 변화를 시작했고, 지금도 조직(org)이 운영 방식을 크게 바꿔 정말 큰 임팩트(impact)를 내기 위해 필요한 방향으로 나아가고 있으면서 사람들을 함께 동참시키고 있어요.
text_zh: 我很快就开始推动变革，朝着组织(org)需要的方向前进，去真正改变我们的运作方式，同时把大家都带上来。
text_es: Así que empecé a introducir cambios con bastante rapidez y seguí avanzando en la dirección necesaria para que la organización tuviera un impacto real en nuestra forma de operar, procurando que el equipo me acompañara.
fullContext: Katie tells the story of when her design team at Airbnb staged an intervention because she hadn't earned their trust as a new leader. After receiving this difficult feedback, Katie learned that while she was making necessary changes to improve the organization, she was imposing changes on people rather than building trust first. She realized that effective change management requires bringing people along with you rather than forcing change upon them.

vocabulary.definition: The strong effect or influence that one thing has on another.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'impact' often refers to the measurable effects of a strategy, decision, or initiative on an organization’s performance or market position.

insight.nuance: While 'impact' generally carries a positive connotation, it can also refer to negative effects, depending on the context.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to the functioning or management of a business or organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'operating' can refer to the day-to-day activities that keep the organization running smoothly, including processes, systems, and workflows.

insight.nuance: The term can imply both efficiency and effectiveness in the context of business operations, and is often used in discussions about operational improvements.

speaker: Katie Dill
text: I think there wasn't really a clear path. I think there was [inaudible]. Exactly. And it was more just like if you understood, again, this is my point around unit economics, there are things where I think you have magical thinking around unit economics.
keySentence: there are things where I think you have magical thinking around unit economics.
text_ko: 사실 뚜렷한 길이 있었다고는 생각하지 않아요. (그 부분은 잘 안 들렸어요.) 맞아요. 그리고 다시 말하지만 제 요지는 유닛 이코노믹스(unit economics)에 관한 건데, 이 분야에 대해 마치 마법처럼 생각하는 경향이 있다고 봐요.
text_zh: 我觉得当时没有一个清晰的路径。我觉得有[听不清]。没错。更多的是，如果你理解的话，这又回到我说的单位经济效益(unit economics)的问题，有些事情你对单位经济效益(unit economics)抱有不切实际的幻想。
text_es: Creo que no había una ruta clara. Creo que había [inaudible]. Exacto. Y era más bien como que si entendías, otra vez, este es mi punto sobre la rentabilidad por unidad (unit economics), hay cosas donde creo que uno se hace ilusiones sobre la rentabilidad por unidad.
fullContext: Lenny asks JZ whether Airbnb Plus could have succeeded with better execution or if the business model was fundamentally flawed. Airbnb Plus was an attempt to create managed, inspected inventory to address trust issues, but it required significant operational investment. JZ explains that the project suffered from 'magical thinking' about unit economics - the belief that profitability would somehow emerge at scale without the fundamental economics working from the start.

vocabulary.definition: Unit economics refers to the direct revenues and costs associated with a particular business model, typically expressed on a per-unit basis.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, understanding unit economics is crucial for assessing profitability and scalability, as it helps entrepreneurs determine how much profit or loss is generated from each unit sold.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a focus on the sustainability of a business model, and it is commonly used in discussions about financial health and growth potential.

vocabulary.definition: Magical thinking refers to the belief that one's thoughts, actions, or words can influence outcomes in a way that defies logic or rationality.
