fullContext: Lenny asks Logan how developers should think about building products that won't be disrupted by OpenAI in the future. Logan explains that OpenAI focuses on general reasoning capabilities rather than specific vertical applications. He uses Harvey, a legal AI company, as an example of how companies can build specialized tools for specific industries that OpenAI won't compete with directly.

vocabulary.definition: Vertical applications are software solutions designed to meet the specific needs of a particular industry or market segment, rather than serving a broad range of sectors.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, vertical applications are often tailored to enhance efficiency and productivity within specialized fields such as healthcare, finance, or manufacturing.

insight.nuance: The term is typically used to emphasize specialization and depth of functionality in contrast to horizontal applications, which serve a wider audience.

speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
text: My whole position on this is prompt engineering is a very human thing. When we want to get some value out of a human, we do this prompt engineering. We try to effectively communicate with that human in order to get the best output.
keySentence: prompt engineering is a very human thing.
text_ko: 제 생각은 프롬프트 엔지니어링(prompt engineering)은 아주 인간적인 일이에요. 사람에게서 어떤 가치를 끌어내고 싶을 때 우리는 바로 이런 프롬프트 엔지니어링을 하고, 최고의 결과를 얻으려면 그 사람과 효과적으로 소통하려고 노력해요.
text_zh: 我的看法是，提示工程(prompt engineering)本质上就是非常“人的”工作。当我们想从一个人那里获得价值时，实际上就是在做这种提示工程——要跟那个人有效沟通，才能拿到最好的产出。
text_es: Mi postura es que la ingeniería de prompts (prompt engineering) es algo muy humano. Cuando queremos obtener valor de una persona, practicamos esa ingeniería: intentamos comunicarnos con ella de la manera más clara y eficaz para conseguir el mejor resultado.
fullContext: Lenny asks Logan to explain prompt engineering and give advice on writing better prompts for ChatGPT. Logan explains that prompt engineering exists because AI models, like humans, need context to give good responses. He draws an analogy between communicating effectively with humans and communicating with AI models - both require providing sufficient context to get valuable output.

vocabulary.definition: In a manner that produces a desired result or outcome; efficiently and successfully achieving objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, being effective often refers to the ability to achieve goals with minimal waste of resources, time, or effort, particularly in project management and communication.

insight.nuance: While 'effectively' implies a successful outcome, it is important to ensure that the methods used are also ethical and sustainable.

vocabulary.definition: To convey information, thoughts, or feelings to others through spoken, written, or non-verbal means.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective communication is vital in business for collaboration, negotiation, and relationship-building, often facilitated through meetings, emails, and presentations.

insight.nuance: The term can imply not just the act of sending a message, but also ensuring that the message is understood by the recipient.

vocabulary.definition: The result or product produced by a process, system, or individual, often measured in terms of quantity or quality.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, output can refer to the performance of employees, the production of goods, or the results of a project, and is often analyzed to improve efficiency and productivity.

insight.nuance: Output can carry a quantitative connotation, but it can also refer to qualitative aspects such as creativity or innovation.

speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
text: Context is the only thing that matters. It's such an important piece of getting a language model to do anything for you.
keySentence: Context is the only thing that matters for language models.
text_ko: 문맥(context)이 전부예요. 언어 모델(language model)에게 뭔가 시키려면 그 문맥이 정말 중요해요.
text_zh: 上下文是唯一重要的东西。想让语言模型(language model)帮你做任何事，这一点太关键了。
text_es: El contexto es lo único que realmente importa. Es clave para lograr que un modelo de lenguaje te funcione como necesitas.
fullContext: Logan continues explaining prompt engineering best practices to Lenny. He emphasizes that the most critical factor in getting good results from AI models is providing adequate context. Logan suggests that if OpenAI made t-shirts, they should say 'Context is all you need' because context is so fundamental to effective AI interaction.

vocabulary.definition: Having significant value or meaning; worthy of attention or consideration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate environment, identifying important issues or tasks is crucial for prioritizing efforts and resources effectively.

insight.nuance: While 'important' denotes significance, it may lack the urgency implied by terms like 'critical' or 'urgent.'

speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
text: I think the thing that surprised me the most was just how quickly everybody got back to business.
keySentence: how quickly everybody got back to business.
text_ko: 가장 놀랐던 건 모두가 얼마나 빨리 다시 본업으로 돌아왔는지였어요.
text_zh: 我觉得最让我惊讶的是大家竟然这么快就回到正事上了。
text_es: Creo que lo que más me sorprendió fue lo rápido que todo el mundo se puso manos a la obra.
fullContext: Lenny asks Logan about the dramatic weekend when OpenAI's board fired and then rehired CEO Sam Altman. Logan describes how the incident occurred during what was supposed to be the company's first major break since ChatGPT launched. He explains that what surprised him most was how quickly the team refocused on work after the crisis, demonstrating their commitment to OpenAI's mission.

vocabulary.definition: Experiencing a sudden feeling of wonder or astonishment due to an unexpected event or outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being surprised can indicate a deviation from anticipated results, such as unexpected market trends or team performance.

insight.nuance: While 'surprised' generally has a neutral connotation, it can imply a lack of preparedness or insight when used in a professional context.

vocabulary.definition: In a rapid manner; with speed or promptness.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the fast-paced world of business and technology, acting quickly is often essential for seizing opportunities and responding to market changes.

insight.nuance: The term 'quickly' suggests efficiency and urgency, but overuse can imply haste without thorough consideration.

vocabulary.definition: Resumed regular activities or tasks after a disruption or interruption.
vocabulary.businessContext: This phrase is commonly used in professional environments to indicate a return to focus on work-related objectives following a break or unexpected event.

insight.nuance: The phrase conveys a sense of professionalism and resilience, suggesting that distractions are managed effectively to maintain productivity.

speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
text: I think 2024 is the year of multimodal AI, but it's also the year that people really push the boundaries of some of these new UX paradigms around AI.
keySentence: 2024 will be the year of multimodal AI and pushing the boundaries of UX paradigms.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 2024년이 멀티모달 AI(multimodal AI)의 해인 것 같아요. 동시에 사람들이 이 새로운 AI 관련 UX 패러다임(UX paradigms)들 중 일부의 경계를 정말로 밀어붙이는 해이기도 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得2024年是多模态AI(multimodal AI)的元年，但同时也是大家真正开始突破AI用户体验(UX)新范式边界的一年。
text_es: Creo que el 2024 va a ser el año de la IA multimodal, pero también va a ser cuando la gente realmente se lance a explorar los límites de estos nuevos paradigmas de experiencia de usuario (UX paradigms) en torno a la IA.
fullContext: Lenny asks Logan about the most mind-blowing AI applications he's seen recently. Logan discusses new interfaces for AI interaction beyond traditional chatbots, mentioning products like the Rabbit R-1 and TL Draw. He explains that while chat is currently the dominant way people use AI, he's excited about new user experience paradigms that move beyond simple text-based interactions.

vocabulary.definition: To challenge the limits of what is currently accepted or possible, often leading to innovation or new ideas.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, this phrase is frequently used to describe efforts to innovate or develop new products and services that exceed existing standards or expectations.

insight.nuance: This phrase carries a positive connotation, suggesting a proactive approach to growth and creativity, and is often used in discussions about innovation.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to the integration of multiple modes or methods of communication, interaction, or operation, often in technology or transportation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, multimodal systems enhance user experience by combining various forms of input and output, such as text, voice, and visual elements, to create more intuitive interfaces.

insight.nuance: While commonly used in technology, the term can also apply to logistics and transportation, emphasizing the versatility and efficiency of using different modes.

vocabulary.definition: Established patterns or models of thinking, behavior, or practices that shape how individuals or organizations understand and approach a particular field.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, paradigms influence strategic decision-making and can dictate the direction of innovation; shifting paradigms often lead to significant changes in industry practices.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a deep-rooted belief system that may be resistant to change, making it a powerful concept in discussions about transformation and disruption.

speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
text: I've got it. It's on a Post-It note that I... Right behind my camera and it's 'Measure in hundreds.' I love this idea of measuring things in hundreds, and it's for folks who are at the beginning of some journey.
keySentence: Measure in hundreds.
text_ko: 찾았어요. 포스트잇에 적어뒀는데 카메라 바로 뒤에 있어요. '백 단위로 측정하라(Measure in hundreds)'고 적혀 있어요. 저는 이런 '백 단위로 측정하기'라는 아이디어가 정말 마음에 들어요. 그리고 이건 이제 막 여정을 시작한 분들에게 좋은 방법이에요.
text_zh: 我记下来了，就贴在我相机后面的便利贴（Post-It）上，上面写着“按百来衡量”。我很喜欢把东西按百来衡量这个想法，特别适合刚起步的人。
text_es: Lo tengo. Está en un post-it que... justo detrás de mi cámara y dice "Mide en centenas". Me encanta esta idea de medir las cosas en centenas, y va dirigida a personas que están empezando un camino.
fullContext: Lenny asks Logan about his favorite life motto during the lightning round. Logan shares his personal motto 'Measure in hundreds' which he keeps on a Post-It note behind his camera. He explains this philosophy helps people understand that success requires many attempts - if you think in terms of hundreds of tries, then failing five times means you've barely started, not that you should give up.

vocabulary.definition: To ascertain the size, amount, or degree of something using a standard unit.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, measuring performance metrics, such as sales growth or customer satisfaction, is crucial for evaluating success and making informed decisions.

insight.nuance: While 'measure' can refer to any quantifiable assessment, it often implies a systematic approach to evaluation in a professional context.

vocabulary.definition: A process of personal or professional development that involves a series of experiences or changes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, a 'journey' often refers to the customer journey, which outlines the stages a customer goes through from awareness to purchase and beyond.

insight.nuance: The term 'journey' conveys a sense of progression and transformation, making it more impactful than simply referring to a 'process.'

vocabulary.definition: The point in time or space at which something starts or originates.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the 'beginning' can refer to the startup phase of a company, where foundational strategies and goals are established.

insight.nuance: The word 'beginning' often carries a sense of potential and opportunity, highlighting the importance of initial actions and decisions.

vocabulary.definition: A thought or suggestion as to a possible course of action or a concept that can be developed into a plan.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, ideas are the foundation of innovation and strategy, often leading to new products, services, or improvements in processes.

insight.nuance: The term 'idea' can imply creativity and originality, but it may also suggest a lack of concrete plans or implementation.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: We talk about the 10X engineer and we don't really talk about the 10X growth advisor or 10X growth person, but the same dynamic applies. You could argue it applies even more because the right growth advisor can have literally company changing impact.
keySentence: The right growth advisor can have literally company changing impact.
text_ko: 우리는 10배 성과 엔지니어(10X engineer)에 대해서는 많이 얘기하지만, 10배 성장 어드바이저(10X growth advisor)나 10배 성장 담당자(10X growth person)에 대해서는 잘 얘기하지 않아요. 같은 원리가 그대로 적용돼요. 오히려 더 크게 적용된다고 주장할 수 있어요. 제대로 된 성장 어드바이저는 말 그대로 회사 판도를 바꿀 수 있는 영향을 미치니까요.
text_zh: 大家都在谈10倍工程师(10X engineer)，却很少有人关注10倍增长顾问(10X growth advisor)或10倍增长型人才(10X growth person)，但道理是一样的。甚至可以说，对增长顾问来说影响更大——合适的人真的能改变一家公司的命运。
text_es: Hablamos del ingeniero 10X (10X engineer) y no hablamos tanto del asesor de crecimiento 10X (10X growth advisor) ni de la persona de crecimiento 10X (10X growth person), pero la misma dinámica se aplica. Se podría decir que aplica incluso más, porque el asesor de crecimiento adecuado puede tener un impacto que literalmente cambia la empresa.
fullContext: Lenny asks Luc about the value and impact of growth advisors compared to other types of advisors or hires. Luc explains that while people often discuss the concept of "10X engineers" - exceptional engineers who provide vastly outsized value - the same principle applies even more strongly to growth advisors. He argues that finding the right growth advisor can literally change a company's trajectory, sometimes delivering hundreds or even thousands of percent improvements when the right strategy is implemented.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by constant change, activity, or progress; energetic and forceful.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a dynamic environment refers to rapidly evolving market conditions that require organizations to adapt quickly to remain competitive.

insight.nuance: While 'dynamic' often has a positive connotation, it can also imply unpredictability or instability in certain contexts.

vocabulary.definition: The strong effect or influence that something has on a situation or person.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, impact often refers to the measurable outcomes of decisions, strategies, or innovations on company performance or market trends.

insight.nuance: Impact can be both positive and negative, so it's important to specify the nature of the impact when discussing outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: A professional who provides strategic guidance and insights to help organizations expand their operations and increase revenue.
vocabulary.businessContext: Growth advisors are often employed by startups and established companies alike to identify opportunities for scaling and optimizing business performance.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a focus on long-term development rather than short-term gains, making it essential for sustainable business practices.

vocabulary.definition: Describing actions, strategies, or individuals that have the potential to significantly alter the direction or success of a business.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the corporate world, company-changing initiatives are often pivotal projects or leadership changes that can redefine a company's trajectory.

insight.nuance: This phrase carries a weighty implication, suggesting that the changes are not merely incremental but transformative in nature.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: It's one of those weird disciplines where the right person at the right time can literally say a sentence that changes the trajectory of your company. You can't say that for a lot of different disciplines, but this is one of them.
keySentence: The right person can literally change the trajectory of your company.
text_ko: 이건 좀 특이한 분야예요. 딱 맞는 사람이 딱 맞는 타이밍에 한 문장만 해도 회사의 방향을 완전히 바꿔놓을 수 있어요. 다른 많은 분야들에 대해선 그렇게 말하기 어렵지만, 이건 그런 경우예요.
text_zh: 这就是那种很奇妙的领域，合适的人在合适的时机说一句话，真的能改变你公司的发展轨迹。很多其他领域都做不到这一点，但这个领域就是有这种魔力。
text_es: Es una de esas disciplinas raras donde la persona indicada en el momento preciso puede literalmente decir una frase que te cambia completamente el rumbo de la empresa. No puedes decir eso de muchas otras disciplinas, pero esta sí es una de ellas.
fullContext: Luc continues explaining why growth advisors can be so valuable to companies. He emphasizes that growth is unique among business disciplines because a single insight or recommendation from an experienced growth expert can fundamentally alter a company's path. This is different from other areas where impact typically requires sustained effort over time - in growth, one conversation or piece of advice can unlock massive improvements.

vocabulary.definition: The path or progression of an object or concept over time, often used to describe growth or development.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'trajectory' often refers to the growth path or strategic direction of a company, indicating how its performance is expected to evolve.

insight.nuance: While 'trajectory' can imply a positive or negative direction, it is often used in a forward-looking context to suggest potential growth or change.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: I think what it highlights is something that Facebook does really, really well, which you get very quickly when you join Facebook and it's why they're such an execution machine and can build a lot of great product.
keySentence: it's why they're such an execution machine and can build a lot of great product.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 이게 보여주는 건 페이스북이 정말 잘하는 한 가지예요. 페이스북에 합류하면 금방 알 수 있고, 그래서 그들이 실행의 기계(execution machine)처럼 빠르게 움직여 많은 훌륭한 제품을 만들어낼 수 있는 이유예요.
text_zh: 我觉得这说明了脸书(Facebook)有一件事做得特别好：你一加入就能很快感受到，这也就是他们执行力那么强、能做出很多优秀产品的原因。
text_es: Creo que lo que pone de manifiesto es algo que Facebook hace muy, muy bien: se nota enseguida cuando te unes, y por eso son una máquina de ejecución (execution machine) capaz de sacar muchos productos excelentes.
fullContext: Luc is sharing a story about his first major review at Facebook with Mark Zuckerberg, where he was asked directly about when they would see results from his strategy. He explains that this experience taught him about Facebook's core cultural value of focusing on impact rather than activities or effort. This laser focus on measurable outcomes is what makes Facebook an "execution machine" capable of building great products consistently.

vocabulary.definition: The act of carrying out or putting into effect a plan, order, or course of action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, execution refers to the implementation of strategies and operational plans to achieve specific goals and objectives.

insight.nuance: While execution emphasizes the practical application of ideas, it can also imply a sense of urgency and efficiency in achieving results.

vocabulary.definition: To construct or develop something, often referring to products, services, or systems.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech and startup world, 'build' often refers to the process of creating software or products from concept to launch, emphasizing innovation and development.

insight.nuance: The term 'build' can imply a collaborative effort and a focus on iterative improvement, rather than just the final product.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: The second one, which I had I suppose never experienced before, was that they made it very personal. I had these reasons why I couldn't leave. So initially I was excited by the opportunity, but I couldn't see myself moving to California for personal reasons.
keySentence: I couldn't see myself moving to California for personal reasons.
text_ko: 두 번째 건은, 솔직히 전에 겪어본 적이 없는 거였는데, 그들이 접근을 아주 개인적으로 했다는 점이에요. 저는 떠날 수 없는 개인적인 이유들이 있었거든요. 그래서 처음엔 그 기회가 마음에 들었지만, 개인적인 사정 때문에 캘리포니아로 이사할 수 있을 것 같지 않았어요.
text_zh: 第二点，应该是我以前没遇到过的——他们把事情弄得很个人化。我有一些脱不开身的私事。起初我对这个机会很兴奋，但因为这些私人原因，我根本想不到自己会搬去加州。
text_es: La segunda, supongo que nunca la había experimentado antes, fue que lo hicieron muy personal. Tenía mis motivos para no irme. Al principio la oportunidad me entusiasmó, pero no me veía mudándome a California por motivos personales.
fullContext: Lenny asks Luc about being personally recruited by Mark Zuckerberg to join Facebook. Luc is sharing the key lessons he learned from that recruitment process about how to effectively hire top talent. He explains that one crucial strategy was making the recruitment process personal by involving family members, recognizing that career decisions affect entire families, not just the individual being hired.

vocabulary.definition: A favorable set of circumstances that makes it possible to do something, often related to career or business advancement.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, opportunities can refer to potential markets, partnerships, or projects that can lead to growth and profitability.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a positive connotation, suggesting potential benefits, but can also imply risk if not approached carefully.

vocabulary.definition: Factors or motivations that are related to an individual's private life or personal circumstances, rather than professional considerations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, employees may cite personal reasons for decisions such as declining a job offer or leaving a position, which can complicate employer-employee relations.

insight.nuance: This phrase often suggests a level of privacy and may indicate that the individual does not wish to disclose specific details.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: Another great sign of excellence, and this was just through reflecting on stars on the team and thinking what makes them unique, what about them.
keySentence: what makes them unique, what about them.
text_ko: 탁월함을 보여주는 또 하나의 좋은 징표였어요. 팀의 스타들을 떠올리며 그들이 어떤 점에서 독특한지, 무엇이 그들을 특별하게 만드는지 생각해본 결과였죠.
text_zh: 另一个体现卓越的明显信号是：回头看看团队里的那些“明星”，想想到底是什么让他们与众不同。
text_es: Otra gran señal de excelencia: surgió simplemente al pensar en las estrellas del equipo y en qué las hace únicas.
fullContext: Lenny asks Luc about his hiring playbook and what he looks for when evaluating talent. Luc is explaining his concept of "signs of excellence" - indicators that someone has repeatedly demonstrated exceptional performance. He describes one particularly strong signal: when a former manager leaves a company and then returns specifically to recruit that person to their new company, which demonstrates the manager's confidence in that person's abilities.

vocabulary.definition: Excellence refers to the quality of being outstanding or extremely good in a particular area or field. It embodies a standard of superiority that is often pursued in professional and academic environments.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, excellence is often associated with high performance, quality assurance, and continuous improvement, serving as a benchmark for organizational goals and employee evaluations.

insight.nuance: While 'excellence' conveys a positive connotation of achievement, it can also imply pressure to maintain high standards, which may not always be sustainable.

vocabulary.definition: Reflecting involves the process of thinking deeply or carefully about something, often to gain insight or understanding. It can also refer to the act of showing or demonstrating certain qualities or characteristics.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, reflecting is crucial for strategic planning and decision-making, as it allows leaders to assess past performances and adapt future strategies accordingly.

insight.nuance: The term 'reflecting' can imply a thoughtful and analytical approach, contrasting with more impulsive or superficial decision-making processes.

vocabulary.definition: Unique describes something that is one of a kind, distinct from others in a significant way. It emphasizes individuality and special characteristics that set an entity apart.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, uniqueness is often leveraged as a competitive advantage, particularly in branding and product differentiation, to attract customers and create loyalty.

insight.nuance: While 'unique' has a positive connotation, it can also suggest a lack of commonality that may not appeal to all target markets or audiences.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: Growth advice is generally always applicable.
keySentence: Growth advice is generally always applicable.
text_ko: 성장 관련 조언은 대개 거의 항상 쓸 수 있어요.
text_zh: 增长方面的建议大多数情况下都管用。
text_es: Los consejos para crecer suelen servir en casi cualquier contexto.
fullContext: Lenny asks Luc to explain why founders should wait until they have product-market fit before focusing on growth, since this advice comes up frequently. Luc explains that while growth advice itself isn't harmful early on, actively growing a product that doesn't satisfy user needs can be damaging. When you use growth tactics to expose more people to a product that provides a poor experience, you're essentially burning through potential customers who are unlikely to return and try your product again later.

vocabulary.definition: Relevant or suitable to a particular situation or context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'applicable' often refers to rules, regulations, or strategies that can be effectively implemented in a specific scenario or industry.

insight.nuance: While 'applicable' suggests relevance, it may imply that certain conditions must be met for its relevance to hold true.

vocabulary.definition: Guidance or recommendations aimed at fostering business expansion and increasing revenue.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, growth advice can encompass strategies for scaling operations, improving customer acquisition, and enhancing product offerings.

insight.nuance: While growth advice is generally beneficial, its effectiveness can vary based on the specific circumstances of the business and market conditions.

speaker: Luc Levesque
text: I mean, one example would be a company that I worked with. Now, a public company. At the time, they weren't. On day one, walked in, they presented their strategy, their plans, their funnels and their landing pages.
keySentence: they presented their strategy, their plans, their funnels and their landing pages.
text_ko: 예를 들면 제가 일했던 회사 하나가 있어요. 지금은 상장사예요. 당시에는 아니었는데, 첫날 들어가자마자 회사에서 전략과 계획, 퍼널(funnel)과 랜딩 페이지(landing page)를 다 보여줬어요.
text_zh: 就是说，举个例子，我以前合作过的一家公司。现在是上市公司，但那时候还不是。我第一天一进门，他们就把战略、计划、漏斗(funnels)和着陆页(landing pages)全都摆出来了。
text_es: O sea, un ejemplo sería una empresa con la que trabajé. Ahora es pública, pero entonces no lo era. Nada más llegar, me presentaron su estrategia, sus planes, sus embudos (funnels) y sus páginas de aterrizaje (landing pages).
fullContext: Lenny asks for an example of the kind of massive impact that a growth advisor can have in a short time. Luc shares a story about advising a company (now public) where he identified an issue with their approach on his first day. Through his experience, he could quickly spot something that seemed off about their strategy. After a brief conversation and simple recommendation, the company implemented his suggestion and saw significant results within three weeks, demonstrating how years of expertise can be distilled into moments of high-impact advice.

vocabulary.definition: A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term or overall aim.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, strategy refers to the comprehensive approach that a company takes to achieve its objectives, often involving market analysis and resource allocation.

insight.nuance: While 'strategy' implies a well-thought-out plan, it can also suggest flexibility and adaptation to changing circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: A model that represents the customer journey from awareness to conversion, often visualized as a funnel shape.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and sales, funnels are used to track and optimize the stages of customer engagement, from initial contact to final purchase.

insight.nuance: The term 'funnel' emphasizes the narrowing of potential customers as they progress through the stages, highlighting the importance of conversion rates.

vocabulary.definition: Web pages specifically designed to capture visitor information through a form or encourage a specific action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In digital marketing, landing pages are crucial for converting visitors into leads or customers, often linked to specific campaigns or advertisements.

insight.nuance: The effectiveness of a landing page can vary significantly based on its design and content, making it a critical focus for marketers.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: I often say to find your audience's cultural erogenous zones. So what it means is people have things that they either care about or don't, and you're not going to change that.
keySentence: Find your audience's cultural erogenous zones to shape your message effectively.
text_ko: 저는 자주 청중의 문화적 민감 지점(cultural erogenous zones)을 찾아보라고 말해요. 그 말은 사람들이 어떤 것에는 관심을 갖고 어떤 것에는 전혀 관심이 없다는 거고, 그건 바꿀 수 없다는 뜻이에요.
text_zh: 我常说，要找到你受众的文化敏感点(cultural erogenous zones)。意思是人们对某些事很在乎，对另一些事毫不关心，而你改变不了这一点。
text_es: Yo suelo decir que hay que identificar los puntos sensibles culturales (cultural erogenous zones) de tu audiencia. Eso significa que hay temas que a la gente le importan y otros que no, y no vas a poder cambiar eso.
fullContext: Lenny asks Lulu about what helps an idea spread effectively. Lulu introduces her framework of finding your audience's 'cultural erogenous zones' - the topics and values that naturally excite and engage specific groups of people. She explains that rather than trying to change people's existing passions or worldviews (which requires enormous effort), it's much more effective to adapt your message to align with what they already care deeply about.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to the ideas, customs, and social behavior of a particular people or society.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding cultural aspects is vital for businesses operating in diverse markets, as it influences consumer behavior and marketing strategies.

insight.nuance: The term 'cultural' often carries a connotation of depth and complexity, suggesting that it encompasses more than just surface-level traits.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people who are intended to receive or engage with a particular message or content.
vocabulary.businessContext: Identifying and understanding the target audience is essential for effective marketing, product development, and communication strategies.

insight.nuance: The term 'audience' can imply a passive group, but in modern contexts, it often suggests an interactive relationship with the content provider.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: You have to make it memorable and you have to make people want to say it of their own volition. And so what doesn't make them want to say it is doing a favor for a corporation.
keySentence: Make people want to say it of their own volition, not just for a corporation.
text_ko: 기억에 남게 만들어야 하고, 사람들이 스스로 말하고 싶게 만들어야 해요. 그런데 기업을 위해 호의를 베푸는 것처럼 느껴지면 사람들은 말하려 하지 않아요.
text_zh: 你得让它朗朗上口，让人愿意自发地说出来。不会让人自发说的，往往就是那种明显在替公司打广告的东西。
text_es: Hay que hacerlo memorable y lograr que la gente quiera decirlo por iniciativa propia. Lo que no les da ganas de decirlo es que parezca que están haciendo un favor a una empresa.
fullContext: Lenny asks Lulu broadly what she's learned about what helps an idea spread. Lulu explains the fundamental principle that ideas spread when people are intrinsically motivated to repeat them, not when they feel like they're doing a favor for a company. She identifies the key motivations that drive people to share content: bringing joy to others, making people laugh, appearing interesting, or expressing their identity.

vocabulary.definition: Easily remembered or recalled; having qualities that make it significant or noteworthy.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, creating memorable branding or marketing campaigns is crucial for customer retention and brand loyalty.

insight.nuance: While 'memorable' often has a positive connotation, it can also imply that something is overly flashy or gimmicky if not executed well.

vocabulary.definition: The power of using one's will to make decisions or take actions; the act of choosing or deciding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, understanding employee volition is essential for fostering a motivated workforce and encouraging initiative.

insight.nuance: The term 'volition' often carries a formal tone and is typically used in discussions about autonomy and decision-making processes.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: I think if you're a startup your enemy is the status quo. And when you don't take risks, when you minimize risk by doing nothing, the best way to minimize risk is to do nothing. You're letting the status quo win.
keySentence: Minimizing risk by doing nothing lets the status quo win by default.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 스타트업(startup)이라면 가장 큰 적은 바로 현상 유지(status quo)예요. 위험(risk)을 감수하지 않고 아무것도 안 하면서 위험을 줄이려 하면, 결국 현상 유지가 이기도록 만드는 거예요.
text_zh: 我觉得，创业公司最大的敌人就是现状（status quo）。如果你不敢冒险，想通过什么都不做来把风险降到最低——毕竟把风险降到最低最直接的办法就是不行动——那你就是在把主动权拱手让给现状。
text_es: Creo que si eres una startup, tu enemigo es el status quo. Y cuando no tomas riesgos —cuando intentas minimizar el riesgo no haciendo nada— la mejor manera de minimizarlo es no hacer nada; así estás dejando que el status quo gane.
fullContext: Lenny asks Lulu about her philosophy of taking risks as a communications person, noting that many comms professionals tend to be very conservative. Lulu explains why startups in particular must take risks in their communications strategy. She argues that for startups, avoiding risk by doing nothing actually allows their biggest competitor - the status quo - to win without any challenge.

vocabulary.definition: The existing state of affairs or current condition in a particular context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the status quo often refers to established practices, norms, or market conditions that companies may seek to challenge or change.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation in innovative contexts, suggesting stagnation or resistance to change.

vocabulary.definition: To reduce the potential for loss or negative outcomes in a given situation.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, minimizing risk is crucial for decision-making, often involving strategies to avoid financial loss or operational failures.

insight.nuance: While minimizing risk is generally seen as prudent, excessive caution can hinder innovation and growth.

vocabulary.definition: To engage in actions that involve exposure to danger or loss in pursuit of a desired outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: Taking risks is often essential for startups aiming for growth, innovation, and competitive advantage in dynamic markets.

insight.nuance: The phrase suggests a willingness to step outside comfort zones, but it should be balanced with calculated decision-making.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: If your natural audience cares about X and you're offering Y, then it's your job to create the API or to create the bridge from X to Y. With messaging, it's not build it and they will come.
keySentence: Create the API to connect your audience's interests with your offerings.
text_ko: 만약 당신의 자연스러운 청중이 X에 관심이 있고 당신이 Y를 제공하고 있다면, X에서 Y로 연결해 주는 API(응용 프로그램 인터페이스)나 다리를 만드는 건 당신 일이에요. 메시징(messaging)은 ‘만들어 놓으면 사람들이 올 거다’처럼 되는 게 아니에요.
text_zh: 如果你的目标受众关心 X，而你提供的是 Y，那你的工作就是把 X 和 Y 连起来——要么做个接口(API)，要么搭座桥把两者连接起来。至于信息传达(messaging)，别指望“建好了他们就会来”。
text_es: Si a tu audiencia natural le importa X y tú ofreces Y, tienes que crear la interfaz de programación (API) o construir el puente entre X y Y. En materia de mensajería (messaging), no basta con construirlo y esperar que vengan.
fullContext: Lenny asks Lulu to elaborate on her 'cultural erogenous zones' framework and wants examples of it in action. Lulu explains that when there's a mismatch between what your audience cares about and what you're offering, your job is to create connections between them. She emphasizes that the 'build it and they will come' approach rarely works in messaging - it's extremely difficult to create content so compelling that it changes someone's fundamental interests.

vocabulary.definition: To establish a connection or pathway between two distinct elements, concepts, or groups.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'creating the bridge' often refers to developing solutions that connect customer needs with product offerings, facilitating better communication and understanding.

insight.nuance: This phrase implies an active role in problem-solving and innovation, suggesting that one must take initiative rather than waiting for solutions to emerge.

vocabulary.definition: The process of conveying information, ideas, or values through various forms of communication.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'messaging' refers to how a company communicates its brand, products, and values to its target audience, often through marketing strategies and public relations.

insight.nuance: Effective messaging is crucial for engagement and persuasion, and it should be tailored to resonate with the specific audience being addressed.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who receive or engage with a particular message or content.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and communications, understanding the 'audience' is critical for tailoring messages and campaigns to effectively reach and influence potential customers.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a specific demographic or psychographic segment, highlighting the importance of targeted communication strategies.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: First, you have to acknowledge that you're the underdog, and you're not going to use the GE playbook from the 1980s or whatever.
keySentence: Acknowledge being the underdog and avoid the GE playbook from the 1980s.
text_ko: 먼저 자신이 언더독(underdog)이라는 걸 인정해야 해요. 그리고 1980년대 GE식 플레이북(playbook)을 그대로 가져다 쓰진 않을 거예요.
text_zh: 先得承认你处于劣势，别指望还能照搬80年代GE那套玩法（GE playbook）什么的。
text_es: Primero tienes que reconocer que eres el que parte en desventaja (underdog), y que no vas a seguir el manual de GE (playbook) de los años 80 ni nada por el estilo.
fullContext: Lenny asks what works best for underdog startups and companies trying to get attention against incumbent competitors. Lulu explains that underdog companies must first acknowledge their position and avoid trying to use the same strategies that work for established corporations with vast resources. She emphasizes that underdogs can't rely on having extensive resources, deep industry relationships, institutional support, or the ability to benefit from existing market narratives.

vocabulary.definition: To recognize the existence, validity, or truth of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, acknowledging a challenge or a competitor's strengths is crucial for strategic planning and decision-making.

insight.nuance: While it implies acceptance, it can also suggest a proactive approach to addressing issues rather than ignoring them.

vocabulary.definition: A set of strategies or guidelines used to achieve specific objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech, a playbook serves as a reference for best practices and operational procedures, often tailored to the unique needs of the organization.

insight.nuance: While it suggests a structured approach, it can also imply rigidity if not adapted to changing circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: A competitor thought to have little chance of winning or succeeding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, underdogs often represent startups or smaller companies that challenge larger, established firms, appealing to consumers' support for the 'little guy.'

insight.nuance: The term can evoke sympathy and support, but may also suggest a lack of resources or experience compared to competitors.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: So you take out your one-page Google Doc. I feel like most comms problems can be solved with one-page Google Doc.
keySentence: Most comms problems can be solved with a one-page Google Doc, not a first world problem.
text_ko: 그럼 한 페이지짜리 구글 문서(Google Doc)를 꺼내 보세요. 대부분의 소통 문제는 그 한 장으로 해결되는 것 같아요.
text_zh: 你把那份一页的 Google 文档 (Google Doc) 拿出来。我觉得大多数沟通问题，一页文档就能解决。
text_es: Así que sacas tu documento de una página (Google Doc). Me parece que la mayoría de los problemas de comunicación (comms) se resuelven con algo así.
fullContext: Lenny asks Lulu for practical advice on how someone should implement her concentric circles framework for spreading messages to different audience groups. Lulu provides a tactical approach, suggesting people create a simple one-page document to map out their target audiences. She emphasizes keeping it manageable by limiting to five or six audience groups, noting that having more audiences than that indicates the company has moved beyond early-stage challenges.

speaker: Lulu Cheng Meservey
role: EVP Corporate Affairs & CCO, Activision Blizzard
text: LinkedIn is super underutilized because it gets a ton of eyeballs in time, but most of the content sucks. 95% of the content this is not scientific - this is my might estimate.
keySentence: LinkedIn is super underutilized despite having a ton of eyeballs.
text_ko: LinkedIn은 정말 활용도가 낮아요. 사람들이 많이 보긴 하는데 대부분의 콘텐츠가 형편없어서 제대로 활용되지 않고 있어요. 제 대략적인 추정으로는 그중 95%는 과학적 근거가 없어요.
text_zh: 领英（LinkedIn）没被好好利用，明明能带来大量曝光，但大部分内容质量很差。我估计大概95%的内容都是这样——这不是科学结论，只是我的粗略估计。
text_es: LinkedIn está muy infrautilizado: consigue muchísima visibilidad con el tiempo, pero el problema es que la mayor parte del contenido es de baja calidad. Diría que el 95% de ese contenido no está basado en evidencia científica —es una estimación mía—.
fullContext: Lenny mentions that he gets more newsletter traffic from LinkedIn than Twitter and asks Lulu for her perspective on this platform choice. Lulu explains why LinkedIn represents an underutilized opportunity for professionals and founders. She argues that while LinkedIn receives significant user attention and engagement, the vast majority of content is low-quality social pleasantries rather than genuinely valuable information, creating an opportunity for those who post substantial content.

vocabulary.definition: Not being used to its full potential or capacity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an underutilized resource, such as a platform or tool, indicates that there is significant untapped value that could be harnessed for greater efficiency or effectiveness.

insight.nuance: This term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that opportunities are being missed due to lack of engagement or investment.

vocabulary.definition: Information or material created and shared for communication, marketing, or educational purposes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of digital marketing and social media, high-quality content is crucial for engaging audiences and driving brand awareness.

insight.nuance: The term can imply varying levels of quality; 'content' alone may suggest a neutral or low-quality standard unless specified otherwise.

vocabulary.definition: An approximate calculation or judgment regarding the value, number, quantity, or extent of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: Estimates are commonly used in project management and financial forecasting to provide a basis for decision-making and resource allocation.

insight.nuance: While estimates are inherently uncertain, they should be based on informed assumptions to maintain credibility.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: The first one is you might land, but you might not expand. As in your eagerness for acquiring, you might have actually given away a lot at less and you have given the farm away, but you don't have anything to expand to.
keySentence: You might land, but you might not expand if you give the farm away.
text_ko: 첫 번째는 딜을 따내는 건(land) 할 수 있어도 그걸 확장(expand)할 게 없을 수 있다는 거예요. 고객을 확보하려는 욕심에 너무 싸게, 많이 퍼줘서 결국 키워갈 자원이 남지 않을 수 있어요.
text_zh: 第一种情况是，你可能把单子拿下了，但扩展不了。因为太急着争取客户，你可能以很低的代价把很多东西都让出去，几乎把家底都掏空了，结果连可供扩张的空间都没留下。
text_es: Lo primero es que puedes conseguir entrar (land), pero quizá no puedas expandirte (expand). En tu afán por captar clientes (acquiring) puedes haber regalado mucho por muy poco, haberlo vendido demasiado barato, y al final no tienes a dónde expandirte.
fullContext: Lenny asks Madhavan about common traps that founders fall into when building their companies. Madhavan is explaining the specific traps that 'disruptor archetype' companies face - those that focus heavily on customer acquisition and market share. He's describing how companies that are overly focused on landing new customers often make the mistake of offering too much value upfront at discounted prices, leaving nothing valuable to sell later for expansion revenue.

vocabulary.definition: The act of obtaining or gaining possession of something, often through purchase or merger.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, acquiring typically refers to the process of one company purchasing another company or its assets to enhance its market position or capabilities.

insight.nuance: While acquiring often has a positive connotation of growth and expansion, it can also imply risk if the acquisition does not yield expected benefits.

vocabulary.definition: To increase in size, scope, or quantity; to grow or develop further.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, expand often refers to a company's efforts to enter new markets, increase product lines, or enhance operational capacity.

insight.nuance: Expand suggests a proactive approach to growth, but it can also imply overextension if not managed carefully.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: When we talk about pricing, many people quickly gravitate to dollar figures. That's just a price point, that's a dollar figure. But when we think about price, we think about it as a measure.
keySentence: Price is a measure of value, not just a dollar figure.
text_ko: 가격 얘기를 할 때 많은 사람들이 금세 달러 액수에만 끌려가요. 그건 그냥 가격대(price point), 달러 금액(dollar figure)에 불과해요. 하지만 가격을 생각할 때는 그걸 하나의 측정(measure)으로 봐야 해요.
text_zh: 很多人一谈到定价就立刻盯着具体金额看，那只是个价格点、就是个数字而已。但我们在考虑价格时，是把它当作一种衡量标准。
text_es: Cuando hablamos de precios, mucha gente tiende a fijarse enseguida en la cifra en dólares. Eso es solo un punto de precio (price point), simplemente una cifra. Pero cuando pensamos en el precio, lo vemos como una medida.
fullContext: Lenny asks Madhavan to introduce the concept of pricing strategy and how to think about it differently. Madhavan explains that most people think about pricing as just dollar amounts, but he argues that price should be viewed as a measurement tool - similar to how liters measure volume, price measures value. This reframing helps entrepreneurs understand that pricing conversations are really about validating whether customers actually want and will purchase their product, which he calls the willingness to pay conversation.

vocabulary.definition: To measure is to ascertain the size, amount, or degree of something, typically using a standard unit of measurement. In business, it often refers to quantifying performance metrics or financial indicators.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, measuring performance is essential for evaluating success and making informed decisions. Metrics such as sales figures, customer satisfaction scores, and market share are commonly analyzed.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a systematic and objective evaluation, often implying the use of data or analytics.

vocabulary.definition: A price point refers to a specific price at which a product or service is offered, often used to categorize products within a market. It helps businesses identify target markets and consumer segments.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding price points is vital for pricing strategies and market positioning, as they can influence consumer perceptions and purchasing decisions.

insight.nuance: The term can carry implications about market segmentation and consumer psychology, suggesting that certain price points may appeal to specific demographics.

vocabulary.definition: To gravitate means to be attracted to or to move toward something, often in a natural or instinctive way. In a business context, it refers to consumer tendencies or preferences.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, understanding what consumers gravitate towards can inform marketing strategies and product development, helping companies align their offerings with customer desires.

insight.nuance: The term often implies an unconscious or instinctual attraction, suggesting that choices may not always be purely rational.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: you think that pricing high actually indicates value, but your price is so high that you actually start hurting your acquisition.
keySentence: your price is so high that you actually start hurting your acquisition.
text_ko: 가격을 높게 책정하면 가치가 있다는 신호라고 생각하실 수 있어요. 그런데 가격이 너무 비싸면 오히려 실제로 고객 확보(acquisition)에 지장을 줘요.
text_zh: 你以为把价格定高能显示价值，但价格定得太高，反而会影响你的获客(acquisition)。
text_es: Crees que fijar un precio alto transmite valor, pero lo subes tanto que terminas perjudicando la captación de clientes (customer acquisition).
fullContext: Madhavan continues explaining founder traps, now focusing on 'moneymaker archetype' companies that prioritize monetization over acquisition. He's describing the price premium paradox - a common mistake where founders believe that higher prices automatically signal higher value to customers. However, when prices become too high, they actually harm customer acquisition because the product becomes unaffordable or irrelevant to most potential buyers.

vocabulary.definition: The act of obtaining or gaining possession of something, typically referring to the purchase of one company by another.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, acquisition often refers to a strategic move to enhance market share, diversify offerings, or gain competitive advantages through the purchase of another company.

insight.nuance: While 'acquisition' can imply a straightforward purchase, it often carries connotations of strategic planning and long-term vision in corporate contexts.

vocabulary.definition: To point out or show something, often used to suggest a conclusion or inference based on evidence.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business analysis, data that indicates trends or consumer behavior can guide strategic decisions and marketing approaches.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a level of certainty or evidence, making it more suitable for formal reports or discussions rather than casual conversation.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: Pricing needs to sit in finance, because my view was finance would be the counterbalance to sales... you can set all the pricing you want, it's human having a human conversation.
keySentence: you can set all the pricing you want, it's human having a human conversation.
text_ko: 가격 책정(pricing)은 재무(finance) 쪽에 있어야 해요. 제 생각엔 재무가 영업(sales)에 대한 균형추 역할을 해 줄 수 있기 때문이에요... 원하는 대로 가격을 다 정할 수는 있지만, 결국엔 사람과 사람 사이의 대화예요.
text_zh: 定价最好放在财务（finance）部门，我觉得财务能对销售（sales）起到制衡作用。你想怎么定价都可以，但归根结底还是人跟人谈出来的。
text_es: La fijación de precios (pricing) tiene que estar en finanzas, porque en mi opinión finanzas sería el contrapeso al equipo de ventas; puedes fijar todos los precios que quieras, pero al final es una conversación entre personas.
fullContext: Lenny asks which department should own pricing strategy within an organization. Madhavan shares how his thinking has evolved over time. He explains that he previously believed pricing should sit in finance because finance teams could serve as a counterbalance to sales teams, who might be tempted to negotiate prices down during deal conversations. The phrase 'checks and balance' refers to creating organizational controls to prevent any one department from making pricing decisions that could hurt the company's profitability.

vocabulary.definition: To offset or balance the effect of something; to provide a compensating force or influence.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, counterbalancing often refers to the need to balance competing interests, such as sales and finance, to ensure sustainable decision-making.

insight.nuance: The term implies a need for equilibrium and is often used in contexts where opposing forces must be managed carefully.

vocabulary.definition: A spoken exchange of thoughts, ideas, or feelings between two or more people; a dialogue.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business environment, effective conversation is crucial for collaboration, negotiation, and relationship-building among team members and stakeholders.

insight.nuance: While it generally refers to informal dialogue, in business, it can also imply a strategic discussion aimed at achieving specific outcomes.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: What if that was available to you instantaneously? Oh, you have now just created a need, right?
keySentence: Oh, you have now just created a need, right?
text_ko: 그게 즉시 제공된다면 어떨까요? 아, 그러면 지금 막 필요를 만들어낸 거예요, 그렇죠?
text_zh: 如果那能立刻用上呢？哦，你不就刚刚创造了一个需求吗？
text_es: ¿Y si eso estuviera disponible al instante? Con eso acabas de crear una necesidad, ¿no?
fullContext: Lenny asks about mastering negotiations, and Madhavan is explaining one of three key components: value selling. Specifically, he's teaching how to 'create needs' rather than just discover them during sales conversations. He provides a concrete example of how a marketing automation AI company should approach potential customers by first understanding their current time-consuming processes, then positioning their solution as an immediate alternative to create urgency and need.

vocabulary.definition: Occurring or done immediately, without any delay.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology and service industries, the ability to deliver solutions instantaneously can be a key competitive advantage, enhancing customer satisfaction and operational efficiency.

insight.nuance: While it suggests speed, it can also imply a lack of thoroughness if not managed properly, so context is important.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: 72% of innovations actually fail from a monetization or commercial perspective, simply because entrepreneurs or companies did not do the check earlier on.
keySentence: 72% of innovations actually fail from a monetization or commercial perspective.
text_ko: 혁신의 72%가 수익화(monetization)나 상업적 관점(commercial perspective)에서 실패해요. 단순히 창업가나 기업들이 그걸 미리 점검하지 않았기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 其实有72%的创新在变现(monetization)或商业化(commercial)上会失败，原因很简单：创业者或公司没在早期做过相应的验证。
text_es: El 72% de las innovaciones fracasa a la hora de monetizar (monetization) o de comercializarse, simplemente porque los emprendedores y las empresas no lo validaron a tiempo.
fullContext: Lenny asks what motivated Madhavan to write his book 'Monetizing Innovation.' Madhavan explains that he was frustrated by companies following a 'spray and pray' approach - building products first and then hoping to monetize them later. He shares a key statistic from their research showing that nearly three-quarters of innovations fail commercially because companies don't validate customer willingness to pay early in the development process. This failure rate could be reduced if companies tested pricing concepts before building the full product.

vocabulary.definition: The process of converting an asset, service, or product into a source of revenue.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, monetization strategies are critical for startups to ensure that their innovations can generate profit and sustain operations.

insight.nuance: Monetization often implies a strategic approach to generating income, and it is important to consider various revenue models to avoid pitfalls.

vocabulary.definition: A particular attitude or way of considering something; a viewpoint.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, having multiple perspectives can lead to more comprehensive decision-making and innovation strategies.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a subjective viewpoint, so it's important to clarify which perspective is being referenced in discussions.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals who start and run their own businesses, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit.
vocabulary.businessContext: Entrepreneurs are often seen as key drivers of innovation and economic growth, particularly in startup ecosystems.

insight.nuance: The term can carry connotations of creativity and risk-taking, and is often associated with a proactive approach to business challenges.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: The right way to think about an ROI model is to actually co-create it with your customers from day one, which means agree and validate on the assumptions and the inputs. So like, 'Hey, how long does this process take today?
keySentence: Co-create it with your customers to validate on the assumptions of an ROI model.
text_ko: ROI 모델(ROI model)을 제대로 생각하려면 처음부터 고객과 실제로 함께 만들어가야 해요. 즉 가정(assumptions)과 입력값(inputs)에 대해 합의하고 검증하는 거예요. 예를 들어, "요즘 이 프로세스는 보통 얼마나 걸리나요?"처럼요.
text_zh: 正确的做法是把ROI模型(ROI model)从第一天就和客户一起共创，也就是说要对那些假设和输入先达成一致并验证。比如，你可以问：“现在这个流程一般要花多长时间？”
text_es: La forma correcta de abordar un modelo de retorno de la inversión (ROI) es, en realidad, desarrollarlo junto con tus clientes desde el primer día; eso significa ponerse de acuerdo y validar las suposiciones y los datos de entrada (inputs). Por ejemplo: "Oye, ¿cuánto tiempo lleva este proceso hoy?"
fullContext: Madhavan is continuing his explanation of value selling techniques within negotiation mastery. He's addressing a common founder mistake: showing up with a pre-built ROI (Return on Investment) model after a proof of concept is complete. Instead, he advocates for co-creating the ROI model with customers from the beginning by getting them to agree on all the underlying assumptions and data inputs, making them much more likely to accept the final calculated value.

vocabulary.definition: To collaboratively develop or design a product, service, or solution with stakeholders, particularly customers or users.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, co-creation emphasizes the importance of customer involvement in the development process to ensure that the final outcome meets their needs and expectations.

insight.nuance: Co-creating implies a partnership and shared responsibility, contrasting with traditional models where the company solely dictates the development process.

vocabulary.definition: To confirm or substantiate the accuracy, effectiveness, or legitimacy of a concept, idea, or product through testing or feedback.
vocabulary.businessContext: Validation is crucial in business settings to ensure that assumptions and hypotheses about a product or market are correct before significant resources are allocated.

insight.nuance: Validation carries a sense of rigor and thoroughness, often involving empirical evidence, and should not be confused with mere approval or agreement.

vocabulary.definition: Beliefs or statements taken for granted without proof, often serving as the foundation for further reasoning or decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business strategy and planning, assumptions are critical as they influence projections, models, and overall strategy; however, they must be regularly reviewed and validated.

insight.nuance: Assumptions can be risky if unexamined, as they may lead to flawed strategies or outcomes if proven incorrect.

vocabulary.definition: The resources, data, or information that are fed into a system, process, or model to produce an output or result.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business analytics and project management, inputs are essential for creating models, forecasts, or strategies, as they directly impact the quality and relevance of the outputs.

insight.nuance: The term 'inputs' can imply a variety of resources, including quantitative data, qualitative insights, or even human effort, and should be specified for clarity.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: You cannot prioritize a product roadmap without having a willingness to pay conversation. If you're just prioritizing based on what you think or what you feel or technical resources, you're getting it wrong.
keySentence: Prioritizing without willingness to pay means you're getting it wrong.
text_ko: 제품 로드맵(product roadmap)의 우선순위를 정하려면 지불 의사(willingness to pay)에 대한 대화가 꼭 있어야 해요. 단지 개인적 판단이나 직감, 기술 자원(technical resources)만으로 우선순위를 매기면 잘못하고 있는 거예요.
text_zh: 在没有就用户的付费意愿(willingness to pay)进行对话之前，别急着给产品路线图(product roadmap)排优先级。要是你只是凭自己的想法、主观感觉，或仅看技术资源来排，那就错了。
text_es: No puedes priorizar la hoja de ruta del producto (product roadmap) sin antes hablar sobre la disposición a pagar (willingness to pay). Si solo priorizas en base a lo que piensas, a tus intuiciones o a los recursos técnicos, estás cometiendo un error.
fullContext: Lenny asks for examples of companies that successfully used willingness to pay conversations. Madhavan shares the story of a two-sided marketplace that tested customer willingness to pay for different features before building them. He emphasizes that product teams cannot effectively prioritize their roadmaps using only internal opinions or technical constraints - they need customer willingness to pay data. This insight helps teams focus their limited resources on building the 20% of features that drive 80% of customer value and payment intent.

vocabulary.definition: To arrange or deal with tasks or items in order of importance or urgency.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and project management, prioritizing is essential for allocating resources effectively and ensuring that critical tasks are completed first to meet strategic goals.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a systematic approach to decision-making, contrasting with arbitrary or emotional choices.

vocabulary.definition: The maximum amount a customer is prepared to spend on a product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding a customer's willingness to pay is crucial for pricing strategies and market positioning, as it directly influences revenue potential and profitability.

insight.nuance: This concept often reflects perceived value and can vary significantly among different customer segments.

vocabulary.definition: A strategic plan that outlines the vision, direction, and milestones for a product or project over time.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology and startups, a product roadmap serves as a communication tool that aligns stakeholders on priorities and timelines for development and release.

insight.nuance: While it provides a high-level overview, a roadmap should remain flexible to adapt to changing market conditions and feedback.

vocabulary.definition: The tools, technologies, and human expertise required to develop and support a product or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech startups, having adequate technical resources is vital for product development, ensuring that teams can effectively implement and maintain solutions.

insight.nuance: This term often implies a focus on the capabilities and skills of the team, as well as the infrastructure needed to support technical initiatives.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: So we coached him to go in with a hundred K, plus 10% on any incremental value that you bring, or it's a 500K fixed. So now this is actually a great situation in negotiation.
keySentence: this is actually a great situation in negotiation.
text_ko: 그래서 우리는 그에게 10만 달러(100K)로 들어가되, 거기에 창출하는 추가 가치(incremental value)에 대해 10%를 더 얹거나, 아니면 50만 달러(500K) 고정(fixed)으로 하라고 조언했어요. 그래서 지금 이건 협상에서 정말 좋은 상황이에요.
text_zh: 所以我们就跟他建议，先出10万（100K），外加你带来的任何增量价值的10%，要不就走固定50万（500K，fixed）。现在这种谈判局面其实挺有利的。
text_es: Por eso le recomendamos que entrara con 100 K, más un 10% sobre cualquier valor incremental (incremental value) que aportara, o que fuera con 500 K fijo (fixed). Así que ahora está en una posición de negociación excelente.
fullContext: Madhavan is sharing a specific negotiation hack for founders who lack courage to ask for higher prices. He describes coaching a founder who believed the customer's budget was $100K but felt their product could justify $500K. Instead of choosing one price, he suggests offering two pricing model options: a lower base price with outcome-based upside, or a higher fixed price. This approach shifts the conversation from pure price negotiation to value discussion.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to small, gradual changes or additions rather than large, significant shifts.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'incremental' often describes improvements or increases in performance, revenue, or product features that occur over time, rather than through a complete overhaul.

insight.nuance: While 'incremental' suggests a positive, manageable approach to growth, it can imply a lack of boldness or innovation if overused.

vocabulary.definition: The process of discussing terms and reaching an agreement between two or more parties.
vocabulary.businessContext: Negotiation is a critical skill in business, often employed in contract discussions, salary agreements, and partnership formations to achieve mutually beneficial outcomes.

insight.nuance: Negotiation can carry a connotation of conflict or competition, but it also implies collaboration and compromise, depending on the context.

vocabulary.definition: To train or instruct someone in a particular skill or area of knowledge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, being 'coached' often refers to receiving guidance or mentorship to enhance performance, especially in areas like sales, leadership, or negotiation tactics.

insight.nuance: The term 'coached' suggests a supportive and developmental approach, which can be more positive than simply 'trained' or 'taught'.

vocabulary.definition: A set of circumstances in which one finds oneself; a state of affairs.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'situation' often refers to the current state of a project, market conditions, or organizational challenges that require strategic analysis and decision-making.

insight.nuance: The word 'situation' can imply complexity or difficulty, so it is often used in contexts where careful consideration is needed.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: People are absolutely meaningless, relatively super smart. What I mean by that is, if you go and ask someone, 'How much should I charge?' You'll get a meaningless answer.
keySentence: You'll get a meaningless answer.
text_ko: 사람들은 절대적으로 보면 무의미하지만, 상대적으로 보면 굉장히 똑똑해요. 제 말은, 누군가에게 '얼마를 청구해야 할까요?'라고 물어보면 아무런 의미 없는 답만 돌아온다는 거예요.
text_zh: 人的意见单独拿出来根本没意义，虽然他们听起来都很聪明。我是说，如果你去问别人“我应该收多少钱？”，你得到的答案基本没什么参考价值。
text_es: La gente, tomada de forma aislada, no sirve de mucho; aunque comparativamente puedan parecer súper listos. Me refiero a que si vas y le preguntas a alguien "¿Cuánto debería cobrar?", te van a dar una respuesta sin sentido.
fullContext: Lenny asks how to actually conduct willingness to pay conversations with customers. Madhavan explains his first method for having these conversations without directly asking customers to set prices. He uses a humorous phrase to describe how people struggle with absolute pricing questions but excel at relative comparisons. Instead of asking 'What should I charge?', he suggests asking customers to compare your product's value to established products like Salesforce, using an indexed scale where the competitor equals 100 and customers rate where your product falls relative to that benchmark.

vocabulary.definition: Lacking significance or purpose; devoid of value or importance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, a 'meaningless' response may indicate that the information provided does not contribute to decision-making or strategic planning.

insight.nuance: While 'meaningless' can imply a lack of value, it may also suggest that the context or criteria for evaluation were not adequately defined.

vocabulary.definition: To set a price for a product or service, or to demand payment for it.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, determining how much to charge for goods or services is a critical aspect of pricing strategy that can influence profitability and market competitiveness.

insight.nuance: The term 'charge' can also imply a transactional nature, and in some contexts, it may carry a negative connotation if perceived as excessive or unfair.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: Yeah, AI pricing is very different from the previous vintage of companies. Why is that so?
keySentence: AI pricing is very different from the previous vintage of companies.
text_ko: 맞아요. AI 가격 책정(AI pricing)은 이전 세대의 기업들과는 확연히 달라요. 왜 그런 걸까요?
text_zh: 是啊，AI 定价 (AI pricing) 跟以前那批公司的定价逻辑完全不一样，为什么会这样？
text_es: Sí, la fijación de precios en la IA (AI) es muy distinta a la de las empresas de la generación anterior. ¿Por qué ocurre eso?
fullContext: Lenny asks how AI pricing differs from traditional software pricing strategies. Madhavan explains that AI companies face fundamentally different challenges compared to previous generations of SaaS companies. Unlike traditional software companies that could focus on growth first and monetization later, AI companies must address pricing from day one due to two key factors: significant cost dynamics from AI infrastructure, and the need to capture value immediately before training customers to expect low prices.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: Segmentation needs to be based on what customers need, what they value, and what are they willing to pay for, and how do you productize package to different segments.
keySentence: Segmentation must focus on customer needs to productize to segments.
text_ko: 세분화(segmentation)는 고객이 무엇을 필요로 하는지, 무엇을 가치 있게 여기는지, 무엇에 기꺼이 비용을 지불할지를 기준으로 해야 하고, 그걸 바탕으로 각 세그먼트별로 어떻게 제품화(productize)하고 패키지(package)로 묶을지 결정해야 해요.
text_zh: 做客户细分(segmentation)得从客户真正需要什么、他们看重什么、愿意为哪些买单出发，然后想清楚怎么把产品/服务产品化(productize)并打包给不同的细分群体。
text_es: La segmentación debe basarse en lo que los clientes necesitan, en lo que valoran y en qué estarían dispuestos a pagar, y en cómo convertir la oferta en producto (productize) y empaquetarla para distintos segmentos.
fullContext: Lenny asks why segmentation is so important for pricing strategy. Madhavan explains that most companies misunderstand segmentation, treating it as a demographics or persona exercise rather than a needs-based approach. He argues that true segmentation must be based on customer needs, values, and willingness to pay, and companies must build different products for different segments rather than building one product and trying to position it differently. The phrase 'you already lost the battle' emphasizes that trying to make one product appeal to all segments is a losing strategy.

vocabulary.definition: Segmentation refers to the process of dividing a market into distinct groups of consumers with similar needs or characteristics. This allows businesses to tailor their marketing strategies to specific segments for better engagement and effectiveness.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and marketing, segmentation is crucial for identifying target audiences and developing personalized marketing campaigns that resonate with different consumer groups.

insight.nuance: Segmentation often implies a strategic approach to understanding customer diversity, and it is best used when discussing targeted marketing efforts rather than general audience descriptions.

vocabulary.definition: To productize means to take a service or idea and develop it into a standardized product that can be marketed and sold. This process often involves defining features, pricing, and packaging for the product.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, productizing is crucial for transforming innovative ideas into market-ready solutions that can be scaled and sold to customers.

insight.nuance: The term carries a connotation of simplification and standardization, and it is best used when discussing the transition from concept to marketable product rather than ongoing service offerings.

speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
text: We usually say how you charge is way more important than how much you charge. Take a quick example and then bring the point home and then we can talk about why this is actually essential.
keySentence: How you charge is more important than how much you charge.
text_ko: 보통은 '얼마를 받느냐'보다 '어떻게 받느냐'가 훨씬 더 중요하다고 말해요. 간단한 예를 하나 들어 요점을 확실히 보여드리고, 그다음에 왜 이게 실제로 필수적인지 이야기해볼게요.
text_zh: 我们经常说，你怎么收费比收多少钱重要得多。我先举个简单的例子，然后把这个道理说透，接下来咱们再聊聊为什么这点其实特别关键。
text_es: Siempre decimos que cómo cobras es mucho más importante que cuánto cobras. Te doy un ejemplo rápido para que se entienda bien el punto, y después hablamos de por qué esto es realmente clave.
fullContext: Lenny introduces the topic of pricing models - the mechanisms companies use to charge customers rather than just the amount they charge. Madhavan emphasizes that the pricing model (how you charge) is more critical than the specific price point (how much you charge). He's about to illustrate this concept with examples from Michelin tires and other companies that transformed their businesses by changing their charging method rather than their prices. The phrase 'bring the point home' means to make the concept clear and convincing through examples.

vocabulary.definition: Absolutely necessary; extremely important.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'essential' often refers to critical components or strategies that are vital for success and operational efficiency.

insight.nuance: While 'essential' denotes necessity, it can imply a level of urgency or priority that may not be present with synonyms like 'important.'

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: If you ever find yourself saying something like, that's not my job, that's probably a thing you should do. And you know what?
keySentence: that's probably a thing you should do.
text_ko: 혹시 '그건 제 일이 아니에요'라고 말하는 자신을 발견한다면, 그 일은 오히려 당신이 해야 할 일일 가능성이 커요. 그리고 있잖아요?
text_zh: 如果你发现自己会说“那不是我的工作”，那很可能正是你该做的事。你知道吗？
text_es: Si alguna vez te sorprendes diciendo "eso no es mi trabajo", probablemente sea justo lo que deberías hacer. ¿Y sabes qué?
fullContext: Lenny asks Maggie about the common threads she's seen across the best product managers she's worked with, hired, and managed. Maggie explains her third key trait, which she calls 'carrying the water' - being willing to do the unglamorous work that needs to get done regardless of whose official responsibility it is. She emphasizes that PMs who succeed are those who focus on getting work done rather than getting frustrated about job boundaries.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project, and you just have to keep that optimism going.
keySentence: you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project
text_ko: 여러분은 보통 팀에서 감정적 중심이 되는 경우가 많아요. 팀원들이 동기부여를 잃지 않고 계속 흥미를 느끼며 프로젝트에 진심으로 몰입하게 만드는 게 여러분의 역할이에요. 그리고 그 낙관적인 분위기를 계속 이어가야 해요.
text_zh: 你很多时候是团队的情绪中心，你的工作就是让大家有干劲、保持热情、继续认同并投入这个项目，而且你得一直把这种乐观情绪维持下去。
text_es: A menudo eres el centro emocional del equipo, y te toca mantener a la gente motivada, entusiasmada y comprometida con el proyecto; tienes que seguir transmitiendo ese optimismo.
fullContext: Lenny asks Maggie about the common threads across successful product managers. Maggie is explaining the concept of 'carrying the water' as a PM - being willing to do work that technically isn't your job. She describes how PMs often serve as the emotional center of their teams, responsible for maintaining team morale and motivation while also being willing to jump into any role needed to ensure project success.

vocabulary.definition: Driven to take action or achieve goals, often fueled by personal ambition or external incentives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being motivated is crucial for employees to meet targets, enhance productivity, and contribute positively to team dynamics.

insight.nuance: While 'motivated' generally has a positive connotation, it can imply pressure or stress if the motivation stems from external demands rather than personal desire.

vocabulary.definition: A hopeful and positive outlook on future outcomes, often leading to proactive behavior.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business, optimism can foster innovation and resilience, encouraging teams to pursue ambitious projects despite uncertainties.

insight.nuance: While optimism is generally seen as beneficial, excessive optimism can lead to unrealistic expectations and poor decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: To accept or adopt an idea, plan, or project, often implying a commitment to its success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, having team members 'bought into' a project is essential for collaboration and achieving collective goals, as it fosters a sense of ownership and accountability.

insight.nuance: This phrase often conveys a deeper level of commitment than simply agreeing with an idea; it suggests emotional and intellectual investment.

vocabulary.definition: The focal point of emotional support and motivation within a group, often responsible for influencing the morale and cohesion of the team.
vocabulary.businessContext: In team dynamics, being the emotional center means facilitating communication, resolving conflicts, and ensuring a positive work environment, which is vital for maintaining productivity.

insight.nuance: While being the emotional center can be a strength, it may also lead to burnout if the individual feels solely responsible for the team's emotional well-being.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: So many people in the spec or the one pager or something will say, okay, here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move. Awesome.
keySentence: Here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move.
text_ko: 스펙(spec)이나 원페이저(one-pager) 같은 문서에 많은 사람들이 “제가 신경 쓰는 지표(metric)는 이거고, 이걸 움직이고 싶어요”라고 적어놔요. 좋아요.
text_zh: 很多人在需求文档（spec）或一页总结（one pager）之类的文档里会说，“好，这是我关心的指标，这是我想去推动的。太好了。”
text_es: Mucha gente, en la especificación (spec) o en un resumen de una página (one pager) o algo así, dirá: “vale, ésta es la métrica que me importa. Esto es lo que quiero mover. Genial.”
fullContext: Lenny asks Maggie about the three traits that make great product managers. Maggie is explaining her second trait: following up on results. She describes how many PMs set metrics and track them initially, but the exceptional ones remember to circle back and report on what actually happened with their launches and initiatives, which is surprisingly rare and highly valued by leadership.
