text: The thing that is hard to really understand for first-time founders that hit breakout success with a consumer product is how draining and how spread thin you get, because everything breaks. Everything that you built needs to be substituted almost every three days.
keySentence: Breakout success leaves founders spread thin as everything breaks.
text_ko: 소비자용 제품(consumer product)으로 대박 성공(breakout success)을 거둔 첫 창업자들이 진짜로 이해하기 어려운 건, 얼마나 지치고 일이 여기저기 분산돼 감당하기 힘들어지는지예요. 모든 게 계속 망가져서 만든 것들을 거의 사흘마다 다시 대체해야 할 정도예요.
text_zh: 第一次创业就做出爆款消费产品的创始人很难理解的一点是，你会被榨干，精力被分散到各个地方，因为什么都会出问题。你搭建的每个系统基本上每三天就得重新来一遍。
text_es: Lo que es difícil de entender para los fundadores primerizos que pegan el golpe con un producto de consumo es lo agotador que se vuelve todo y cómo te quedas sin recursos, porque todo se rompe. Todo lo que construiste hay que cambiarlo prácticamente cada tres días.
fullContext: Lenny asks what other lasting lessons Nikita learned from building tbh that he brings to new apps today. Nikita explains the intense operational challenges that come with viral success - when your app suddenly scales massively, all your systems break and need to be replaced constantly. This creates absolute chaos that founders need to be prepared for, requiring ruthless prioritization to keep the app running as it grows exponentially.

vocabulary.definition: A significant and rapid achievement in popularity or sales, often surpassing initial expectations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, a breakout success typically refers to a product or service that quickly gains traction in the market, leading to substantial revenue growth and brand recognition.

insight.nuance: This term conveys a sense of unexpected achievement and can imply both excitement and pressure to maintain momentum.

vocabulary.definition: Causing fatigue or exhaustion, often due to excessive demands or stress.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups, the term draining can describe the emotional and physical toll that rapid growth and constant problem-solving take on founders and their teams.

insight.nuance: While it often refers to physical exhaustion, it can also imply mental fatigue and the challenges of sustaining high levels of performance.

vocabulary.definition: To be stretched too far in terms of resources, time, or attention, leading to diminished effectiveness.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, being spread thin can occur when a team takes on too many projects or responsibilities, resulting in reduced quality of work and increased stress among team members.

insight.nuance: This phrase often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that the individual or team may not be able to perform optimally due to overcommitment.

speaker: Nikita Bier
text: I was sleeping three hours a day for three months. It was extraordinarily difficult to do it all. Our team was also relentless though. They would come over to my house, 9:00 AM, stay until midnight and just do that seven days a week.
keySentence: Our team was relentless, working from morning until midnight every day.
text_ko: 세 달 동안 하루에 세 시간밖에 못 잤어요. 모든 걸 다 해내기가 정말 힘들었어요. 그래도 우리 팀은 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요. 매일 오전 9시에 제 집에 와서 자정까지 머물면서 주 7일 내내 그렇게 일했어요.
text_zh: 那三个月我每天只睡三个小时，真的是太难熬了。不过我们团队也是拼了命的，他们早上九点就到我家，一直干到半夜，就这样一周七天不停歇。
text_es: Dormía tres horas al día durante tres meses. Era increíblemente difícil hacer todo eso. Pero nuestro equipo también era imparable. Se aparecían en mi casa a las 9 de la mañana, se quedaban hasta medianoche y así siete días a la semana, sin parar.
fullContext: Lenny asks what it was like managing viral growth while simultaneously fighting false rumors that Gas was used for human trafficking. Nikita describes the intense physical and mental demands of scaling a viral app while dealing with crisis management. The human trafficking hoax threatened to kill the company, requiring around-the-clock effort from the entire team to combat false information spreading faster than their app itself.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by an unyielding or persistent attitude, often in pursuit of a goal or objective.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a relentless approach can be crucial for overcoming challenges and achieving success, particularly in competitive environments or during product development.

insight.nuance: While 'relentless' conveys determination, it can also imply a lack of consideration for balance or well-being, so it should be used carefully.

vocabulary.definition: To a very great degree; exceptionally or unusually.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, describing a challenge or achievement as extraordinarily difficult or successful emphasizes its significance and the effort required.

insight.nuance: This term often carries a positive connotation, suggesting that the subject is noteworthy or remarkable, making it suitable for highlighting exceptional cases.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: And some folks, myself included at certain points, swung way too far on the outcomes train and forgot that output is an indicator of that.
keySentence: swung way too far on the outcomes train and forgot that output is an indicator of that.
text_ko: 어떤 분들은, 저도 어떤 시점에는 그랬는데, 성과(outcomes)에 너무 치중하다 보니 산출물(output)이 그걸 나타내는 지표라는 걸 잊었어요.
text_zh: 有些人——包括我有时候也会——在追求结果(outcomes)上走得太远，忘了产出(output)只是个指标而已。
text_es: Algunos —y me incluyo en ciertos momentos— nos obsesionamos tanto con los resultados (outcomes) que olvidamos que la producción (output) es un indicador de eso.
fullContext: Lenny asks Nikita about lessons she's learned about building successful teams. Nikita explains a common problem she's observed across companies where teams become too focused on outcomes (like setting goals and OKRs) while neglecting output (actual shipping and execution). She argues that while having the right goals is important, teams also need to monitor how quickly they're actually delivering products to market, as output serves as a key indicator of whether the outcomes-focused approach is working.

vocabulary.definition: Outcomes refer to the results or consequences of a particular action, decision, or process. They are often used to evaluate the effectiveness of strategies or initiatives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, outcomes are critical for assessing project success, measuring performance, and determining the impact of various initiatives on organizational goals.

insight.nuance: While outcomes are often viewed as final results, they can also imply ongoing processes and should be evaluated in the context of both short-term and long-term objectives.

vocabulary.definition: An indicator is a measurable variable that provides insight into a specific condition or trend, often used to assess performance or progress.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, indicators are essential for tracking key performance metrics, guiding decision-making, and identifying areas for improvement within an organization.

insight.nuance: Indicators can be quantitative or qualitative, and it is important to choose the right indicators that align with strategic goals to avoid misleading conclusions.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: the exercise especially with leaders in an org is to have them sit down and write them for each other.
keySentence: Leaders should sit down and write down roles and responsibilities for each other.
text_ko: 특히 조직의 리더들과 할 때는, 리더들이 앉아서 서로를 위해 그것들을 적어보게 하는 연습이에요.
text_zh: 这个练习，尤其是针对组织里的领导，就是让他们坐下来，互相把这些写清楚。
text_es: El ejercicio, sobre todo con los líderes de una organización, consiste en que se sienten y se escriban entre sí.
fullContext: Lenny asks Nikita about her biggest lessons for building successful teams. Nikita describes her framework for creating clear roles and responsibilities within cross-functional product teams. She advocates for expanding the traditional product-design-engineering triad to include data scientists as a fourth member. Her approach involves having each team member write down not only their own role but also their expectations of their counterparts, then reviewing these together to create a shared agreement or 'contract' about how the team will work together.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: From my experience as a product manager, it was always a blocker. Getting your hands on the data, maybe having someone to troubleshoot with if as a PM you couldn't kind of understand or figure it out yourself, it was just always a blocker.
keySentence: Getting your hands on data was always a blocker for product managers.
text_ko: 프로덕트 매니저(product manager, PM)로 일하면서 제 경험상 그건 항상 걸림돌이었어요. 데이터를 직접 확보하는 것도 문제였고, PM이 혼자서 이해하거나 해결하기 어려울 때 같이 트러블슈팅(troubleshoot)해줄 사람이 없으면 늘 막혔어요.
text_zh: 以我做产品经理(product manager)的经验来看，这一直是个绊脚石。拿到数据本身就是问题，要是作为产品经理(PM)你自己弄不明白、也没人能一起排查(troubleshoot)，事情就彻底卡住了。
text_es: En mi experiencia como responsable de producto (product manager, PM), siempre fue un cuello de botella: acceder a los datos y no tener a alguien con quien resolver problemas cuando no podías entenderlo o solucionarlo por tu cuenta.
fullContext: Lenny asks why Nikita pushes to embed data scientists directly into product teams rather than having them in a centralized data team. Nikita explains that when data scientists are centralized, product managers constantly face delays in getting data analysis done. They have to negotiate with other teams for data science resources and wait in queues, which slows down product development. Having a dedicated data scientist on each product team eliminates these bottlenecks and allows for faster decision-making.

vocabulary.definition: A blocker is an obstacle or hindrance that prevents progress or completion of a task or project.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, blockers often refer to issues that delay project timelines or impede workflow, requiring resolution before moving forward.

insight.nuance: While 'blocker' typically has a negative connotation, it can also be used constructively to identify areas needing attention.

vocabulary.definition: To troubleshoot means to identify, analyze, and resolve problems or issues, particularly in technical systems or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup settings, troubleshooting is a critical skill for product managers and engineers to ensure systems function correctly and efficiently.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a systematic approach to problem-solving, distinguishing it from casual or superficial fixes.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: I'll tell you what I do. I don't know, I think folks might get defensive sometime. But I'll tell you what I try.
keySentence: But I'll tell you what I try.
text_ko: 제가 하는 걸 말씀드릴게요. 음, 가끔 사람들 반응이 방어적일 때가 있는 것 같아요. 그래도 제가 시도해 보는 방법은 이런 식이에요.
text_zh: 我跟你说说我是怎么做的吧。我也不太确定，有时候人会有点防备。不过我可以讲讲我通常会怎么尝试。
text_es: Te cuento lo que hago. No sé, creo que a veces la gente se pone a la defensiva. Pero te digo qué intento.
fullContext: Lenny asks how to help teams recognize when they're not delivering enough output without making them defensive. Nikita shares her approach of asking direct but non-accusatory questions about actual deliverables. Rather than making statements about poor performance, she focuses on understanding what was actually shipped to production and how long it took. This questioning approach helps teams self-reflect on their execution velocity while avoiding defensiveness that comes from direct criticism.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by a protective or guarded stance, often in response to perceived criticism or threat.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being defensive can manifest during feedback sessions or negotiations, where individuals may react protectively to critiques or challenges.

insight.nuance: While being defensive can indicate a lack of openness to feedback, it may also reflect a strong commitment to one's ideas or work.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: When I reflect back on what works across my early career, it really comes down in a nutshell to this career concept of explore and exploit.
keySentence: it really comes down in a nutshell to this career concept of explore and exploit.
text_ko: 제가 경력 초반에 무엇이 잘 통했는지 돌이켜보면, 한마디로 말해 커리어 관점에서 '탐색과 활용(explore and exploit)'이라는 개념으로 요약돼요.
text_zh: 回头看我早期职业生涯里什么管用，归根结底就是这条职业策略：探索与利用（explore and exploit）。
text_es: Cuando pienso en lo que realmente funcionó al principio de mi carrera, todo se reduce a esto: el concepto de explorar y aprovechar (explore and exploit).
fullContext: Lenny asks about Nikita's biggest lessons for building successful teams, and she shifts to discussing team building fundamentals. Nikita explains that successful team building starts with clearly defining individual roles and responsibilities, particularly within cross-functional product teams. She advocates for what she calls a 'quartet' approach - expanding the traditional product-design-engineering triad to include data scientists as a fourth core member of product teams.

vocabulary.definition: To think deeply or carefully about something, often in relation to past experiences or decisions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, reflecting is crucial for evaluating past strategies and outcomes to inform future decisions and improvements.

insight.nuance: While reflecting can imply a thoughtful consideration, it may also suggest a degree of introspection that is not always appropriate in fast-paced business environments.

vocabulary.definition: To investigate or examine a subject or area in depth, often to discover new information or opportunities.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and innovation, exploring can refer to researching market trends, customer needs, or new technologies to identify potential avenues for growth.

insight.nuance: Exploring carries a sense of curiosity and openness to new ideas, making it suitable for brainstorming sessions but less so for situations requiring decisive action.

vocabulary.definition: To make full use of and benefit from a resource or opportunity, often with a connotation of taking advantage.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, exploiting can refer to leveraging existing assets, capabilities, or market conditions to maximize returns and competitive advantage.

insight.nuance: While exploiting can have a positive connotation in terms of resource optimization, it may also imply unethical practices if it suggests taking unfair advantage of others.

speaker: Nikita Miller
role: SVP & Head of Product, The Knot Worldwide
text: So when I say outcome, you're saying here's the goal they're achieving or the impact they're having, or is it just the idea we know what our outcome will be but they're not actually shipping anything?
keySentence: here's the goal they're achieving or the impact they're having
text_ko: 그러니까 제가 '결과(outcome)'라고 말할 때, 당신은 그들이 달성하는 목표나 주는 임팩트(impact)를 말하는 건가요? 아니면 우리가 결과를 알고는 있지만 실제로는 아무것도 출시(shipping)하지 않는, 단지 아이디어 수준인 건가요?
text_zh: 所以我说成果(outcome)，你的意思是这是他们要达成的目标或带来的影响，还是只是我们心里有个预期，但他们根本没真正把东西交付出来？
text_es: Entonces, cuando digo "resultado (outcome)", ¿estás diciendo que esa es la meta que están alcanzando o el impacto que están teniendo, o que es solo la idea — sabemos cuál será el resultado pero en realidad no están lanzando (shipping) nada?
fullContext: Lenny asks Nikita to clarify what she means by outcomes versus output after she mentioned teams focusing too heavily on outcomes. Nikita explains that outcomes refer to understanding goals and strategy (like OKRs), but teams often get stuck in planning mode. She emphasizes that successful execution requires multiple attempts and iterations - the more experiments and products you ship to market, the higher your chances of achieving your desired outcomes. The key is balancing strategic thinking with actual delivery.

vocabulary.definition: An outcome is the result or consequence of a particular action, process, or event.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, outcomes are often measured to evaluate the effectiveness of strategies, projects, or initiatives, helping organizations assess their performance and make informed decisions.

insight.nuance: While 'outcome' generally refers to the end result, it can imply a focus on measurable results rather than qualitative aspects.

vocabulary.definition: Impact refers to the strong effect or influence that one thing has on another.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, impact is often used to describe the significance of a project or initiative on stakeholders, market trends, or financial performance.

insight.nuance: The term 'impact' carries a connotation of importance and can suggest both positive and negative effects, making it crucial to specify the nature of the impact when discussing it.

vocabulary.definition: Achieving refers to the act of successfully reaching a desired objective or completing a task.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business realm, achieving is often linked to meeting targets, fulfilling strategic goals, or delivering on promises to stakeholders.

insight.nuance: The term 'achieving' implies effort and accomplishment, and is typically used in contexts where success is measurable and recognized.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: Some people focus on conversion rate, like, "I'm going to make this really, really slick." And that's cool. You get a bit more growth. But to get to recommendation, you're going to blow your user socks off.
keySentence: To get recommendations, you must blow your user socks off with unique experiences.
text_ko: 어떤 사람들은 전환율(conversion rate)에만 집중해요. "정말정말 세련되게 만들 거야" 이렇게요. 그건 좋아요 — 성장도 좀 더 나와요. 그런데 진짜 추천(recommendation)을 얻으려면 사용자들을 완전히 놀라게 해서 강한 인상을 남겨야 해요.
text_zh: 有些人只盯着转化率（conversion rate），想着“我要把这做得特别顺滑、特别有质感。”这确实能带来点增长，但要做到用户愿意主动推荐你，你得把他们彻底惊艳。
text_es: Algunas personas se centran en la tasa de conversión (conversion rate), tipo: "voy a dejar esto súper, súper pulido". Y eso está bien — consigues un poco más de crecimiento. Pero para llegar a la recomendación (recommendation), tienes que dejar boquiabiertos a tus usuarios.
fullContext: Lenny is discussing with Nilan how to drive word-of-mouth growth for products. Nilan is explaining that most teams stop when their product simply works, or they focus on incremental improvements like conversion rate optimization. However, to get customers to actively recommend your product to others, you need to exceed their expectations dramatically. He argues that you must create experiences that customers never knew were possible before - essentially doing something completely new rather than just improving existing solutions.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage of users who take a desired action, such as making a purchase or signing up for a newsletter, out of the total number of visitors.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, conversion rate is a critical metric used to evaluate the effectiveness of marketing strategies and user experience design.

insight.nuance: While a high conversion rate indicates successful user engagement, it is important to also consider the quality of the conversions and customer satisfaction.

vocabulary.definition: A suggestion or endorsement made by an individual or organization, often based on personal experience or expertise.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, recommendations can significantly influence consumer behavior, often driving sales and fostering brand loyalty through trust and credibility.

insight.nuance: Recommendations carry weight when they stem from genuine experiences, making them more impactful than mere advertisements.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: So building a brand led money transfer business, the brand's got to be pretty damn good, right? You're going to feel pretty special afterwards, in order to have less money afterwards.
keySentence: the brand's got to be pretty damn good, right?
text_ko: 브랜드 주도형 송금 사업(brand-led money transfer business)을 만들려면 브랜드가 정말 끝내줘야 해요, 그렇죠? 결국엔 돈은 덜 남는데도 ‘그래도 기분은 특별하잖아’ 하면서 스스로 위로하게 될 거예요.
text_zh: 所以想把汇款业务做成以品牌为主导(brand-led money transfer business)，品牌得足够出色，对吧？最后你会觉得自己很了不起，但手里的钱反而更少了。
text_es: Si vas a montar un negocio de transferencias de dinero centrado en la marca (brand-led money transfer business), la marca tiene que ser realmente buena, ¿no? Te vas a sentir muy especial… para luego quedarte con menos dinero.
fullContext: Lenny asks about the biggest shift that helped Wise grow word-of-mouth significantly. Nilan explains why word-of-mouth was essential for Wise's business model. Since money is the ultimate commodity and customers end up with less money after using any money transfer service, building a brand-led business in this space requires an exceptionally good customer experience. He's outlining the challenge of finding marketing channels that can scale broadly while having very low distribution costs, which led them to focus on word-of-mouth growth.

vocabulary.definition: A brand is a unique name, symbol, or design that identifies and differentiates a product or service from others in the market. It encompasses the perceptions and experiences associated with a company or product.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a strong brand can lead to customer loyalty, higher perceived value, and competitive advantage, making it a crucial element for startups and established companies alike.

insight.nuance: While 'brand' often refers to the visual identity, it also implies the emotional connection and reputation a company builds over time.

vocabulary.definition: Money transfer refers to the process of sending funds from one individual or entity to another, often facilitated by financial institutions or digital platforms. It can occur domestically or internationally.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the fintech sector, money transfer services are critical for enabling seamless transactions, especially in global markets where traditional banking may be less accessible.

insight.nuance: The term can imply various methods, including electronic transfers, wire transfers, or remittances, and is often associated with speed and security.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: We only got the advocacy when we were eight to 10 times cheaper. That's when people started talking about it. So the bar is all the way up there. And to put that in context, that means figuring out how to move money instantly.
keySentence: Advocacy only emerged when we were all the way down to 0.35.
text_ko: 사람들이 얘기하기 시작한 건 우리가 8~10배나 더 싸졌을 때뿐이에요. 그때야 고객 추천(advocacy)이 나왔죠. 그래서 기준이 아주 높아진 거예요. 맥락을 더하면, 결국 돈을 즉시 이체하는 방법(즉시 자금 이체, move money instantly)을 찾아내야 한다는 뜻이에요.
text_zh: 只有当我们的价格便宜到8到10倍，才会有人开始主动推荐(advocacy)。那时候大家才开始讨论它。所以门槛被拉得很高。换句话说，这就得想明白怎么做到资金即时到账(move money instantly)。
text_es: Solo conseguimos apoyo (advocacy) cuando éramos entre ocho y diez veces más baratos. Fue entonces cuando empezó a correr la voz. Así que el listón está por las nubes. Y para que te hagas una idea, eso significa averiguar cómo mover dinero al instante.
fullContext: Nilan is explaining a key insight about driving word-of-mouth for Wise. When entering new markets, they discovered that being marginally better (like pricing at 5.9% versus competitors at 6%) would get customers to use their service, but wouldn't generate recommendations. Only when they achieved dramatically better pricing - 8 to 10 times cheaper than alternatives - did customers become evangelical and start talking about the product. This taught them that the bar for recommendation is extremely high, requiring breakthrough improvements rather than incremental ones.

vocabulary.definition: Advocacy refers to the act of supporting or promoting a cause or proposal, often through persuasive communication and action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, advocacy can involve lobbying for policy changes, promoting a product, or rallying support from stakeholders to influence decision-making.

insight.nuance: While advocacy is generally positive, it can sometimes carry a connotation of bias or partisanship, so it's important to ensure that the support is based on sound reasoning and evidence.

vocabulary.definition: Context refers to the circumstances or background information surrounding a particular event, situation, or concept that helps to clarify its meaning.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, providing context is crucial for understanding market trends, customer behavior, or the rationale behind strategic decisions.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a broader perspective, so it's important to use it when the surrounding details significantly affect interpretation or understanding.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: It's this thing around growth rate. So, especially product net growth, which is what we're talking about. So you can imagine, we're going to open a new market to Indonesia, and the fastest way to do it is to take...
keySentence: the fastest way to do it is to take...
text_ko: 이건 성장률에 관한 얘기예요. 특히 지금 말하는 건 제품 순성장(product net growth)이구요. 인도네시아처럼 새 시장에 진출한다고 상상해보세요. 그럴 때 가장 빠른 방법은 ... 하는 거예요.
text_zh: 关键在于增长率这事儿。尤其是产品净增长（product net growth），也就是我们在说的那个。你可以想象，我们要进军印尼这个新市场，最快的办法就是...
text_es: Es toda esta cuestión de la tasa de crecimiento. Sobre todo del crecimiento neto del producto (product net growth), que es de lo que estamos hablando. Así que imagínate: vamos a abrir un nuevo mercado en Indonesia, y la forma más rápida de hacerlo es...
fullContext: Lenny asks about common mistakes people make when trying to drive word-of-mouth growth. Nilan explains a key misstep that many companies, including Wise, have made. When entering new markets, the tempting shortcut is to use existing infrastructure solutions that others have already built - for example, plugging into existing money transfer systems for Indonesia. While this approach can quickly acquire some users, it doesn't create the exponential growth curve needed for strong word-of-mouth because it hasn't fundamentally solved the underlying problems customers face.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage increase in a company's revenue, customer base, or market share over a specific period of time.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the growth rate is a critical metric used to assess the performance and potential of a company, especially in evaluating investment opportunities and market strategies.

insight.nuance: While a high growth rate is generally viewed positively, it is important to consider the sustainability of that growth and the context in which it occurs.

vocabulary.definition: The overall increase in a company's size or value after accounting for losses or reductions, such as customer churn or product returns.
vocabulary.businessContext: Net growth is often used to provide a more accurate picture of a company's performance, as it reflects the actual gain after subtracting any losses.

insight.nuance: Net growth can sometimes mask underlying issues if not analyzed alongside gross growth figures, making it essential to consider both metrics.

vocabulary.definition: The process of introducing a product or service to a new geographical area or demographic segment where it has not previously been available.
vocabulary.businessContext: Opening a new market is a strategic move for businesses seeking to expand their customer base and increase revenue, often requiring market research and tailored marketing strategies.

insight.nuance: This phrase implies not just entry into a new market but also the establishment of a presence and the cultivation of customer relationships in that area.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: So it comes from a very logical place, how do I get users quickly? I can take a shortcut in doing this, but that, you kind of realize is wasted effort. So the step then becomes this much harder question of these types of questions.
keySentence: but that, you kind of realize is wasted effort.
text_ko: 그래서 출발점은 아주 논리적이에요. ‘어떻게 하면 빠르게 사용자를 확보할까?’라고 생각하죠. 이걸 위해 지름길(shortcut)을 택할 수도 있는데, 그러다 보면 그게 결국엔 헛수고라는 걸 깨닫게 돼요. 그래서 그다음엔 훨씬 더 어렵고 복잡한, 이런 종류의 질문들을 고민해야 해요.
text_zh: 这出发点很合理：怎么能快速获取用户(users)？可以走捷径，但你会意识到那是在浪费力气。于是下一步反而成了一个更难的问题——像这种问题该怎么解决？
text_es: Surge de algo muy lógico: ¿cómo consigo usuarios rápido? Podría tomar un atajo para lograrlo, pero te das cuenta de que al final es un esfuerzo desperdiciado. Entonces lo que viene es una pregunta mucho más difícil de ese tipo.
fullContext: Continuing his explanation about avoiding shortcuts in product development, Nilan describes how teams naturally want to find quick wins to acquire users rapidly. However, he learned that these shortcuts ultimately represent wasted effort because they don't create the transformative experiences needed for word-of-mouth growth. Instead, teams should ask fundamental questions about the theoretical limits of what's possible - like the absolute minimum cost or maximum speed achievable - and work backwards from those ideals rather than making incremental improvements.

vocabulary.definition: A quicker or more direct route to achieve a goal or complete a task, often bypassing standard procedures.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, taking a shortcut may refer to using less rigorous methods to achieve results faster, which can sometimes compromise quality or thoroughness.

insight.nuance: While shortcuts can save time, they may lead to incomplete solutions or future complications, so they should be used judiciously.

vocabulary.definition: Exertion or resources spent on a task that yields little to no productive outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, wasted effort often refers to time and resources that could have been better allocated to more impactful projects or strategies.

insight.nuance: This phrase carries a negative connotation, suggesting inefficiency and lack of foresight in planning or execution.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by clear, sound reasoning or consistent principles that lead to rational conclusions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business realm, logical thinking is crucial for decision-making, problem-solving, and strategic planning, ensuring that actions are based on evidence and rationality.

insight.nuance: While 'logical' suggests a rational approach, it may sometimes imply a lack of creativity or emotional consideration in decision-making.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: You can't split test your way to love. So, this experiment led product management approach, where you throw a bunch of things on the wall, and then you kind of see what sticks, and generally we don't advocate this.
keySentence: You can't split test your way to love.
text_ko: 사용자의 사랑을 스플릿 테스트(split test)로 얻을 수는 없어요. 그래서 여러 가지를 벽에 막 던져보고 뭐가 붙는지 보는, 이른바 실험 주도형 제품 관리 접근법(experiment led product management approach)은 보통 우리가 권하지 않아요.
text_zh: 靠 A/B 测试(split test) 是让用户真正喜欢起来的办法。 所以那种以实验为主导的产品管理方法(experiment-led product management approach)，就是把很多点子都试一遍，看看哪个能站得住脚——我们一般不建议这么干。
text_es: No vas a lograr que los usuarios lo amen solo con pruebas A/B (split tests). Por eso, ese enfoque de gestión de producto (product management) dirigido por experimentos —en el que lanzas un montón de cosas a ver cuál pega— no es algo que, en general, recomendemos.
fullContext: Lenny and Nilan are discussing Wise's approach to product development and experimentation. Nilan is explaining why Wise doesn't rely heavily on A/B testing and experiment-driven product management. He argues that constantly running experiments to see what works is ineffective for building products that customers will love and recommend. Instead of this "throw things at the wall" approach, he advocates for building conviction about what matters to customers through direct customer feedback and insights before building features, since engineering resources are expensive and limited.

vocabulary.definition: The process of overseeing the development, marketing, and lifecycle of a product from conception to market launch and beyond.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, product management involves coordinating cross-functional teams to ensure that products meet customer needs and align with business goals.

insight.nuance: While product management focuses on strategic planning and execution, it is often seen as a collaborative role that requires balancing various stakeholder interests.

vocabulary.definition: To publicly support or recommend a particular cause, policy, or idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, advocating for a product or strategy often involves rallying support from stakeholders and influencing decision-making processes.

insight.nuance: While 'advocate' implies strong support, it can also suggest a level of persuasion that may not always be welcomed, especially in contentious discussions.

vocabulary.definition: A way of dealing with a situation or problem; a method or strategy.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the term 'approach' is often used to describe the strategy taken to achieve goals, whether in project management, marketing, or product development.

insight.nuance: The term can imply flexibility and adaptability, but may also suggest a lack of specificity if not defined clearly.

speaker: Nilan Peiris
text: And closing this delta between what you've done, and what's perceived to be done is what I call product marketing within the product. And that in its own right is a discipline, I've learned.
keySentence: Closing this delta between actions and perceptions is product marketing in its own right.
text_ko: 여러분이 실제로 해놓은 것과 사람들이 해놓은 것으로 인식하는 것 사이의 격차를 줄이는 것이 제가 말하는 제품 안에서의 프로덕트 마케팅(product marketing within the product)이에요. 그리고 그게 그 자체로 하나의 전문 분야라는 걸 배웠어요.
text_zh: 要缩小你实际做的事情和别人认为你做的事情之间的差距，我把这叫做产品内的产品营销(product marketing within the product)。我发现这本身就是一门学问。
text_es: Y cerrar esa brecha entre lo que realmente has hecho y lo que se percibe que has hecho es lo que yo llamo marketing del producto dentro del producto. Y eso por sí solo es toda una disciplina, he aprendido.
fullContext: Nilan is sharing insights about a breakthrough that 3x'd their referral sharing rates. He discovered that customers were getting great value from Wise but weren't fully aware of how much value they were receiving. For example, customers saved money but didn't believe the actual savings amount, or received instant transfers without realizing they were instant. The key was creating visual comparisons and animations within the product to help customers understand the true value they received, which then made them more likely to share with others.

vocabulary.definition: Regarded or understood in a particular way, often based on subjective interpretation rather than objective reality.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and branding, 'perceived' is crucial as it influences customer attitudes and behaviors toward products or services.

insight.nuance: This term often carries a connotation of subjectivity, suggesting that perceptions may not always align with facts, making it important to clarify the distinction in discussions.

vocabulary.definition: A field of study or a branch of knowledge, often characterized by a systematic approach to learning and practice.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'discipline' refers to the structured methodologies and practices that guide teams in achieving goals, such as product marketing or project management.

insight.nuance: While it can refer to a specific area of expertise, it also implies a level of rigor and commitment to standards, making it suitable for discussions about professional development.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: I went to Alibaba and I bought myself one of these flip phones from China like we used to have in the 1990s with no apps, no internet connection.
keySentence: I bought myself one of these flip phones from China like we used to have in the 1990s with no apps, no internet connection.
text_ko: 알리바바에서 중국산 폴더폰(flip phone) 하나 샀어요. 90년대에 쓰던 것처럼 앱도 없고 인터넷 연결도 없어요.
text_zh: 我在阿里巴巴(Alibaba)上买了个国产翻盖手机(flip phone)，就像90年代我们用的那种，没应用(App)，也上不了网。
text_es: Entré en Alibaba y me compré uno de esos teléfonos plegables (flip phones) de China, como los que teníamos en los 90: sin aplicaciones (apps) ni conexión a Internet (internet connection).
fullContext: Lenny asks Nir about his personal experience with distraction and what techniques he tried. Nir explains how he attempted to solve his distraction problem by completely removing technology from his environment - buying a basic flip phone and an old word processor. However, he discovered that even without any digital distractions, he still found ways to procrastinate and avoid the important work he needed to do. This led him to realize that the root cause of distraction isn't external technology, but internal discomfort.

vocabulary.definition: A connection is a relationship or link between two or more entities, which can be physical, emotional, or digital in nature. It often implies a sense of engagement or interaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, connections are vital for networking, collaboration, and building partnerships that can lead to new opportunities and growth.

insight.nuance: The term can carry different weights depending on the context, such as a personal connection versus a professional one, and is often used to emphasize the importance of relationships in achieving success.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: identify what is that internal trigger... that is the source of 90% of our distractions... it's just a feeling... it's just an emotion.
keySentence: identify what is that internal trigger... that is the source of 90% of our distractions...
text_ko: 그 '내적 트리거(internal trigger)'가 뭔지 찾아보세요... 그게 우리를 90%나 산만하게 만드는 원인이에요... 사실 그건 그냥 느낌이에요, 그냥 감정이에요.
text_zh: 弄清楚到底是哪种内在触发(internal trigger)——它造成了我们90%的分心，实际上不过就是一种感觉、一种情绪。
text_es: Identifica cuál es ese desencadenante interno (internal trigger) que está detrás del 90% de nuestras distracciones; no es más que un sentimiento, una emoción.
fullContext: Nir continues explaining his discovery about the true source of distraction. He reveals that research shows 90% of distractions come from internal triggers (emotions like boredom, anxiety, or discomfort) rather than external triggers like notifications. He emphasizes that understanding this is empowering because emotions are temporary and manageable. The 'arrows in your quiver' metaphor refers to having multiple strategies prepared to handle uncomfortable feelings when they arise, rather than escaping them through distraction.

vocabulary.definition: An internal trigger refers to a psychological or emotional stimulus that prompts a specific response or behavior within an individual. It often relates to feelings or thoughts that initiate actions, particularly in the context of habits or decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, understanding internal triggers can help organizations design products or marketing strategies that resonate with users' emotional states, thereby enhancing user engagement and retention.

insight.nuance: While 'internal trigger' often implies a personal or psychological aspect, it is important to differentiate it from external triggers, which are environmental or situational stimuli.

vocabulary.definition: A source is the origin or starting point from which something derives or is obtained. It can refer to information, materials, or causes that lead to a particular outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, identifying the source of problems or opportunities is crucial for effective decision-making and strategic planning, as it allows organizations to address root causes rather than symptoms.

insight.nuance: The term 'source' can imply reliability or credibility, particularly in contexts involving information or data; thus, it is essential to evaluate the trustworthiness of a source.

vocabulary.definition: Emotion is a complex psychological state that encompasses subjective experience, physiological response, and behavioral or expressive response. It plays a significant role in influencing human behavior and decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding emotions can enhance customer relations, marketing strategies, and team dynamics, as emotional intelligence is key to effective leadership and communication.

insight.nuance: While 'emotion' generally refers to feelings, it can carry different weights depending on context; for instance, in negotiations, emotions can be both a powerful motivator and a potential source of conflict.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: What I tell myself is, "Okay, I'm just going to wait 10 minutes before I check email, before I scroll social media, before I Google something that is just trying to procrastinate doing the work." I can do that. I'm a grown man.
keySentence: I'm just going to wait 10 minutes before I check email, before I scroll social media, before I Google something that is just trying to procrastinate doing the work.
text_ko: 저는 스스로에게 이렇게 말해요. "이메일 확인하기 전에, SNS를 스크롤하기 전에, 일을 미루려고 하는 구글 검색을 하기 전에 10분만 기다릴게요." 그 정도는 할 수 있어요. 저는 어른이니까요.
text_zh: 我跟自己说，‘先等十分钟再去看邮件、刷社交媒体，或者去谷歌(Google)搜那些只是为了拖延工作的东西。’我可以做到的——我又不是小孩子了。
text_es: Lo que me digo es: "Bueno, voy a esperar diez minutos antes de revisar el correo (email), antes de entrar a las redes sociales (social media), antes de buscar algo en Google (Google) que solo me sirve para perder el tiempo en lugar de ponerme a trabajar." Puedo hacerlo. Soy un hombre hecho y derecho.
fullContext: Nir explains his '10-minute rule' technique for managing distraction urges. When he feels tempted to check social media or email instead of doing important work, he sets a timer for 10 minutes and tells himself he can do those distracting activities after the timer goes off - but not yet. During those 10 minutes, he either returns to his intended task or 'surfs the urge' by acknowledging and experiencing the uncomfortable emotion without trying to escape it. This technique treats the urge as temporary rather than permanent.

vocabulary.definition: To delay or postpone action or tasks, often by engaging in less urgent activities.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, procrastination can lead to missed deadlines and decreased productivity, impacting overall team performance and project timelines.

insight.nuance: While procrastination often carries a negative connotation, it can sometimes be a symptom of deeper issues like burnout or lack of motivation.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from. I'll say that again. You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from.
keySentence: You can't call something a distraction without knowing what it distracted you from.
text_ko: 무엇으로부터 주의가 뺏겼는지 모르면 그걸 산만하다고 부를 수 없어요. 다시 말할게요. 무엇으로부터 주의가 뺏겼는지 모르면 그걸 산만하다고 부를 수 없어요.
text_zh: 别急着把某件事贴上“分心”(distraction)的标签，关键是你得先搞清楚它把你从哪件事上拉走了。我再说一遍：别随便把什么事叫做“分心”(distraction)，除非你知道它到底让你没做成哪件事。
text_es: No puedes considerar algo una distracción si no sabes de qué te apartó. Lo repito: no puedes considerar algo una distracción si no sabes de qué te apartó.
fullContext: Nir discusses the importance of having a scheduled plan to identify what constitutes distraction versus traction. He explains that without a clear calendar showing what you intended to do at specific times, it becomes easy to justify any work-related activity as productive. The key insight is that even checking work email can be a distraction if it's not what you planned to do during that time block. This justification trap keeps people from focusing on their most important tasks.

vocabulary.definition: A distraction is anything that diverts attention away from a primary focus or task. It can be an external stimulus or an internal thought that interrupts concentration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business environments, distractions can hinder productivity and efficiency, impacting project timelines and team performance. Identifying distractions is crucial for maintaining focus in a fast-paced work setting.

insight.nuance: While distractions are often viewed negatively, they can sometimes lead to creative insights or necessary breaks, making context important in their evaluation.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: What you want to do instead is to book time in your schedule for this reflective work time, which is where you do the kind of work that requires you to work without distraction.
keySentence: Book reflective work time in your schedule to avoid distractions and plan effectively.
text_ko: 대신 할 일은 일정에 성찰 업무 시간(reflective work time)을 따로 잡아두는 거예요. 그 시간에는 방해받지 않고 집중해야 하는 일을 하면 돼요.
text_zh: 你应该在日程里专门留出反思工作时间(reflective work time)，在那段时间里专心做那些不能被打断、需要不受干扰的工作。
text_es: En lugar de eso, reserva en tu agenda bloques para trabajo reflexivo: ahí haces las tareas que requieren concentración sin distracciones.
fullContext: Nir explains the importance of scheduling 'reflective work time' - periods dedicated to deep thinking, planning, and strategizing that require full attention. He distinguishes this from reactive work (responding to emails and notifications). He argues that to-do lists are inadequate because they lack time constraints - you can always add more items without considering how much time you actually have. A time-blocked calendar forces you to make realistic trade-offs and prioritize what truly matters.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by deep thought or consideration, often involving introspection about past experiences or decisions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, reflective practices are crucial for evaluating past strategies and improving future decision-making processes.

insight.nuance: While 'reflective' often carries a positive connotation of thoughtful analysis, it can imply indecisiveness if overused.

vocabulary.definition: Anything that diverts attention away from a primary task or focus, often leading to decreased productivity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, distractions can significantly hinder performance, making it essential for teams to create environments that minimize interruptions.

insight.nuance: The term 'distraction' typically has a negative connotation, suggesting a loss of focus that can be detrimental to achieving goals.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: You don't tell your boss no, you ask your boss to help you prioritize. That is your boss' most important job is to prioritize. So, you're not saying no. You're saying, "Here's my calendar. Here's this list of stuff you've asked me to do.
keySentence: Ask your boss to help you prioritize tasks instead of saying no.
text_ko: 상사에게 '안 돼요'라고 딱 못 한다고 말하는 게 아니라, 우선순위(priority)를 정하는 걸 도와 달라고 요청하세요. 상사의 가장 중요한 역할은 우선순위를 정하는 거예요. 그러니까 '아니요'라고 거절하는 게 아니라, '제 일정표는 이렇고, 요청하신 일 목록은 여기예요'라고 말하는 거예요.
text_zh: 你别直接跟老板说“不”，你应该请老板帮你排优先级（prioritize）。给事情排优先级（prioritize）才是老板最重要的工作。所以你并不是在说不，你是在说：“这是我的日程表（calendar），这是你交给我的任务清单。”
text_es: No le dices que no a tu jefe; le pides que te ayude a priorizar. La labor más importante de tu jefe es establecer prioridades. No estás diciendo “no”, estás diciendo: “Mira mi calendario. Aquí tienes la lista de tareas que me has pedido que haga.”
fullContext: Nir addresses how to manage competing demands from your manager without saying 'no' directly. He calls this technique 'schedule syncing' or 'managing your manager.' Instead of refusing requests, you show your boss your time-blocked calendar and a separate list of additional tasks they've requested. You then ask them to help prioritize what's most important. This approach leverages the fact that prioritization is a key management responsibility while giving you control over your time.

vocabulary.definition: To arrange or deal with tasks or responsibilities in order of importance or urgency.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, prioritizing helps teams focus on high-impact activities that align with strategic goals, ensuring efficient use of resources.

insight.nuance: While prioritizing is generally viewed positively, it can imply that some tasks may be deprioritized, which could lead to tension if not communicated effectively.

speaker: Nir Eyal
text: The antidote for impulsiveness is forethought. The antidote for impulsiveness is forethought. Fundamentally, distraction is an impulse control issue. That's all it is, and it's a skill like any other. We learn skills.
keySentence: The antidote for impulsiveness is forethought; distraction is an impulse control issue.
text_ko: 충동성(impulsiveness)을 다스리는 해독제는 사전 숙고(forethought)예요. 충동성(impulsiveness)을 다스리는 해독제는 사전 숙고(forethought)예요. 근본적으로 산만함(distraction)은 충동 조절(impulse control)의 문제예요. 그게 전부고, 다른 기술들처럼 배워서 익힐 수 있는 거예요. 우리는 기술을 배워요.
text_zh: 应对冲动最好的办法就是提前想清楚。说到底，分心不过是个冲动控制(impulse control)的问题。就是这样，它只是一项技能，和别的技能一样，都能学会。
text_es: La mejor forma de combatir la impulsividad es pensar antes (forethought). La mejor forma de combatir la impulsividad es pensar antes (forethought). En esencia, la distracción es un problema de control de impulsos (impulse control). Eso es todo: es una habilidad como cualquier otra y se aprende.
fullContext: Nir provides his core philosophy for becoming indistractable. He emphasizes that distraction is fundamentally about impulse control, which is a learnable skill rather than an inherent character trait. His key insight is that the solution lies in planning ahead - taking deliberate steps today to prevent tomorrow's distractions. This forward-thinking approach empowers people to take control of their attention rather than feeling helpless against distraction.

vocabulary.definition: In a basic or essential way; at the core or foundation of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'fundamentally' is often used to emphasize the underlying principles or values that drive a company's strategy or operations.

insight.nuance: This term conveys a sense of depth and importance, suggesting that the point being made is not just superficial but central to understanding the issue.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to resist immediate temptations or urges in order to achieve long-term goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business, impulse control is critical for decision-making, particularly in financial management and strategic planning, where hasty decisions can lead to negative outcomes.

insight.nuance: This term often implies a struggle against natural instincts, highlighting the importance of discipline and self-regulation in professional settings.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to perform tasks and solve problems effectively, often acquired through practice and experience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business environment, skills are essential for employee performance, innovation, and competitive advantage, with companies often investing in training to develop these capabilities.

insight.nuance: While 'skill' can refer to both hard and soft abilities, it often emphasizes the proficiency gained through experience rather than innate talent.

vocabulary.definition: A thing that prevents someone from giving full attention to something else; a diversion of focus.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, distractions can significantly reduce productivity and efficiency, prompting organizations to implement strategies for minimizing interruptions and enhancing focus.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting that distractions are obstacles to achieving goals or maintaining concentration.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: We have this mental metaphor that we talk a lot about, getting to the next hill.
keySentence: getting to the next hill.
text_ko: 우리가 자주 하는 얘기 중에 마음속 은유(mental metaphor) 하나 있어요: 바로 '다음 언덕으로 가는 것(getting to the next hill)'이에요.
text_zh: 我们常提的一个心理比喻就是“翻过下一座山头”。
text_es: Hay una metáfora mental de la que hablamos mucho: llegar a la siguiente colina.
fullContext: At the beginning of the podcast, Noah explains Slack's approach to product innovation and avoiding incremental thinking. He describes how product teams can get trapped in constant small improvements without seeing bigger opportunities. The metaphor of "getting to the next hill" refers to moving beyond immediate tasks to see the broader landscape of possibilities that exists beyond current projects.

vocabulary.definition: A figure of speech that describes an object or action in a way that isn’t literally true, often used to illustrate a concept or idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: Metaphors are commonly used in business communication to simplify complex ideas and make them more relatable to stakeholders.

insight.nuance: While effective for illustration, metaphors can sometimes obscure meaning if overused or poorly chosen.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: I think the biggest probably lesson learned, frankly, is that we were really close with the Instagram folks early on. They were big developers on our platform. They used the Foursquare API before they were bought by Facebook.
keySentence: we were really close with the Instagram folks early on.
text_ko: 솔직히 제가 생각하기에 가장 큰 교훈은 초기에 인스타그램 쪽과 우리가 정말 가까웠다는 점이에요. 그들은 우리 플랫폼에서 중요한 개발자들이었고, 페이스북에 인수되기 전에 포스퀘어 API(Foursquare API)를 사용했어요.
text_zh: 老实说，我觉得最重要的一个教训，大概就是我们当年和 Instagram（Instagram）团队走得很近。他们当时是我们平台上很重要的开发者，在被 Facebook（Facebook）收购之前就一直在用 Foursquare 的 API（Foursquare API）。
text_es: Creo que, para ser sincero, la lección más importante fue que desde el principio teníamos muy buena relación con la gente de Instagram. Eran de los desarrolladores (developers) más importantes de nuestra plataforma y usaban la interfaz de programación (API) de Foursquare antes de que Facebook la comprara.
fullContext: Lenny asks Noah whether Foursquare could have built a massive consumer business or if pivoting to B2B data was inevitable. Noah reflects on what went wrong with Foursquare's social strategy. He explains that they focused on location-based sharing (person + place) while Instagram succeeded with experience-based sharing (person + moment), which sometimes included location but wasn't dependent on it.

vocabulary.definition: A platform is a foundational technology or service that enables the development and deployment of applications, products, or services, often facilitating interactions between users and providers.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, platforms like social media networks or software ecosystems serve as critical infrastructures that support third-party developers and enhance user engagement.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a broader ecosystem of services and users, and is often associated with scalability and network effects.

vocabulary.definition: Developers are individuals or teams responsible for creating, building, and maintaining software applications or systems, often possessing specialized technical skills.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology companies, developers play a crucial role in product development, innovation, and the implementation of new features that meet user needs.

insight.nuance: The term can encompass a range of roles, from front-end to back-end developers, and is often associated with collaboration and problem-solving in tech environments.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: I would say to folks in general, if you're joining company and the CEO does the role that is your functional area of expertise, it's probably the area where you'll learn the most because they're hopefully world class at it.
keySentence: Joining a company with a CEO in your functional area of expertise offers less agency.
text_ko: 일반적으로 사람들에게 이렇게 말하고 싶어요. 회사에 합류할 때 최고경영자(CEO)가 당신의 전문 분야(functional area)를 직접 맡고 있다면, 그게 아마 당신이 가장 많이 배우는 분야일 거예요. 그분이 그 일을 세계적 수준으로 잘할 가능성이 크기 때문이에요.
text_zh: 我一般会跟大家说，如果你要加入的公司里，首席执行官（CEO）亲自负责的恰好是你擅长的那个职能领域，那通常就是你能学到最多的地方，因为你可以指望他们在这方面是世界级的。
text_es: Diría, en general, que si entras a una empresa y el CEO desempeña el rol de tu área funcional (functional area), probablemente sea el área donde más vas a aprender, porque con suerte será de primer nivel (world-class) en eso.
fullContext: Lenny asks Noah about working with strong product-minded founders like Dennis Crowley and Stewart Butterfield. Noah shares advice for product managers joining companies where the CEO is deeply involved in product decisions. He explains the trade-off between learning opportunities and potential frustration when working under a product-focused founder who may limit your decision-making authority.

vocabulary.definition: A specific division or department within an organization that focuses on a particular set of tasks or responsibilities.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, functional areas such as marketing, finance, and human resources are essential for the overall operation and strategic direction of the company.

insight.nuance: While often used to describe distinct departments, 'functional area' can also imply a specialization within a broader role, highlighting the importance of expertise in that domain.

vocabulary.definition: A high level of knowledge or skill in a particular area or field, often acquired through experience and education.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, having expertise is crucial for making informed decisions, driving innovation, and maintaining competitive advantage.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a connotation of authority and trustworthiness, suggesting that the individual is not only knowledgeable but also respected in their field.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to the highest standard of quality or performance, often recognized internationally as exemplary.
vocabulary.businessContext: Companies strive to achieve world-class status to enhance their reputation, attract top talent, and gain a competitive edge in the global market.

insight.nuance: The phrase implies not just excellence, but also a benchmark against which others are measured, making it a powerful descriptor in marketing and branding.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: I think what we would wind up doing with Stewart at Slack, for example, is we would get the entire development team, engineers design product, user research and Stewart together in a room and we almost do a bug bash together.
keySentence: We wind up doing a bug bash together to clean up the mess collaboratively.
text_ko: 예를 들어 Slack의 스튜어트와 함께라면 개발팀 전체—엔지니어, 디자이너, 제품팀, 사용자 리서치(user research) 담당자와 스튜어트를 한 방에 모아놓고 사실상 함께 버그 바시(bug bash)를 하곤 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得像跟 Slack 那边的 Stewart 合作时，我们会把整个开发团队、工程师、设计、产品、用户研究这些人连同 Stewart 一起叫到一个房间，然后大家一起集中找 bug（bug bash）。
text_es: Creo que, por ejemplo, con Stewart en Slack lo que acabaríamos haciendo sería reunir en una sala a todo el equipo de desarrollo —ingeniería, diseño, producto e investigación de usuarios— y prácticamente hacer entre todos una revisión masiva de errores (bug bash).
fullContext: Noah explains how to successfully involve product-minded founders in the final stages of product development. He describes Slack's collaborative approach where the entire team, including founder Stewart Butterfield, would gather to review and refine products before launch. A "bug bash" is a collaborative session where team members test software together to find and fix issues.

vocabulary.definition: A group of professionals, typically including software engineers, designers, and product managers, responsible for creating and improving products or services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech companies, the development team plays a crucial role in the product lifecycle, from initial concept through to deployment and maintenance.

insight.nuance: The term can vary in composition and focus depending on the organization, with some teams emphasizing agile methodologies or cross-functional collaboration.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: What we started doing with these complaints storms and idea was really simple, which is we'd get a team together often Stewart myself would also join and we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces and we'd say, "Okay.
keySentence: we'd actually start off with other products first in adjacent spaces
text_ko: 우리가 이런 불만 폭주(complaints storms)와 아이디어로 시작할 때 한 일은 정말 단순했어요. 팀을 모으고 스튜어트도 자주, 저도 함께 참여했는데, 실제로 먼저 인접 분야(adjacent spaces)의 다른 제품들부터 살펴보면서 "좋아요."라고 말하곤 했어요.
text_zh: 我们开始用这些“投诉风暴”(complaints storms)和想法着手做的事其实很简单：把团队凑在一起，Stewart 常来，我也会参加。我们通常先从相近领域的其他产品下手，然后会说，“好。”
text_es: Lo que empezamos a hacer con estas oleadas de quejas (complaints storms) fue muy sencillo: reuníamos a un equipo —a menudo Stewart se unía y yo también— y, en realidad, empezábamos por otros productos en áreas afines y decíamos: "vale".
fullContext: Lenny asks Noah about Slack's "Complaint-Storms" process. Noah explains this method for helping teams look at their product with fresh eyes and build empathy for new users. The process involves teams critically examining customer journeys in competing products first, then applying the same critical lens to their own product to identify pain points and areas for improvement.

vocabulary.definition: Next to or adjoining something else; having a common boundary.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'adjacent' often refers to markets or sectors that are closely related or similar to a company's current operations, allowing for potential expansion or synergy.

insight.nuance: While 'adjacent' implies proximity, it often carries a connotation of strategic relevance, suggesting that the adjacent area is worth exploring for growth opportunities.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals working collaboratively towards a common goal.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, a 'team' is essential for leveraging diverse skills and perspectives, driving projects forward, and fostering innovation through collaboration.

insight.nuance: The term 'team' often implies a sense of unity and shared responsibility, but it can also carry implications of hierarchy or role differentiation depending on the context.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: I think teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it. Take bigger boulder bets. Get to the next hill to see what the horizon wants around you.
keySentence: Take bigger boulder bets to see what the horizon wants around you.
text_ko: 팀들은 종종 그 언덕을 기어 오르다 길을 잃고, 그 뒤에 거대한 멋진 산맥이 있다는 걸 깨닫지 못해요. 더 과감한 베팅(boulder bets)을 해보세요. 다음 언덕까지 올라가서 지평선을 보면 주변에 어떤 기회들이 있는지 알 수 있어요.
text_zh: 很多团队常常在眼前这座小坡上耗着，没看到背后有一大片更宏大、更漂亮的天地。要敢下更大的赌注（boulder bets）。爬到下一个山头，看看地平线周围有哪些机会。
text_es: Creo que los equipos a menudo se pierden arrastrándose cuesta arriba por esa colina, sin darse cuenta de que detrás hay una cordillera enorme e increíblemente hermosa. Hagan apuestas más grandes (boulder bets). Suban a la siguiente colina para ver qué hay en el horizonte.
fullContext: Lenny asks how Slack enables innovation and zero-to-one bets despite being a large company. Noah explains Slack's strategic philosophy using a mountain climbing metaphor. He describes how teams can get trapped focusing on immediate incremental improvements ("crawling up that hill") without seeing the much larger opportunities that exist beyond their current scope.

vocabulary.definition: The line at which the earth's surface and the sky appear to meet; metaphorically, it refers to the limit of one's knowledge, experience, or interest.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'horizon' is often used to describe future opportunities or challenges that an organization may face, encouraging teams to look beyond immediate concerns.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a sense of optimism and potential, suggesting that there are greater opportunities ahead if one looks beyond current limitations.

vocabulary.definition: A term used to describe significant, high-stakes investments or decisions that have the potential for substantial returns or consequences.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business strategy, 'boulder bets' refer to bold moves that can define a company's future direction and success, often involving considerable risk.

insight.nuance: This phrase suggests a willingness to take calculated risks for potentially transformative outcomes, and it is typically used in discussions about innovation and growth strategies.

speaker: Noah Weiss
text: I think when we have those teams, I think it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process of, "Okay.
keySentence: it's important to just give them space to run, to give them ... get a gel free card for maybe the normal process
text_ko: 그런 팀이 생기면 그냥 마음껏 달려보라고 여지를 주는 게 중요하다고 생각해요. 평소 프로세스에서 잠깐 벗어날 수 있는 일종의 면죄부(get-out-of-jail-free card)를 줘야 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得有那样的团队时，重要的是放手给他们空间去运作，甚至在某些常规流程上给他们一张免死金牌(get-out-of-jail-free card)。
text_es: Creo que cuando tenemos esos equipos, es importante darles espacio para que actúen, darles una especie de carta blanca para saltarse el proceso normal de “vale…”.
fullContext: Noah continues explaining how Slack structures innovation teams to work on new product areas like AI. He emphasizes giving these teams freedom from normal corporate processes and focusing on learning velocity rather than traditional planning cycles. The goal is rapid prototyping and user learning that eventually leads to breakthrough products that exceed customer expectations.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: it's like a whole different game where when you see a team that's sort of down and out... sometimes they just need a change of scene, a change of pace.
keySentence: A motivated team has inertia; a down and out team needs a change of scene.
text_ko: 완전히 다른 판이에요. 기운 없고 맥 빠진 팀을 보면... 가끔은 그저 분위기 전환이나 템포 변화가 필요한 것뿐이에요.
text_zh: 感觉完全是另一回事：当你看到一个团队有点低迷、士气不振的时候，有时候他们只是需要换个环境、换换节奏。
text_es: Es como un juego totalmente distinto: cuando ves a un equipo que está pasando por un bache, a veces lo único que necesitan es un cambio de aires y de ritmo.
fullContext: Lenny asks how long you should stick with a project that isn't going well before deciding to move on. Noam explains that while most projects and early companies fail due to lack of stamina rather than running out of money, the key indicator for when to pivot or kill a project is when the team loses motivation and energy. He emphasizes that high-ambiguity projects require tremendous faith and stamina to succeed.

vocabulary.definition: A shift in environment or surroundings that can lead to new perspectives or ideas.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a change of scene can refer to relocating a team or department to foster creativity and innovation, especially when facing stagnation.

insight.nuance: This phrase often implies a refreshing break from routine, but it may not always guarantee improved outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: An alteration in the speed or rhythm of an activity, often to enhance engagement or productivity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate setting, a change of pace might involve varying work schedules or introducing new project management techniques to reinvigorate team dynamics.

insight.nuance: While it suggests a positive shift, it can also imply that the previous pace was ineffective or unproductive.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: I think that one important lesson from that is, no one can be a bystander on product strategy. Just because you've got product in your title doesn't mean you're the only one that should be thinking about product strategy certainly at that level.
keySentence: No one can be a bystander in product strategy; everyone needs a seat at the table.
text_ko: 제 생각에 그걸 통해 얻을 수 있는 중요한 교훈 중 하나는 제품 전략(product strategy)에 대해 누구도 방관자일 수 없다는 거예요. 직함에 '제품'이 들어간다고 해서 그 수준에서 제품 전략을 고민해야 할 사람이 그 사람뿐이라는 건 절대 아니에요.
text_zh: 我觉得从这件事里学到的一个重要教训是：在产品策略 (product strategy) 上没人能置身事外。别以为头衔上写着“产品”就代表只有你该去想，尤其是在那个层面上。
text_es: Creo que una lección importante de eso es que nadie puede quedarse al margen de la estrategia de producto (product strategy). Tener "producto" en el título (product) no significa que seas el único que deba pensar en ella, especialmente a ese nivel.
fullContext: Lenny asks about lessons from Noam's time at Thumbtack during their turnaround period. Noam explains that when companies face challenges like negative growth, the entire leadership team must unite around product strategy rather than leaving it solely to the product team. He emphasizes that at the leadership level, cross-functional collaboration becomes critical for navigating difficult periods.

vocabulary.definition: A person who is present at an event or incident but does not take part in it.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, a bystander may refer to individuals who observe strategic decisions without contributing to the dialogue or decision-making process.

insight.nuance: The term often carries a negative connotation, implying passivity or a lack of engagement in important matters.

vocabulary.definition: A plan that outlines how a company will develop, market, and manage its products to achieve business objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, product strategy is critical for aligning product development with market needs and competitive positioning.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a comprehensive approach that includes research, planning, and execution, rather than just a focus on individual products.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: If you're a large organization and you do some performance management process twice a year and you're 0 to 1 incubator, you've already killed it. It's the wrong incentive.
keySentence: you've already killed it. It's the wrong incentive.
text_ko: 만약 큰 조직인데 연 2회 정도 성과관리 프로세스(performance management process)를 운영하면서 0에서 1을 만드는 인큐베이터(0 to 1 incubator)를 하신다면, 이미 그걸 망쳐버린 거예요. 그건 잘못된 인센티브(incentive)예요.
text_zh: 如果你是大公司，一年只做两次绩效管理（performance management process），还自称是0到1孵化器（0 to 1 incubator），那你基本上已经把它扼杀了。问题在于，这种激励（incentive）机制就是错的。
text_es: Si eres una gran empresa, aplicas un proceso de gestión del desempeño (performance management process) dos veces al año y además te consideras una incubadora 0 to 1 (0 to 1 incubator), ya lo has arruinado. Es el incentivo equivocado.
fullContext: Lenny asks for advice on creating effective startup-within-a-startup initiatives at large companies. Noam discusses the critical importance of designing proper incentive systems for innovation teams. He explains that traditional corporate performance management cycles are fundamentally incompatible with early-stage product development, which requires different timeframes and success metrics than established business operations.

vocabulary.definition: The process of ensuring that an organization's goals are consistently met in an effective and efficient manner through the assessment and improvement of employee performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, performance management is often implemented through regular reviews, feedback mechanisms, and goal-setting to align individual contributions with organizational objectives.

insight.nuance: While performance management can enhance productivity, it may also be perceived as bureaucratic if not executed thoughtfully, particularly in innovative environments.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: Growth masks all problems. You don't really have a, I think, true understanding of what is working well and what is not working well when you have incredible growth.
keySentence: Growth masks all problems.
text_ko: 성장(growth)은 모든 문제를 가려요. 엄청난 성장 상황에서는 뭐가 잘 되고 있고 뭐가 잘 안 되는지 진짜로 제대로 알기 어려워요.
text_zh: 增长(growth)会把所有问题掩盖住。增长特别快的时候，你其实看不清什么起作用、哪里出了问题。
text_es: El crecimiento oculta los problemas. Cuando creces a ritmo vertiginoso no tienes una visión clara de lo que funciona y de lo que no.
fullContext: Lenny asks about lessons from Noam's experience at Thumbtack during their challenging period when growth went negative. Noam explains how rapid growth can hide fundamental business problems that only become apparent when growth slows or reverses. At Thumbtack specifically, strong user acquisition was masking supply-side liquidity issues in their marketplace.

vocabulary.definition: To conceal or hide something, often referring to underlying issues or problems.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'masks' can refer to how rapid growth can obscure operational inefficiencies or challenges that need addressing.

insight.nuance: While 'masks' implies a temporary concealment, it suggests that the underlying issues will eventually resurface if not addressed.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to comprehend or grasp the significance of something, often involving insight and knowledge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, 'understanding' is crucial for evaluating performance metrics, market trends, and customer needs to make informed decisions.

insight.nuance: This term implies a depth of knowledge that goes beyond surface-level awareness, often requiring analysis and critical thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Difficult to believe; extraordinary or remarkable in nature.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business growth, 'incredible' often describes exceptional performance metrics or achievements that surpass expectations.

insight.nuance: While 'incredible' conveys a positive connotation, it can also imply skepticism if used in contexts where results seem too good to be true.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: I always tell people I feel like I'm an IC trapped in a manager's body sometimes. Fundamentally, I like to build, that's why I do this. I like to make things.
keySentence: I feel like an IC trapped in a manager's body; I prefer to lead through teams.
text_ko: 저는 늘 사람들한테 가끔 관리자 몸에 갇힌 개인 기여자(Individual Contributor, IC) 같다고 말해요. 근본적으로 만드는 걸 좋아해서 이 일을 해요. 무언가를 만들어내는 과정을 좋아해요.
text_zh: 我常跟人说，有时候觉得自己像个个人贡献者（IC），可偏偏成了经理。归根结底，我就是喜欢动手做东西，这也是我做这份工作的原因——我就是喜欢把东西做出来。
text_es: Siempre les digo a la gente que a veces me siento como un colaborador individual (individual contributor, IC) atrapado en el cuerpo de un gerente (manager). En el fondo me gusta construir; por eso hago esto. Me gusta crear cosas.
fullContext: Lenny asks about Noam's diverse career experiences across different types of product challenges. Noam explains his motivation for changing roles and companies frequently, describing his core drive to build and create products. An IC refers to an individual contributor - someone who does hands-on work rather than managing others. Noam describes the tension between wanting to build directly versus leading teams to build.

vocabulary.definition: In a basic or essential way; at the core or foundation of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'fundamentally' is often used to emphasize the underlying principles or beliefs that drive decisions and strategies.

insight.nuance: This term conveys a sense of depth and importance, suggesting that the point being made is not just surface-level but integral to understanding the issue.

vocabulary.definition: To create or develop something, often through a process of construction or assembly.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech and startup sectors, 'build' frequently refers to the development of products, services, or systems, emphasizing the act of creation and innovation.

insight.nuance: While 'build' can refer to physical construction, in business, it often implies a more abstract process of developing ideas or strategies.

speaker: Noam Lovinsky
text: When you're thinking about career opportunities and what job to take, it's really, really hard to sniff out really well in a high degree of certainty like success.
keySentence: it's really, really hard to sniff out really well in a high degree of certainty like success.
text_ko: 커리어 기회나 어떤 직업을 택할지 고민할 때, 그 선택이 성공으로 이어질지를 높은 확신으로 가늠해내기는 정말, 정말 어려워요.
text_zh: 当你在考虑职业机会、决定要不要接某份工作的时候，很难有十足把握地判断哪份工作能让你成功。
text_es: Cuando estás valorando oportunidades de carrera y qué puesto aceptar, es muy difícil saber con un alto grado de certeza qué te va a llevar al éxito.
fullContext: Lenny asks for general career advice based on Noam's successful journey across multiple companies. Noam explains that while it's difficult to predict which companies or roles will be successful, you can develop skills for evaluating people and teams. He emphasizes choosing roles that will stretch you and create significant personal growth, even when that growth involves discomfort.

vocabulary.definition: Career opportunities refer to the various job openings and professional paths available to individuals in their field of expertise. They encompass positions that can lead to personal and professional growth.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, career opportunities are often discussed in relation to talent acquisition, employee development, and succession planning, as organizations seek to attract and retain skilled professionals.

insight.nuance: The term carries a positive connotation, suggesting potential for advancement and fulfillment, and is often used in discussions about job markets and recruitment strategies.

vocabulary.definition: A high degree of certainty indicates a strong level of confidence in the accuracy or outcome of a prediction or decision. It reflects a situation where the likelihood of an event occurring is perceived to be very high.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business decision-making, a high degree of certainty is crucial for risk assessment and strategic planning, as it influences investment choices and operational strategies.

insight.nuance: This phrase is often used in contexts where data and analysis support a conclusion, but it may imply an overconfidence if not backed by thorough research.

speaker: Oji Udezue
text: So I guess while I love mental models, while I love frameworks, what I want people who listen to me and maybe listen to you to understand is you have to go deeper.
keySentence: you have to go deeper.
text_ko: 사고 모델(mental models)도 좋아하고 프레임워크(frameworks)도 좋아하긴 한데요, 제 얘기를 듣는 분들하고 아마 당신 얘기를 듣는 분들에게 진짜로 전하고 싶은 건 더 깊이 들어가야 한다는 거예요.
text_zh: 我倒是挺喜欢心智模型(mental models)和各种框架(frameworks)，但我想让听我说话的人——也可能在听你的人——明白的是：别只停在表面，要更深入。
text_es: Supongo que, aunque me encantan los modelos mentales (mental models) y los marcos (frameworks), quiero que la gente que nos escucha entienda que hay que ir más a fondo.
fullContext: Lenny asks Oji about his perspective on frameworks broadly after noting that Oji had an interesting response when asked about frameworks. Oji explains that while he appreciates frameworks and mental models as shortcuts for dense thinking, he believes product managers need to understand the fundamentals behind frameworks rather than applying them blindly. He emphasizes that product management isn't a science and involves significant uncertainty, so practitioners must adapt frameworks to their specific stage and situation.

vocabulary.definition: Frameworks are structured systems or models that provide a foundation for understanding complex concepts or processes. They help organize thoughts and guide decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, frameworks are often used to develop strategies, project management methodologies, or software development processes, enabling teams to work more efficiently and cohesively.

insight.nuance: While frameworks offer valuable guidance, they can sometimes be seen as rigid or limiting if not adapted to specific contexts.
