text_zh: 你要把两件事身体力行：一是有种不服输的韧劲儿——永不松懈、全力以赴，始终把精力放在能产生成果的方向；二是不断改进，总是在想办法把事情做得更好。
text_es: Tienes que encarnar dos cosas. La primera: perseverancia implacable —una entrega total y constante, siempre orientada a la productividad y a obtener resultados positivos. La segunda: mejorar las cosas; siempre debes esforzarte por dejarlas mejor.
fullContext: Lenny asks Robby about his philosophy of 'embodying relentless improvement' and what that means for building successful products. Robby explains that this concept has two key components: relentlessness (complete effort always directed toward positive productivity) and continuously making things better while never being content with the current state. This philosophy drives the constant improvement needed for breakthrough products.

vocabulary.definition: The effective and efficient output of work that not only meets but exceeds expectations, contributing to overall success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business environment, positive productivity is often measured through metrics such as project completion rates, quality of work, and employee engagement, reflecting a healthy work culture.

insight.nuance: This term emphasizes not just quantity but quality and impact, making it preferable in discussions about workplace efficiency and morale.

vocabulary.definition: The act of bringing something into reality or making it visible; a tangible expression of an idea or concept.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, manifestation often refers to the realization of strategic goals, visions, or innovations, translating abstract concepts into concrete outcomes.

insight.nuance: This term carries a sense of intentionality and clarity, making it suitable for discussions about goal-setting and vision execution, but may be seen as vague in more technical contexts.

speaker: Robby Stein
text: Not every great thing is going to be invented by you. Facebook probably created the modern feed, but there's a feed for every single product. At the end of the day, you're just robbing your user base of the opportunity to have a better product.
keySentence: Robbing your user base denies them a better product opportunity.
text_ko: 모든 멋진 걸 여러분이 다 발명해야 하는 건 아니에요. 페이스북이 현대적 피드(feed)를 만든 건 맞지만, 사실 거의 모든 제품(product)에 피드가 있어요. 결국엔 여러분이 사용자 기반(user base)에게 더 나은 제품(product)을 가질 기회를 빼앗고 있는 거예요.
text_zh: 不是所有好东西都得你自己发明出来。Facebook可能创造了现代信息流(feed)的概念，但现在每个产品都有信息流(feed)功能。说到底，你这样做就是让用户失去了用更好产品的机会，这不是坑自己的用户吗？
text_es: No todo lo genial lo vas a inventar tú. Facebook probablemente creó el feed moderno, pero ahora hay un feed para cada producto. Al final del día, solo le estás quitando a tus usuarios la oportunidad de tener un mejor producto.
fullContext: Lenny brings up the controversial launch of Instagram Stories, which was criticized for copying Snapchat's format. Robby defends the decision by explaining that not every innovation needs to be original - formats like feeds become universal primitives across products. He argues that refusing to adopt better formats would be robbing users of improved experiences, emphasizing that the focus should be on serving users rather than claiming originality.

vocabulary.definition: A favorable circumstance or situation that allows for the potential to achieve a desired outcome or benefit.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business development, identifying and capitalizing on opportunities is essential for growth and market expansion.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a time-sensitive chance, suggesting urgency in decision-making and action.

vocabulary.definition: An item or service created to meet the needs or desires of consumers, typically offered for sale in the market.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a product can be a physical good or a digital service, and its development is often guided by market research and consumer feedback.

insight.nuance: The term can encompass a wide range of offerings, from tangible goods to intangible services, and is often associated with branding and customer experience.

speaker: Robby Stein
text: I think the most recent one, and this is true, something even within the last week or two, is that it's so obvious how human-like the interface is becoming with how you can communicate and steer AI.
keySentence: it's so obvious how human-like the interface is becoming with how you can communicate and steer AI.
text_ko: 가장 최근의 변화라고 생각하는 건—사실 지난 일주일이나 이주일 안에 생긴 일인데요—인공지능(AI)와 소통하면서 원하는 방향으로 이끌 수 있게 되면서 인터페이스(interface)가 얼마나 사람처럼 돼 가는지가 너무 확실해졌어요.
text_zh: 我觉得最近这点越来越明显，甚至在过去一两周就能看出来：和人工智能(AI)的交互界面(interface)越来越像真人，你可以像跟人交流一样去沟通和引导它。
text_es: Creo que lo más reciente, y esto es verdad incluso en la última semana o dos, es lo evidente que resulta lo humano que se está volviendo la interfaz, por cómo puedes comunicarte con la IA (AI) y guiarla.
fullContext: Lenny asks Robby what he's learned about building AI products that might surprise people. Robby shares that one of the most surprising recent developments is how human-like AI interfaces have become. He explains that just months ago, users had to do extensive prompt engineering and use specific techniques to get AI to perform tasks, but now the interaction is becoming much more natural and conversational.

vocabulary.definition: A point of interaction or communication between two systems, devices, or entities, often referring to user interfaces in technology.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, an interface is crucial for ensuring that users can effectively interact with software applications, impacting user experience and productivity.

insight.nuance: While 'interface' can refer to any interaction point, it is often used in a tech context to emphasize user-friendliness and design quality.

vocabulary.definition: To convey information or express thoughts and feelings through verbal, non-verbal, or written means.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective communication is essential in business for collaboration, negotiation, and relationship-building among team members and stakeholders.

insight.nuance: While 'communicate' is a broad term, it often implies clarity and effectiveness, particularly in professional settings where miscommunication can lead to significant issues.

vocabulary.definition: To guide or control the direction or course of something, often used in the context of leadership or decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, to steer a project or initiative means to influence its direction and ensure it aligns with strategic goals and objectives.

insight.nuance: The term 'steer' suggests an active role in guiding processes, as opposed to merely observing or allowing events to unfold passively.

vocabulary.definition: Having qualities or characteristics that resemble those of a human being, often used to describe technology that mimics human behavior or appearance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In technology and AI, 'human-like' attributes are increasingly sought after to enhance user interaction and improve the effectiveness of automated systems.

insight.nuance: While 'human-like' can imply advanced capabilities, it may also raise ethical considerations regarding the boundaries between human and machine interactions.

speaker: Robby Stein
text: I think that you need to be the physical manifestation of two pieces of things. One is just relentlessness, just complete effort, but is always exerted in a direction of positive productivity. And then the second is make things better.
keySentence: Be the physical manifestation of relentlessness and always make things better.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 두 가지를 직접 보여줘야 해요(physical manifestation). 하나는 단순한 끈질김이에요 — 전력을 다해 노력하되 그 노력이 항상 생산적인 방향으로 향해야 해요. 그리고 두 번째는 뭔가를 더 좋게 만드는 태도예요, 계속 개선하려고 하는 거죠.
text_zh: 你得把两点具体体现出来：一是要有不懈的劲头、全力以赴，但要把这种努力放在能带来正向成果的方向上；二是要不断把事情做得更好。
text_es: Creo que tienes que encarnar dos cosas: primero, una persistencia implacable —darlo todo, pero siempre orientado a generar productividad y resultados positivos—; y segundo, hacer que las cosas mejoren.
fullContext: Lenny asks about Robby's core philosophy for building successful products. Robby explains his concept of 'embodying relentless improvement' which came from a personal story where his wife described him as 'dissatisfied' - meaning he's driven by a desire to make the world better. He breaks this philosophy into two components: relentless effort in a productive direction, and never being content with the current state of things.

vocabulary.definition: The quality of being persistent and unyielding in pursuit of a goal, often characterized by continuous effort and determination.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, relentlessness is crucial for overcoming challenges and achieving long-term objectives, particularly in competitive environments where perseverance can lead to success.

insight.nuance: While relentlessness is often viewed positively, it can imply a lack of flexibility or consideration for alternative approaches if taken to an extreme.

vocabulary.definition: The state of being productive in a manner that not only achieves results but also contributes positively to overall goals and well-being.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, positive productivity emphasizes not just output quantity but also the quality of work and its alignment with organizational values and objectives.

insight.nuance: This term suggests a holistic approach to productivity, where the means of achieving results are as important as the results themselves, and it is often used in discussions about workplace culture.

speaker: Robby Stein
text: I think there's typically three things I think about. If I were to write a book about how to build great products, there'd be three chapters.
keySentence: there'd be three chapters.
text_ko: 제가 보통 생각하는 건 세 가지예요. 훌륭한 제품을 만드는 방법에 대해 책을 쓴다면 장을 세 개로 나눌 것 같아요.
text_zh: 我通常会想到三件事。要是写一本教你怎么打造优秀产品的书，我会把它分成三章。
text_es: Suelo centrarme en tres cosas. Si tuviera que escribir un libro sobre cómo desarrollar productos excelentes, serían tres capítulos.
fullContext: Lenny asks Robby to share his core product principles that have helped him build successful products across Instagram and Google. Robby outlines his framework for a hypothetical three-chapter book on building great products, starting with the first principle of deeply understanding people. He references Clayton Christensen's 'jobs to be done' framework from 'Competing Against Luck' as a key methodology for understanding why people hire products to solve their problems.

vocabulary.definition: To build means to construct or develop something systematically, often involving the integration of various components or resources. It implies a process of creation that can be tangible or intangible.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and technology, 'build' frequently refers to the development of products, services, or systems, emphasizing the iterative process of creation and improvement.

insight.nuance: While 'build' suggests a proactive and constructive approach, it can also imply a long-term commitment; use it when discussing the creation of complex systems or products that require ongoing effort.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: What's taught now in business schools generally sucks. People aren't prepared educationally, and they sure don't get prepared for it in companies. It's intellectually challenging and it's emotionally intimidating.
keySentence: Business schools generally suck; they don't prepare students for intellectually challenging environments.
text_ko: 지금 경영대학원(business schools)에서 가르치는 건 대체로 형편없어요. 사람들은 교육적으로 준비가 안 돼 있고, 회사에서도 전혀 준비시켜 주지 않아요. 그건 지적으로는 도전적이고 정서적으로는 위압적이에요.
text_zh: 现在商学院教的那些东西基本上都不怎么样。学生在学校里没学到什么真本事，进了公司也得不到什么像样的培训。这活儿既烧脑又让人压力山大。
text_es: Lo que enseñan ahora en las escuelas de negocios es bastante malo. La gente no viene preparada desde la educación, y desde luego tampoco los preparan en las empresas. Es un desafío intelectual enorme y emocionalmente te puede intimidar muchísimo.
fullContext: Lenny asks Roger why so many people are bad at strategy. Roger explains that there are multiple reasons why strategy is difficult for most people. He identifies that business schools have moved away from teaching practical strategy and instead focus on theoretical approaches that don't work in the real world. Companies also don't provide good strategic training, leaving people unprepared for the intellectual and emotional challenges that strategy work requires.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to tasks or concepts that require significant cognitive effort and critical thinking to understand or solve.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business environments, projects that are intellectually challenging often drive innovation and strategic thinking, pushing teams to develop creative solutions.

insight.nuance: This phrase is often used to highlight the complexity of a task, suggesting that it is not only difficult but also rewarding for personal and professional growth.

vocabulary.definition: Describing situations or environments that provoke feelings of fear, anxiety, or self-doubt, particularly in interpersonal or competitive contexts.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate settings, emotionally intimidating scenarios can arise during high-stakes presentations, negotiations, or performance evaluations, affecting employee confidence and engagement.

insight.nuance: This term often conveys a sense of vulnerability, suggesting that the emotional stakes are high and can impact decision-making and performance.

vocabulary.definition: Indicating that an individual has received adequate training or knowledge through formal education to perform effectively in a specific field.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business, being prepared educationally means having the necessary skills and knowledge to meet industry demands and contribute to organizational goals.

insight.nuance: This phrase implies a foundational level of competence that is expected in professional settings, often contrasted with real-world experience.

vocabulary.definition: Institutions that provide education and training in various aspects of business management, finance, marketing, and entrepreneurship.
vocabulary.businessContext: Business schools play a crucial role in shaping future leaders and entrepreneurs by equipping them with theoretical knowledge and practical skills necessary for success in the corporate world.

insight.nuance: While business schools are often associated with high-quality education, there is ongoing debate about their relevance and effectiveness in preparing students for real-world challenges.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: Strategy is an integrated set of choices that compels desired customer action.
keySentence: Strategy is an integrated set of choices that compels desired customer action.
text_ko: 전략(strategy)은 우리가 원하는 고객 행동(customer action)을 하게 만드는, 서로 연계된 선택들의 일관된 집합이에요.
text_zh: 战略 (strategy) 就是一套相互配合的选择，用来促使客户按我们希望的方式行事。
text_es: La estrategia es un conjunto integrado de decisiones que impulsa a los clientes a tomar la acción que buscamos.
fullContext: Lenny asks Roger to define what strategy actually is. Roger provides his core definition of strategy and explains the fundamental challenge - companies can control their internal decisions like factories, R&D spending, and hiring, but they cannot control what customers ultimately choose to do. Strategy is therefore about making the right internal choices to influence customer behavior in your favor.

vocabulary.definition: Combined or coordinated in a way that creates a unified whole.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'integrated' often refers to systems or processes that work together seamlessly to enhance efficiency and effectiveness.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a holistic approach, implying that all components are interconnected and function together, rather than in isolation.

vocabulary.definition: To drive or force someone to take a specific action or adopt a particular behavior.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and sales, understanding what compels customers to act is crucial for developing effective strategies that encourage purchases or engagement.

insight.nuance: The word carries a sense of urgency or necessity, suggesting that the action is not merely encouraged but almost required.

vocabulary.definition: Something that is wished for or sought after; a goal or objective that one aims to achieve.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, 'desired' often refers to customer preferences or outcomes that a company aims to fulfill through its products or services.

insight.nuance: The term implies a level of aspiration or ambition, indicating that the outcome is not just favorable but actively sought after.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: You have to be either differentiated or low cost, there's no way to protect yourself if you're not one of those two.
keySentence: There's no way to protect yourself without being differentiated or low cost.
text_ko: 차별화(differentiated)를 하든지 아니면 저비용(low cost) 전략을 취하든지, 둘 중 하나여야 해요. 둘 중 하나가 아니면 자신을 지킬 방법이 없어요.
text_zh: 要么做到差异化，要么走低成本路线，做不到这两点之一就没法保护自己。
text_es: Tienes que ser o estar diferenciado (differentiated) o ser de bajo coste (low cost); si no estás en uno de esos dos, no hay forma de protegerte.
fullContext: Lenny asks about the two routes to winning that Roger describes - being the lowest cost option or being differentiated. Roger emphasizes that these are the only two viable competitive positions, referencing Michael Porter's foundational strategy work. He uses a vivid analogy to explain what happens to companies that get stuck in the middle - they become vulnerable to competitors who can push them around at will because they have no defensible position.

vocabulary.definition: Characterized by distinct features that set a product or service apart from competitors. This uniqueness can be based on quality, design, or customer experience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a differentiated strategy is crucial for attracting customers in saturated markets, allowing companies to command higher prices and foster brand loyalty.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a positive connotation of innovation and creativity, but can also suggest a risk if the differentiation does not resonate with the target market.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to products or services offered at a price significantly lower than competitors, often achieved through economies of scale or streamlined operations.
vocabulary.businessContext: A low-cost strategy is commonly employed by companies aiming to capture price-sensitive customers and gain market share by undercutting competitors.

insight.nuance: While low cost can attract a broad customer base, it may also imply lower quality, which can affect brand perception if not managed carefully.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: You'll know you're playing to play if you're not aiming to, and accomplishing, having either an offer where Lenny walks into the store, whatever kind of store it is, and says to the person in the store, I want that brand.
keySentence: You're playing to play if Lenny walks into the store and wants that brand.
text_ko: 당신이 플레이 투 플레이(playing to play) 하고 있다는 건, 그런 상태를 목표로 삼지도 않고 또 그걸 이루지도 못하고 있을 때 알 수 있어요. 예를 들어 렌니가 어떤 가게에 들어가서 점원에게 "저건 그 브랜드로 할래요"라고 말하게 만드는 제안이 없다면, 플레이 투 플레이 하는 거예요.
text_zh: 当你并不是刻意去实现“让像 Lenny 那样的人走进店里就说‘我要那个牌子’”这种结果，但最后却做到了，你就知道自己是在“玩票”（playing to play）了。
text_es: Sabrás que estás "jugando por jugar" (playing to play) cuando ni te plantes —y mucho menos consigas— tener una oferta que haga que Lenny entre en cualquier tienda y le diga a la persona que atiende: "quiero esa marca".
fullContext: Lenny asks how to recognize if you're just "playing to play" rather than "playing to win" in your strategy. Roger explains that customers provide the clearest signal - if customers specifically request your brand by name rather than seeing you as interchangeable with competitors, you're truly winning. He uses Lego as an example of a brand that has achieved this level of customer preference and loyalty.

vocabulary.definition: The act of successfully completing a task or achieving a goal.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, accomplishing often refers to meeting project milestones, achieving sales targets, or fulfilling strategic objectives.

insight.nuance: This term conveys a sense of fulfillment and success, often implying that effort and planning were involved.

vocabulary.definition: A name, term, design, symbol, or other feature that distinguishes one seller's goods or services from those of others.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, branding is essential for creating customer loyalty, establishing market presence, and differentiating products or services.

insight.nuance: The term 'brand' encompasses not just the visual identity but also the values and perceptions associated with a company or product.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: I have never met this mythical beast called a great natural strategist. Great strategists have all one thing in common, they just practice.
keySentence: Great strategists are not mythical beasts; they just practice.
text_ko: 저는 '타고난 훌륭한 전략가(great natural strategist)'라는 전설 같은 존재를 만난 적이 없어요. 훌륭한 전략가들에게는 한 가지 공통점이 있어요. 바로 꾸준히 연습한다는 거예요.
text_zh: 我从没见过那种传说中天生的战略家。真正厉害的战略家只有一个共同点：他们都是靠练出来的。
text_es: Nunca me he topado con ese mito del "gran estratega nato". Lo único que tienen en común los grandes estrategas es que practican.
fullContext: As Roger wraps up the conversation, Lenny asks if there's any final advice he'd like to share. Roger addresses a common misconception that some people are just naturally gifted at strategy while others aren't. He argues that strategic thinking is a learned skill that improves with practice, not an innate talent. He encourages listeners to start practicing strategic thinking rather than waiting or assuming they're not cut out for it.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to or resembling a myth; often used to describe something that is imaginary or not based in reality.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'mythical' can refer to concepts or ideals that are often idealized but rarely achieved, such as a 'mythical' perfect product or leader.

insight.nuance: While 'mythical' can imply something fantastical, it can also suggest skepticism about the feasibility of certain business aspirations.

vocabulary.definition: A person skilled in planning and directing overall military operations or the operations of an organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, a strategist is someone who formulates plans to achieve specific goals, often analyzing market trends and competitive landscapes.

insight.nuance: The term carries a connotation of expertise and foresight, implying that a strategist is not just a planner but also a visionary.

vocabulary.definition: The repeated exercise of an activity or skill to acquire or maintain proficiency.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, practice is essential for skill development, team cohesion, and the refinement of strategies, often leading to improved performance and outcomes.

insight.nuance: While 'practice' can imply routine, it also suggests a commitment to continuous improvement and learning.

speaker: Roger Martin
text: I just think of it as a problem solving tool. And what problem should you attempt to solve? You should attempt to solve something where your current outcomes that you're getting are lower than the outcomes you wish you were getting.
keySentence: I see it as a problem solving tool to address a gap.
text_ko: 저는 그걸 그냥 문제 해결 도구(problem-solving tool)로 생각해요. 어떤 문제를 해결해야 하냐고요? 지금 얻고 있는 결과(outcomes)가 원하던 결과보다 낮을 때 그 문제를 해결하려고 시도해봐야 해요.
text_zh: 我就把它当成一个解决问题的工具。那你该解决什么问题？先去解决那些眼下结果达不到你期望的地方。
text_es: Yo lo veo simplemente como una herramienta para resolver problemas. ¿Qué problema deberías intentar resolver? Aquel en el que los resultados que estás obteniendo ahora están por debajo de los que te gustaría tener.
fullContext: Lenny asks Roger for a tactical approach to help people who feel overwhelmed by strategy work. Roger introduces his concept of "betterment over perfection" as a practical starting point. Instead of trying to solve everything at once, he recommends identifying the most painful gap between current performance and desired outcomes, then using strategic thinking to close that specific gap before moving to the next one.

vocabulary.definition: The results or consequences of actions taken, often measured against predefined objectives or goals. Outcomes can be both quantitative and qualitative.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, outcomes are used to evaluate the effectiveness of strategies, projects, and initiatives, guiding future decision-making.

insight.nuance: Outcomes can imply both intended results and unintended consequences, making it important to analyze them comprehensively.

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: I'm very clear that I'm a big fan of test everything, which is any code change that you make, any feature that you introduce has to be in some experiment.
keySentence: any code change that you make, any feature that you introduce has to be in some experiment.
text_ko: 저는 'test everything'(모든 것 테스트) 철학의 열렬한 신봉자라는 걸 분명히 말하고 싶어요. 어떤 코드 변경이든, 어떤 기능을 도입하든 반드시 실험(experiment) 안에서 검증해야 해요.
text_zh: 我很清楚自己非常支持“全部测试”（test everything）的做法：你做的任何代码改动、上线的任何新功能，都要以某个实验（experiment）来验证。
text_es: Quiero dejar claro que soy un gran defensor de "test everything" (test everything): cualquier cambio de código (code change) que hagas o cualquier funcionalidad (feature) que introduzcas tiene que estar dentro de algún experimento (experiment).
fullContext: Lenny asks whether you can be too experiment-driven, mentioning concerns that experimentation leads only to micro-optimizations and prevents big innovations. Ronny responds by advocating for testing everything through experiments, explaining that even seemingly minor changes like small bug fixes can have unexpected impacts on user behavior and business metrics.

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: You have to allocate sometimes to these high risk, high reward ideas. We're going to try something that's most likely to fail. But if it does win, it's going to be a home run.
keySentence: Allocate to high risk, high reward ideas for potential home runs.
text_ko: 때때로 고위험·고보상(high risk, high reward) 아이디어에 자원을 할당해야 해요. 이번엔 성공 가능성이 낮은 시도를 해볼 거예요. 그런데 만약 성공하면 큰 성과, 즉 홈런(home run)이 될 거예요.
text_zh: 有时候得把资源投到那些高风险高回报的点子上。我们要试一个很可能会翻车的做法，但要是成功了，那就是一记全垒打。
text_es: A veces hay que destinar recursos a ideas de alto riesgo y alta recompensa (high risk, high reward). Vamos a probar algo que probablemente fracase. Pero si sale bien, será un éxito rotundo (home run).
fullContext: Continuing his response about experimentation strategy, Ronny explains that teams need a portfolio approach to experiments. While some experiments should focus on incremental improvements with higher success rates, teams must also dedicate resources to ambitious, risky ideas that have low probability of success but could deliver breakthrough results if they work.

vocabulary.definition: To distribute resources or responsibilities for a specific purpose or task.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, allocation often refers to the distribution of budget, personnel, or time to various projects or departments to optimize efficiency and achieve strategic goals.

insight.nuance: While 'allocate' is often used in a formal context, it can imply a strategic decision-making process that involves prioritizing certain areas over others.

vocabulary.definition: A principle suggesting that investments or ventures with greater potential for loss also have the potential for greater returns.
vocabulary.businessContext: This concept is frequently referenced in investment strategies and entrepreneurial ventures, where taking calculated risks can lead to significant financial gains or innovations.

insight.nuance: This phrase is often used to justify pursuing ambitious projects, but it also carries the implication that one must be prepared for potential failures.

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: And it's amazing how many times I've seen people come up with new designs or a radical new idea. And they believe in it, and that's okay.
keySentence: And they believe in it, and that's okay.
text_ko: 정말 놀라운 건 사람들이 새로운 디자인이나 파격적인 아이디어를 내는 걸 제가 생각보다 자주 본다는 거예요. 그리고 그들이 그걸 믿는다고 해도 괜찮아요.
text_zh: 我见过很多次有人想出新的设计或激进的新点子，他们相信自己的想法，这没问题。
text_es: Me sorprende cuántas veces veo a personas que proponen diseños nuevos o ideas radicales. Creen en ellas, y eso está bien.
fullContext: Ronny continues discussing the balance between incremental and revolutionary experiments. He acknowledges that it's natural for people to believe strongly in their big ideas, but emphasizes the importance of setting realistic expectations about failure rates, especially for ambitious experiments that attempt major changes to user experiences.

vocabulary.definition: To have confidence in the truth, existence, or reliability of something or someone.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, believing in a product, idea, or team can drive motivation and commitment, influencing decision-making and investment.

insight.nuance: This phrase often conveys a deeper emotional or personal commitment, rather than just a rational assessment.

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: Of these experiments, 92% failed to improve the metric that we were trying to move. So only 8% of our ideas actually were successful at moving the key metrics.
keySentence: Only 8% of our ideas successfully move the key metrics.
text_ko: 이 실험들(experiments) 중 92%는 우리가 움직이려고 했던 지표(metric)를 개선하지 못했어요. 그래서 결국 우리 아이디어(ideas) 중 실제로 핵심 지표(key metrics)를 움직인 건 단 8%뿐이었어요.
text_zh: 这些实验里面，92%都没能把我们想要提升的指标搞上去。所以我们的想法中，真正能推动关键指标的其实只有8%。
text_es: De todos estos experimentos, el 92% no logró mejorar la métrica que queríamos impactar. O sea que solo el 8% de nuestras ideas realmente funcionaron para mover las métricas clave.
fullContext: Ronny is explaining the reality of experiment success rates at Airbnb's search team, where he ran approximately 250 experiments during his tenure. Despite these experiments ultimately contributing to a 6% overall improvement in revenue, the vast majority of individual experiment ideas failed to move their target metrics, illustrating the humble reality of how difficult it is to predict what will actually work.

vocabulary.definition: Metrics are quantitative measures used to assess, compare, and track performance or progress towards specific goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, metrics are essential for evaluating the effectiveness of strategies, products, or processes, often guiding decision-making and resource allocation.

insight.nuance: While metrics imply a focus on numerical data, they can also encompass qualitative assessments when evaluating broader performance indicators.

vocabulary.definition: Successful refers to achieving desired outcomes or goals, often resulting in positive recognition or financial gain.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, a successful initiative or project typically meets or exceeds its objectives, contributing to overall company growth and profitability.

insight.nuance: The term can carry subjective connotations, as success may vary based on individual or organizational standards and expectations.

vocabulary.definition: Experiments are systematic trials or tests conducted to investigate hypotheses or explore new ideas, often involving controlled conditions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech, experiments are frequently employed to test product features, marketing strategies, or user engagement methods to gather data and inform future decisions.

insight.nuance: While experiments imply a level of uncertainty and risk, they are essential for innovation and learning, distinguishing them from routine operations.

vocabulary.definition: To improve means to make something better or enhance its quality, performance, or effectiveness.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, improving processes, products, or services is crucial for maintaining competitiveness and meeting customer needs, often driven by data analysis and feedback.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a positive change but can imply varying degrees of enhancement depending on the context and specific goals.

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: I think one of the mistakes that some company makes is they launch a lot of experiments and never go back and summarize the learnings.
keySentence: they launch a lot of experiments and never go back and summarize the learnings.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 어떤 회사들이 실수로 많이 하는 것 중 하나가 실험(experiments)을 잔뜩 해 놓고 그 배운 점(learnings)을 돌아와서 정리하지 않는 거예요.
text_zh: 我觉得有些公司常犯的一个错误，就是做了很多实验（experiments），却不回头总结学到的东西（learnings）。
text_es: Creo que uno de los errores que cometen algunas empresas es lanzar muchos experimentos y luego no volver para resumir lo aprendido (learnings).
fullContext: Lenny suggests using AI to create product roadmaps from experiment patterns, which leads Ronny to discuss the importance of institutional memory in experimentation. He explains that many companies fail to capture and share learnings from their experiments, missing opportunities to build organizational knowledge that could inform future decisions and prevent repeating mistakes.

vocabulary.definition: To condense and present the main points or findings of a larger body of information in a concise manner.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, summarizing is crucial for reporting results of projects, meetings, or research, enabling stakeholders to quickly grasp essential insights without wading through extensive details.

insight.nuance: Summarizing should focus on clarity and relevance, ensuring that key messages are communicated effectively without oversimplifying complex information.

vocabulary.definition: Insights or knowledge gained from experiences, particularly from mistakes or successes in a specific context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, learnings are often documented after projects or initiatives to inform future strategies and avoid repeating past errors.

insight.nuance: The term 'learnings' can sometimes be perceived as informal; in formal reports, it may be preferable to use 'insights' or 'findings.'

speaker: Ronny Kohavi
text: Document it. We had a large deck internally of these successes and failures, and we encourage people to look at them. The other thing that's very beneficial is just to have your whole history of experiments and do some ability to search by keywords.
keySentence: Document a large deck internally to track successes and failures, searchable by keywords.
text_ko: 문서로 남겨 두세요. 저희는 내부적으로 이런 성공·실패 사례를 모아둔 큰 슬라이드 덱(deck)이 있었고, 사람들에게 그걸 보라고 권장해요. 또 정말 유용한 건 전체 실험(experiments) 이력을 남겨서 키워드(keywords)로 검색할 수 있게 해두는 거예요.
text_zh: 把这些都记录下来。我们内部有一套很全的材料，把这些成功和失败的案例都整理在里面，我们也鼓励大家多去看看。另外还有一个特别有用的做法，就是把你们所有的实验历史都保存好，然后可以按关键词来搜索查找。
text_es: Documéntalo todo. Nosotros teníamos internamente una presentación bien grande con todos estos éxitos y fracasos, y animábamos a la gente a revisarla. Lo otro que es súper útil es tener todo el historial de experimentos y poder buscar por palabras clave.
fullContext: Lenny asks for practical advice on how teams can remember surprising experiment results when people leave the company years later. Ronny recommends systematic documentation and searchable experiment histories, noting that at Microsoft they were running 20-25,000 experiments per year, making searchability crucial for finding relevant past learnings before launching new experiments.

vocabulary.definition: A written or electronic record that provides information or evidence regarding a particular subject or activity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, documentation is essential for maintaining clear communication, tracking progress, and ensuring compliance with regulations.

insight.nuance: The term 'document' can imply a formal record, so it is best used in contexts where accuracy and permanence are important.

vocabulary.definition: Systematic tests or trials conducted to discover or validate information, hypotheses, or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech companies, experiments are often employed to test new ideas, products, or strategies, allowing for data-driven decision-making.

insight.nuance: The term 'experiments' carries a connotation of innovation and risk-taking; it's best used in contexts where exploration and learning are valued.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: I first opened up my DMs- I had 'em closed, which is like traditionally the default on Twitter for a long time.
keySentence: I had 'em closed, which is like traditionally the default on Twitter for a long time.
text_ko: 제가 처음으로 다이렉트 메시지(DMs)를 열었어요 — 원래는 닫아놨었거든요. 트위터에서는 오랫동안 그게 기본값이었어요.
text_zh: 这是我第一次把私信(DMs)打开——之前一直关着，推特(Twitter)长期默认就是关着的。
text_es: La primera vez que abrí mis mensajes directos (DMs), los tenía cerrados —algo que durante mucho tiempo fue la opción por defecto en Twitter.
fullContext: Lenny asks Ryan about his practice of offering free advice to founders who DM him on Twitter. Ryan explains how he initially hesitated to open his direct messages because he expected to receive spam, but was surprised to find that wasn't the case. This led to him actively inviting founders to reach out for advice, which he then sometimes shares publicly (anonymized) as a form of micro-blogging.

vocabulary.definition: A default is a preset option or value that is automatically selected unless an alternative is specified by the user. In technology, it often refers to settings or configurations that are applied when no other choice is made.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, understanding defaults is crucial for user experience design, as they can significantly influence user behavior and decision-making processes.

insight.nuance: The term 'default' can imply a lack of active choice, which may carry a negative connotation in contexts where proactive decision-making is valued.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: And maybe the biggest surprise was a lot of people are pretty vulnerable. These are strangers, founders who DM me saying, "Hey, I'm- we have three months runway left. We're running out of money. Here's a situation.
keySentence: a lot of people are pretty vulnerable.
text_ko: 그리고 아마도 가장 놀랐던 건 많은 사람들이 꽤 취약하다는 점이었어요. 낯선 창업자들(founders)이 다이렉트 메시지(DM)로 저한테 "저희 런웨이(runway)가 세 달밖에 남지 않았어요. 자금이 거의 바닥나가고 있어요. 이런 상황이에요"라고 보내요.
text_zh: 也许最让我意外的是，很多人其实很脆弱。这些都是陌生人，都是创始人，会私信我 (DM) 说：“嗨，我……我们只剩三个月的跑道 (runway)，资金快见底了，情况是这样的：”
text_es: Y quizá lo que más me sorprendió fue que mucha gente estaba bastante vulnerable. Eran personas que no conocía, fundadores que me escribían por mensajes directos (DM) diciendo: "Oye, eh... nos quedan tres meses de margen de caja (runway). Se nos está acabando el dinero. Te explico la situación."
fullContext: Lenny asks what Ryan has learned from founders who DM him questions. Ryan explains that he was surprised by how vulnerable and authentic people are willing to be in private messages, sharing serious problems like running out of funding. He reflects on how founders typically have to project confidence publicly while dealing with significant challenges privately.

vocabulary.definition: Exposed to the possibility of being harmed or attacked, either physically or emotionally.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, being vulnerable often refers to a company's financial or operational weaknesses that could be exploited by competitors or lead to failure.

insight.nuance: While vulnerability can imply weakness, it can also indicate openness and honesty, especially in discussions about challenges faced by startups.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of time a company can operate before it runs out of cash, typically measured in months.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, runway is a critical metric for assessing a company's financial health and sustainability, influencing investment decisions and strategic planning.

insight.nuance: Runway is often discussed in terms of cash flow management and can indicate urgency for fundraising or cost-cutting measures.

vocabulary.definition: A set of circumstances in which one finds oneself; a state of affairs.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'situation' often refers to the current state of a company or market, particularly when assessing challenges or opportunities.

insight.nuance: The term can be neutral but may carry negative connotations depending on the context, especially if it refers to a crisis or problematic scenario.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: I do spend time, ironically, like. challenging founders sometimes when they're thinking about raising or thinking about an idea to- to not raise. Um, people who are in tech, uh, especially, are certain bubbles of tech, that's the default.
keySentence: In certain bubbles of tech, that's the default to raise money immediately.
text_ko: 아이러니하게도 저는 때때로 창업자들(founders)이 자금 조달(raising)을 고민하거나 오히려 투자를 받지 않는 쪽을 생각할 때, 그 판단을 도전적으로 물어보는 데 꽤 시간을 써요. 특히 테크(tech) 업계에 있는 사람들은 특정 테크 버블(bubbles of tech)에 갇혀 있는 게 기본값(default)인 경우가 많아요.
text_zh: 说来有点讽刺，我有时会花时间去反问创始人 (founders)：当他们在考虑要不要融资 (raising) 或者在琢磨一个点子时，我会劝他们别急着去融资。特别是在科技圈 (tech) 的某些小圈子里，去融资几乎是默认的做法。
text_es: A veces, irónicamente, suelo retar a los fundadores: cuando están pensando en levantar fondos (raising) o cuando surge una idea, les planteo que quizá no deberían levantar fondos. La gente que está en tecnología, sobre todo en ciertas burbujas del sector, da por hecho que esa es la opción por defecto.
fullContext: Lenny asks Ryan about his advice to founders considering whether to start a company, given how difficult startups are. Ryan explains that he often challenges founders who assume they need to raise venture capital immediately after having an idea. He points out that in certain tech circles, fundraising has become the default first step, even when it may not be necessary or appropriate.

vocabulary.definition: Default refers to a pre-set condition or standard that is automatically applied unless an alternative is specified.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, default settings in software applications can significantly influence user behavior and decision-making processes.

insight.nuance: The term can also imply a lack of action or choice, suggesting complacency or an unexamined status quo.

vocabulary.definition: Founders are individuals who establish or create a company or organization, often taking on significant risk and responsibility.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, founders are crucial as they drive the vision, culture, and initial growth of their ventures, often seeking investment to scale their ideas.

insight.nuance: The term 'founder' carries a sense of innovation and leadership but can also imply a level of inexperience in navigating business challenges.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: I think it's super important that founders see a line of sight to work on this for ... I think my rule of thumb is a decade, just do you see yourself working on this for a decade?
keySentence: Founders should see a line of sight to work on this for a decade.
text_ko: 창업자가 앞으로 이 일을 계속해나갈 수 있겠다는 그림을 그려볼 수 있는지가 정말 중요해요. 제 경험칙은 대략 10년이에요. 스스로 이걸 10년 동안 해나갈 수 있을 것 같으세요?
text_zh: 我觉得特别重要的一点是，创始人得能看出这件事有长期可走的路。我的经验是把时间拉到十年：你能想象自己为这件事坚持十年吗？
text_es: Creo que es muy importante que los fundadores puedan ver una vía clara para trabajar en esto. Mi regla general es una década; es decir, ¿se ven trabajando en esto durante diez años?
fullContext: Ryan continues discussing his advice for founders considering starting a company. He explains his framework for evaluating startup commitment - founders should be able to envision working on their idea for a decade. While acknowledging that most startups fail before reaching that timeframe, he believes this long-term perspective serves as an important litmus test for genuine passion and commitment to the problem they're trying to solve.

vocabulary.definition: A general principle or guideline based on practical experience rather than a strict rule.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a rule of thumb can help entrepreneurs make quick decisions based on past experiences or common practices, especially in uncertain situations.

insight.nuance: While useful, a rule of thumb should not replace thorough analysis or data-driven decision-making.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: I don't know how to articulate that- that feeling, but that flutter in your stomach that you wake up with in the morning of just anxiety and stress and- and worry.
keySentence: that flutter in your stomach that you wake up with in the morning of just anxiety and stress and- and worry.
text_ko: 그 느낌을 어떻게 표현해야 할지 모르겠어요. 아침에 일어나자마자 속이 울렁거리고 불안하고 스트레스 받고 걱정으로 가득한 그런 기분이에요.
text_zh: 我说不上来那种感觉，就是早上醒来心里七上八下、肚子里翻腾，满是焦虑、压力和担忧。
text_es: No sé cómo explicarlo: esa sensación, ese nudo en el estómago con el que te despiertas por la mañana, simplemente de ansiedad, estrés y preocupación.
fullContext: Ryan is describing the emotional toll of being a founder during difficult periods at Product Hunt. He's explaining to Lenny the physical manifestation of startup stress - the stomach flutter of anxiety upon waking. He emphasizes how being in a leadership position compounds this difficulty because founders must project confidence externally while dealing with internal anxiety, creating additional pressure beyond the underlying business challenges.

vocabulary.definition: To express an idea or feeling fluently and coherently. It involves the ability to convey thoughts clearly and effectively.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being articulate is crucial for effective communication during presentations, meetings, and negotiations, as it helps convey complex ideas succinctly.

insight.nuance: While 'articulate' generally has a positive connotation, it may imply that someone is overly verbose if used inappropriately.

vocabulary.definition: A feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease about something with an uncertain outcome. It can manifest physically and mentally.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, anxiety can affect employee performance and decision-making, often leading to decreased productivity and morale.

insight.nuance: Anxiety can be a normal response to stress, but excessive anxiety may indicate deeper issues that require attention.

vocabulary.definition: A state of mental or emotional strain resulting from challenging or adverse circumstances. It can impact both physical and psychological well-being.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business environments, stress is often linked to tight deadlines, high expectations, and workload, which can lead to burnout if not managed effectively.

insight.nuance: While stress can sometimes motivate individuals to perform better, chronic stress is detrimental and should be addressed proactively.

speaker: Ryan Hoover
text: The biggest surprise has probably been ... There are cases when I didn't think the company would make it.
keySentence: There are cases when I didn't think the company would make it.
text_ko: 가장 놀라웠던 건 아마도… 회사가 버티지 못할 거라고 생각했던 순간들이 있었다는 점이에요.
text_zh: 最大的惊讶大概是……有好几次我都觉得公司撑不下去了。
text_es: Probablemente lo que más me ha sorprendido... Ha habido momentos en los que no creí que la empresa iba a salir adelante.
fullContext: Lenny asks Ryan what has surprised him most about angel investing. Ryan explains that his biggest surprise has been seeing companies he had mentally written off as failures eventually succeed through pivots or unexpected breakthroughs. This taught him never to count portfolio companies out until they're definitively done, highlighting the unpredictable nature of startup journeys and the importance of backing resilient founders.

vocabulary.definition: An unexpected event or occurrence that causes astonishment or shock.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a surprise can refer to unforeseen outcomes in market trends, financial results, or project developments that can significantly impact strategic planning.

insight.nuance: While 'surprise' can have a positive connotation, such as a pleasant surprise in sales growth, it can also imply negative outcomes, making it essential to clarify the context.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: Copilot is essentially that magnified by many lines of code. It is multi-line autocomplete that is fundamentally powered by an AI model called CodeX, which is a derivative of another one that you might be familiar with, GPT-3.
keySentence: Copilot is fundamentally powered by an AI model called CodeX.
text_ko: 코파일럿(Copilot)은 본질적으로 많은 코드 줄로 확장된 기능이에요. 여러 줄을 한꺼번에 자동완성해 주는 멀티라인 자동완성(multi-line autocomplete)이고, 근본적으로는 코드엑스(CodeX)라는 AI 모델(AI model)이 구동해요. 코드엑스는 아마 들어보셨을 GPT-3(GPT-3)의 파생 모델이에요.
text_zh: Copilot 本质上就是把自动补全放大到多行代码，换句话说就是一种多行自动补全(multi-line autocomplete)。它背后由一个叫 CodeX 的 AI 模型(CodeX) 驱动，而 CodeX 又是从你可能熟悉的 GPT-3(GPT-3) 衍生出来的。
text_es: Copilot es, básicamente, lo mismo pero ampliado para manejar muchas líneas de código. Es un autocompletado multilínea (multi-line autocomplete) que se alimenta de un modelo de IA (AI) llamado CodeX, que a su vez deriva de otro con el que quizá ya estés familiarizado: GPT-3.
fullContext: Lenny asks Ryan to explain what GitHub Copilot is for listeners who aren't familiar with it. Ryan describes how Copilot evolved from basic autocomplete features that developers have used for decades. He explains that while traditional autocomplete only suggests simple completions like variable names, Copilot uses advanced AI to suggest entire blocks of code based on context, comments, and surrounding code patterns.

vocabulary.definition: In a basic and essential way; at the core or root of something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, 'fundamentally' is often used to emphasize the underlying principles or assumptions that drive a strategy or decision.

insight.nuance: This term conveys a sense of depth and importance, suggesting that the point being made is not merely superficial.

vocabulary.definition: Something that is based on another source; not original but derived from something else.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, 'derivative' often refers to products or technologies that build upon or adapt existing innovations, highlighting their relationship to prior developments.

insight.nuance: While 'derivative' can imply a lack of originality, it can also suggest a valuable evolution of existing ideas.

vocabulary.definition: A feature that predicts and suggests completions for text input based on prior data or patterns.
vocabulary.businessContext: In software development and user interface design, 'autocomplete' enhances user experience by increasing efficiency and reducing errors during data entry.

insight.nuance: This term is often associated with technology products that aim to streamline user interactions, making it a positive feature in most contexts.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: That's just labor. It's not creating. It's just typing.
keySentence: That's just labor, not creating, just typing.
text_ko: 그건 그냥 단순 노동이에요. 창조하는 일이 아니고요. 그냥 타이핑만 하는 거예요.
text_zh: 那只是体力活，不是创造性工作，就是在敲键盘而已。
text_es: Eso es trabajo rutinario, no es creación. Es solo teclear.
fullContext: Ryan continues explaining the value proposition of Copilot by describing common frustrations developers face. He argues that much of a developer's time is spent on mundane tasks like remembering API syntax or creating test data, rather than the creative problem-solving aspects of programming. Ryan positions Copilot as a tool that eliminates this 'busy work' so developers can focus on the creative and strategic aspects of coding.

vocabulary.definition: Labor refers to the physical or mental effort exerted in the production of goods or services, often associated with work performed by employees.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, labor is a critical factor of production, and understanding labor costs and productivity is essential for financial planning and operational efficiency.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a sense of hard work or effort, and it is often used in discussions about workforce management, labor laws, and economic conditions.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: We had actually created a snapshot of GitHub's public code for what we call the Arctic Code Vault, right? Essentially, this is up in like way in the Northlands of Finland, there's a seed vault. We were like, you know what?
keySentence: we had actually created a snapshot of GitHub's public code for what we call the Arctic Code Vault
text_ko: 사실 저희는 GitHub 공개 코드 전체를 스냅샷(snapshot)으로 만들어 ‘아틱 코드 볼트(Arctic Code Vault)’에 보관해뒀어요. 요컨대, 이건 핀란드 북부에 있는 종자 저장고(seed vault) 같은 곳이에요. 그래서 우리는 “그래, 해보자”라고 했어요.
text_zh: 其实我们当时把 GitHub 上的公开代码做了个快照，放到我们叫“北极代码库”(Arctic Code Vault)的项目里。它基本上就放在芬兰北部，有点像一个种子库(seed vault)。然后我们就想，干脆……
text_es: En realidad habíamos creado una instantánea (snapshot) del código público de GitHub para lo que llamamos la Bóveda de Código Ártico (Arctic Code Vault). O sea, está muy al norte de Finlandia, donde hay una bóveda de semillas (seed vault). Y nos dijimos: “¿sabes qué?”
fullContext: Ryan tells the origin story of how Copilot began when OpenAI was aggressively downloading GitHub's repositories for training data. He explains that GitHub had previously created the Arctic Code Vault - a physical preservation project storing code on silver film in Finland, similar to seed vaults that preserve plant genetics. This existing dataset became the foundation for training the AI model that would become Copilot.

vocabulary.definition: A snapshot is a representation or capture of a system's state at a specific point in time. It allows users to view or restore the system as it was at that moment.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech, snapshots are frequently used in version control systems to capture the state of code or data, enabling developers to revert to previous versions or analyze changes over time.

insight.nuance: The term implies a temporary or momentary capture, and while it is useful for tracking changes, it may not reflect ongoing developments unless regularly updated.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: The original team that was working on Copilot at GitHub was the team that we call GitHub Next. Essentially their job is to work on second and third horizon projects. What some folks might call moonshots, right?
keySentence: GitHub Next works on second and third horizon projects, or moonshots.
text_ko: GitHub에서 코파일럿(Copilot)을 원래 작업하던 팀이 바로 우리가 깃허브 넥스트(GitHub Next)라고 부르는 팀이에요. 본질적으로 그들의 일은 제2·제3 호라이즌(horizon) 프로젝트를 맡아서 진행하는 거예요. 어떤 사람들은 이런 걸 문샷(moonshots)이라고 부르기도 하죠, 그렇죠?
text_zh: 最早在 GitHub 负责 Copilot 的那支团队，就是我们叫 GitHub Next 的团队。简单来说，他们主要做第二、第三阶段的未来探索项目（second- and third-horizon projects），也就是有些人说的“登月式”项目（moonshots），对吧？
text_es: El equipo original que trabajaba en Copilot en GitHub es el que llamamos GitHub Next. En esencia se ocupan de proyectos a mediano y largo plazo (second and third horizon projects), lo que algunos podrían llamar «moonshots» (moonshots).
fullContext: Lenny asks whether there was a clear moment when leadership decided to double down on Copilot as a major investment. Ryan explains GitHub's organizational structure for innovation, describing GitHub Next as their R&D team focused on long-term experimental projects. He defines horizon projects as initiatives organized by time and uncertainty rather than calendar dates, with different horizons representing different levels of risk and timeline expectations.

vocabulary.definition: Horizon projects refer to initiatives that are focused on long-term goals and future innovations, typically extending beyond the immediate operational scope of an organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, horizon projects are often pursued to explore new markets or technologies that may not yield immediate returns but are essential for future growth and competitiveness.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a forward-thinking approach, emphasizing the importance of balancing current operations with future possibilities.

vocabulary.definition: Moonshots are ambitious, exploratory projects aimed at achieving significant breakthroughs or innovations, often with high risks and uncertain outcomes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech and startup world, moonshots are typically associated with transformative ideas that could disrupt industries or create entirely new markets, often requiring substantial investment and visionary leadership.

insight.nuance: The term conveys a sense of grand ambition and the willingness to take risks for potentially revolutionary results, making it suitable for visionary discussions.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: Making sure that you've got a good mix of engineers who are comfortable maintaining a service, as well as engineers and researchers who are really thinking about... what is the new thing that we've brought to market.
keySentence: A good mix of engineers can bring that vision to it.
text_ko: 서비스(service)를 안정적으로 운영·유지하는 데 익숙한 엔지니어(engineers)들과, 우리가 시장에 내놓은 것이 진짜로 무엇이 새롭고 의미 있는지 진지하게 고민하는 연구원(researchers)과 엔지니어들이 적절히 섞여 있어야 해요.
text_zh: 要确保团队里有合适的人才搭配：既有对维护服务得心应手的工程师(engineers)，也有真正去思考我们能向市场带来什么新东西的工程师和研究人员(researchers)。
text_es: Asegúrate de contar con una buena mezcla: ingenieros que se sientan cómodos manteniendo el servicio, y otros ingenieros e investigadores que realmente se pregunten qué es lo nuevo que estamos llevando al mercado.
fullContext: Ryan shares lessons learned about transitioning experimental R&D projects to operational products within large companies. He emphasizes the importance of creating hybrid teams that combine researchers who understand the original innovation with engineers who have the skills to scale and maintain production services. This advice comes from GitHub's experience moving Copilot from their experimental Next team to their production engineering teams.

vocabulary.definition: Researchers are individuals who systematically investigate and study various subjects to develop new knowledge or insights.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the tech industry, researchers play a crucial role in innovation, helping to identify market needs and develop new technologies or products that can be brought to market.

insight.nuance: The term often implies a rigorous, methodical approach to inquiry, and is typically used in contexts where evidence-based findings are valued.

speaker: Ryan J. Salva
text: As a general rule, as a general principle, I certainly try to make sure that we're always reserving some capacity for bold, audacious experimental research projects. You can think of those really uncertain bets as being five to 10% of the team's capacity.
keySentence: We reserve capacity for bold, audacious experimental research projects.
text_ko: 일반적으로는 저는 대담하고 과감한 실험적 연구 프로젝트(experimental research projects)를 위해 항상 일정한 여력을 남겨두려고 해요. 그런 정말 불확실한 베팅(bets)은 팀 역량의 약 5~10% 정도로 보면 돼요.
text_zh: 通常我会确保团队总留出一点带宽，去做那些大胆、冒险的实验性研究。把这些高度不确定的尝试当作占团队能力大概5%到10%就行。
text_es: Como regla general, procuro que siempre reservemos algo de capacidad para proyectos de investigación experimentales y audaces. Puedes ver esas apuestas muy inciertas como entre el 5% y el 10% de la capacidad del equipo.
fullContext: Lenny asks Ryan for advice on balancing bold bets versus incremental improvements when managing product portfolios at large companies. Ryan provides specific percentage recommendations for resource allocation: 5-10% on experimental moonshots, 25-30% on maintaining existing products, and about 60% on incremental improvements to in-market products. He notes this framework works for larger teams, while startups typically must go all-in on single big bets.

vocabulary.definition: Showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks; daring.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'audacious' often describes innovative strategies or projects that challenge the status quo and require significant investment and commitment.

insight.nuance: While 'audacious' conveys a sense of bravery, it can also imply recklessness if not supported by sound reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to or based on untested ideas or methods; involving trial and error.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and tech, 'experimental' refers to projects or initiatives that are in the testing phase, often aimed at innovation or discovering new market opportunities.

insight.nuance: The term suggests a focus on innovation and learning, but may also imply uncertainty and potential failure.

vocabulary.definition: The maximum amount that something can contain or produce; the ability to hold or accommodate.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'capacity' often refers to the resources available for production, including human resources, technology, and financial assets, which can impact strategic planning.

insight.nuance: While 'capacity' generally denotes potential, it can also imply limitations when resources are fully utilized.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: I often use this analogy of if you're doing a home renovation, you can have the most beautiful rendering of the new bedroom and we're going to have these lamps on the side of the bed that are coming out from the wall.
keySentence: you can have the most beautiful rendering of the new bedroom
text_ko: 저는 집 리모델링 비유를 자주 들어요. 집을 고친다고 하면 새 침실을 가장 멋지게 렌더링(rendering)해 놓고 침대 옆에 벽에서 나오는 조명을 달 거예요, 하는 식이에요.
text_zh: 我经常打个比方：做房屋装修的时候，你可以把新卧室的效果图做得很漂亮，比如在床头两侧装那种从墙面伸出来的壁灯。
text_es: Suelo usar esta analogía: si estás haciendo una reforma en casa, puedes tener el render (rendering) más bonito del nuevo dormitorio y decidir que vas a poner unas lámparas al lado de la cama que salen de la pared.
fullContext: Ryan uses this home renovation analogy to explain why technical feasibility must be explored during the shaping phase, not after committing to build something. He's illustrating how beautiful designs or plans can fall apart when they encounter technical reality - just like planning wall-mounted lamps without checking if electrical wiring exists in that wall. This speaks to the core Shape Up principle of de-risking projects upfront rather than discovering problems mid-build.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison between two different things that highlights some form of similarity, often used to explain a concept or idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, analogies are frequently employed to simplify complex ideas, making them more relatable to stakeholders or team members.

insight.nuance: While analogies can clarify, they should be used carefully to avoid oversimplification or misleading comparisons.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: We're not going to start something unless we can see the end from the beginning.
keySentence: We won't start a big concept unless we can see the end from the beginning.
text_ko: 처음부터 끝이 보이지 않으면 시작하지 않아요.
text_zh: 除非一开始就能看清最后的结果，否则我们不会着手去做。
text_es: No empezamos nada si desde el principio no vemos cómo va a acabar.
fullContext: Ryan explains a core Shape Up principle about project clarity before starting work. Instead of estimating big, vague concepts, Shape Up requires creating clear diagrams during shaping sessions where all team members - engineers, product managers, and designers - can understand exactly what needs to be built. This ensures everyone can visualize the end result before committing engineering time to the project.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: We're going to go the other way around and we're going to say, what is the maximum amount of time we're willing to go before we actually finish something?
keySentence: what is the maximum amount of time we're willing to go before we actually finish something?
text_ko: 이번엔 반대로 해볼게요. 어떤 일을 실제로 끝내기까지 우리가 기꺼이 허용할 수 있는 최대 시간을 얼마로 잡을까요?
text_zh: 我们换个角度，反过来问：在真正把一件事做完之前，我们最多愿意等多久？
text_es: Vamos a hacerlo al revés y preguntarnos: ¿cuánto tiempo, como máximo, estamos dispuestos a dejar pasar antes de terminarlo de verdad?
fullContext: Ryan describes the fundamental Shape Up approach of working backward from time constraints rather than forward from scope. Instead of estimating how long a feature will take to build, Shape Up starts by setting a maximum time budget (appetite) and then shapes the solution to fit within that constraint. This forces teams to make deliberate trade-offs and ensures projects don't drag on indefinitely.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: There was always this really intense urgency from both Jason and David, 'We've got to get to something we can ship. We have to finish this and move on.
keySentence: We've got to get to something we can ship.
text_ko: 제이슨과 데이비드 양쪽에서 항상 정말 강한 긴박감이 있었어요. "우리가 실제로 출시(ship)할 수 있는 수준까지 만들어야 해요. 이걸 마무리하고 다음으로 넘어가야 해요."
text_zh: Jason 和 David 一直很着急，总是催着说：“我们得赶出可以上线（ship）的版本，先把这事做完再往下走。”
text_es: Siempre había una sensación de urgencia enorme por parte de Jason y David: "Tenemos que llegar a algo que podamos lanzar (ship). Tenemos que terminar esto y seguir adelante."
fullContext: Ryan describes the cultural foundation that led to Shape Up at Basecamp's early days. Founders Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson maintained intense urgency around shipping, refusing to let projects become unclear or drag on indefinitely. This drive to reach concrete, shippable outcomes quickly became a core principle that later evolved into the formal Shape Up methodology when the company needed to scale this approach.

vocabulary.definition: A strong and immediate sense of importance or necessity to act quickly.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, particularly in startups, intense urgency often drives teams to prioritize tasks that lead to rapid product development or market entry.

insight.nuance: This phrase conveys a heightened level of pressure and can imply a need for swift decision-making, often associated with high-stakes environments.

vocabulary.definition: To deliver or release a product or service to customers or the market.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, 'shipping' refers to the completion and deployment of a product, often marking a significant milestone in development.

insight.nuance: While 'ship' is commonly used in tech, it can imply a sense of finality and readiness, so it should be used when a product is truly prepared for launch.

vocabulary.definition: To complete a task or project, bringing it to a conclusion.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, finishing a project is crucial for meeting deadlines and achieving objectives, often linked to performance metrics and accountability.

insight.nuance: The term can suggest a sense of closure, but it may also imply that the quality of the work should not be compromised for the sake of speed.

vocabulary.definition: To progress to the next stage or task after completing a previous one.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, moving on is essential for maintaining momentum and ensuring that teams do not linger on completed projects, which can hinder innovation.

insight.nuance: This phrase can carry a sense of urgency to transition quickly, but it should be used carefully to avoid implying disregard for the work that has been done.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: Those sessions with Jason, they were these short, very, very intense sessions where you're trying to crack the nut together. Where's the idea? What's the concept? How can we go...
keySentence: Those sessions with Jason were intense, trying to crack the nut together.
text_ko: 제이슨과의 그 세션들은 짧지만 정말 정말 강렬해서, 우리가 같이 머리를 맞대고 해법을 찾아내려 애쓰는 시간이었어요. 아이디어는 어디에 있죠? 컨셉(concept)은 뭐죠? 어떻게 풀어가야 할까요...
text_zh: 跟Jason开的那些会都很短，但节奏超快、强度很大，大家就是一起攻坚：点子在哪？概念是什么？我们接下来怎么推进……
text_es: Esas sesiones con Jason eran cortas, muy, muy intensas: intentábamos entre todos dar con la idea. ¿Dónde está la idea? ¿Cuál es el concepto? ¿Cómo lo llevamos adelante...?
fullContext: Ryan describes the early collaborative sessions with Jason Fried that became the foundation for Shape Up's shaping process. These were intense, focused sessions aimed at 'cracking the nut' - finding the core idea that could be built quickly and effectively. With David only available 10 hours per week for programming, they needed absolute clarity on what to build before he started coding, which forced them to do deep thinking upfront.

vocabulary.definition: Having a strong or extreme degree of force, energy, or concentration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, 'intense' often describes high-pressure situations or focused efforts to achieve specific outcomes, such as during brainstorming sessions or project deadlines.

insight.nuance: While 'intense' can imply a positive drive towards productivity, it may also suggest stress or overwhelming pressure if not managed properly.

vocabulary.definition: An abstract idea or a general notion that serves as the foundation for a theory or plan.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startups, a 'concept' often refers to the initial idea behind a product, service, or strategy that guides development and marketing efforts.

insight.nuance: While 'concept' suggests a theoretical framework, it may lack the specificity needed for execution, making it important to clarify and develop further.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: That was one of those moments where you're like, 'Oh, this isn't going to automatically, organically just keep it spreading as we hire forever.' You know what I mean?
keySentence: Oh, this isn't going to automatically, organically just keep it spreading as we hire forever.
text_ko: 그건 딱 “아, 이건 사람을 계속 뽑기만 한다고 해서 저절로 자연스럽게 계속 퍼지진 않겠구나” 싶었던 순간 중 하나였어요. 이해되시죠?
text_zh: 那会儿你会想，‘别指望它会自己自然地随着我们不断招人就一直传播下去。’懂我意思吗？
text_es: Fue uno de esos momentos en los que piensas: "esto no va a seguir ocurriendo solo y de forma orgánica si seguimos contratando sin parar", ¿me entiendes?
fullContext: Ryan recounts the moment Basecamp realized their organic way of working wouldn't scale indefinitely. After about 10 years of organic growth, they encountered their first project that didn't go well due to team members not understanding the implicit processes. This was the catalyst for formalizing their approach into what became Shape Up - they needed to systematize what had been working intuitively so new hires could participate effectively.

vocabulary.definition: In a natural or inherent manner, without external influence or intervention.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'organically' often refers to growth or expansion that occurs through internal efforts rather than through acquisitions or mergers.

insight.nuance: The term carries a connotation of sustainability and authenticity, suggesting that growth is genuine rather than artificially stimulated.

speaker: Ryan Singer
text: You can't put 10 pounds of crap in a five pound bag.
keySentence: You can't put 10 pounds of crap in a five pound bag by cutting away scope.
text_ko: 5파운드짜리 가방에 10파운드어치의 물건을 억지로 넣을 수는 없어요.
text_zh: 别指望把十磅的东西塞进五磅的袋子里。
text_es: No puedes meter 10 libras de cosas en una bolsa de 5 libras.
fullContext: Ryan, quoting Bob Moesta, explains why proper shaping is crucial before giving teams time-boxed projects. He's addressing a common Shape Up misapplication where teams try to take massive, undefined projects and force them into six-week cycles by cutting scope. This approach fails because without proper upfront shaping work to define what's actually achievable, teams can't meaningfully reduce an oversized project to fit the time constraint.

speaker: Sachin Monga
text: I really think that we're just starting into this golden era of what it might mean to be a writer on the internet. The economic model for supporting great writing on the internet has been generally pretty terrible for the entirety of the internet's history.
keySentence: We're starting into a golden era of what it means to be a writer.
text_ko: 저는 우리가 이제 막 인터넷에서 작가로 산다는 것의 의미가 새롭게 정의되는 황금기에 접어들기 시작했다고 정말 생각해요. 그동안 인터넷 역사 전반에 걸쳐 훌륭한 글을 경제적으로 뒷받침하는 모델은 대체로 형편없었어요.
text_zh: 我真心觉得，我们才刚刚开始进入网络写作者的黄金时代，才开始弄清楚在网上写作到底意味着什么。支持优秀网络写作的经济模式 (economic model) 在互联网的整个历史里一直都很差。
text_es: Creo que apenas estamos empezando a entrar en lo que podría ser una edad de oro para ser escritor en internet. El modelo económico para financiar la escritura de calidad en internet ha sido, en general, bastante deficiente durante casi toda la historia de internet.
fullContext: Sachin is discussing his long-term vision for where Substack is heading as a product. He's explaining how the internet has historically failed to properly compensate quality writers, but Substack is changing this landscape. He mentions that beyond established writers like Matt Taibbi who joined early, there are now many newer writers finding success who don't even identify primarily as writers but are making substantial income from their work.

vocabulary.definition: An economic model is a theoretical construct that represents economic processes through a set of variables and logical relationships. It is used to analyze and predict economic behavior and outcomes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, economic models are essential for understanding market dynamics, pricing strategies, and the financial viability of new ventures or products.

insight.nuance: While 'economic model' can refer to various frameworks, it is often used in discussions about sustainability and profitability in business strategies.

vocabulary.definition: Supporting refers to the act of providing assistance, resources, or validation to help someone or something succeed. It can involve emotional, financial, or logistical aid.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, supporting often relates to backing initiatives, projects, or employees to enhance productivity and morale.

insight.nuance: The term can imply a secondary role, suggesting that the subject is not the primary focus but is essential for success.

speaker: Sachin Monga
text: We're still pretty early, but we have something going now.
keySentence: We're still pretty early, but we have something going now.
text_ko: 아직 초반이긴 하지만, 지금은 뭔가 잘 돌아가고 있어요.
text_zh: 我们还在起步阶段，不过现在已经开始有起色了。
text_es: Todavía estamos en una fase muy temprana, pero ya tenemos algo en marcha.
fullContext: Lenny asks Sachin about how Substack's product team is structured and how it might evolve as they scale. Sachin explains that when he joined Substack a year ago, they had zero product managers, but they've now built out a proper product organization. He describes their current structure of three full-stack teams aligned around different user types rather than product features.

speaker: Sachin Monga
text: I think the first thing was really treating my role in the beginning more as a facilitator than a decision maker when it comes to product. When I first joined, I felt like my main role was actually just solving that.
keySentence: Treating my role as a facilitator was my main role in the beginning.
text_ko: 처음에는 제품(product)에 관해서 제 역할을 의사결정자(decision maker)라기보다 조율자(facilitator)로 보는 게 맞다고 생각했어요. 합류했을 때는 제 주된 역할이 사실 그 부분을 해결하는 것뿐이라고 느꼈어요.
text_zh: 关于产品，我一开始更把自己当成推动者(facilitator)，而不是决策者(decision maker)。刚加入那会儿，我觉得自己主要的工作就是把这事儿处理好。
text_es: Creo que al principio enfoqué mi rol más como facilitador que como quien toma las decisiones sobre el producto (product). Cuando me uní, sentía que mi papel principal era precisamente resolver eso.
fullContext: Lenny asks about the challenge of being a head of product at a small company with a founder who has strong product opinions. Sachin explains his approach to working with Chris, Substack's CEO. Rather than trying to be the primary decision maker immediately, Sachin focused on being a bridge between Chris and the product teams, ensuring clear communication of vision and priorities as the company grew beyond the point where Chris could be involved in every decision.

vocabulary.definition: A facilitator is an individual who helps a group of people understand their common objectives and assists them in achieving those goals by guiding discussions and processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, facilitators often lead meetings, workshops, or training sessions to ensure productive collaboration and effective communication among team members.

insight.nuance: The term implies a supportive role rather than a directive one, emphasizing collaboration over authority.

vocabulary.definition: A decision maker is a person who has the authority to make choices or determine a course of action within an organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate environments, decision makers are typically senior executives or managers who evaluate options and make strategic decisions that impact the direction of the company.

insight.nuance: This term carries a connotation of responsibility and authority, often implying a higher level of accountability for outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: Solving refers to the process of finding a solution to a problem or addressing a challenge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business and technology, solving often involves analytical thinking and creative problem-solving skills to overcome obstacles and improve processes.

insight.nuance: This term suggests an active engagement in overcoming difficulties, often requiring critical thinking and resourcefulness.

speaker: Sachin Monga
text: Maybe that leads into my answer to the second question, which is that's not really for everyone. I think there's almost like a personality type that has to be okay with being humbled all the time and feeling like you don't know what you're doing.
keySentence: Being humbled all the time is necessary for this trajectory.
text_ko: 아마 그게 두 번째 질문에 대한 제 답으로 이어지는 것 같아요. 근데 그건 모든 사람에게 맞는 건 아니에요. 늘 겸손해지고 내가 뭘 하는지 모른다는 기분을 계속 견뎌낼 수 있는 성향이 있어야 해요.
text_zh: 这大概就是我对第二个问题的回答：这并不适合每个人。我觉得这更像是一种性格——得能接受不断被打击，常常觉得自己不太知道自己在干什么。
text_es: Quizá eso me lleva a la respuesta de la segunda pregunta: no es para todo el mundo. Creo que se necesita casi un tipo de personalidad que esté bien con que te pongan en evidencia todo el tiempo y con la sensación de no saber qué estás haciendo.
fullContext: Lenny asks about what type of person isn't a good fit for the role of head of product at a fast-growing startup with a product-minded founder. Sachin explains that the constant change and growth at startups means processes become obsolete quickly, requiring someone comfortable with uncertainty. He contrasts this with working at more stable companies where you can master established processes and systems.

vocabulary.definition: A classification of individuals based on their characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving. Different personality types can influence how individuals interact with others and approach challenges.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, understanding personality types can enhance team dynamics, improve communication, and inform leadership styles, particularly in roles that require collaboration and conflict resolution.

insight.nuance: While often used in team-building and recruitment contexts, it is important to avoid overgeneralizing individuals based on personality types, as this can lead to stereotyping.

vocabulary.definition: Feeling a sense of modesty or insignificance, often as a result of a challenging experience or realization. It can also refer to being brought down to a lower status or position.
